POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 22:52:23 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.12 Tusk government ‘facing armageddon’ as European court resumes cases against Poland https://www.politico.eu/article/donald-tusk-government-facing-armageddon-as-european-court-resumes-cases-against-poland/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 25 Nov 2026 20:45:59 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9392259 Europe’s top human rights court resumed proceedings against Poland on Wednesday, putting fresh pressure on Prime Minister Donald Tusk to deliver on his promise to restore the independence of the country’s courts.

The European Court of Human Rights said it has around 1,600 cases pending over judicial changes introduced by Poland’s former nationalist Law and Justice government. It suspended proceedings in 2023 to give Warsaw time to restore judicial independence.

Tusk’s promise to restore the rule of law helped unlock billions in frozen EU funding following his return to power in 2023. But his efforts have been hampered by two successive PiS-backed presidents, most recently Karol Nawrocki.

Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek has estimated that compensation payments could exceed €12 million. Speaking by phone Wednesday evening, he said the bill could grow considerably as judges appointed under the disputed system continued to hear cases, creating fresh grounds for compensation claims.

“So we’re facing armageddon,” Żurek said. He blamed PiS for undermining Poland’s judicial system and accused Nawrocki of obstructing efforts to repair it.

The decision comes amid a wider confrontation between Tusk and Nawrocki over Poland’s courts, including the Constitutional Tribunal.

At the heart of the ECHR cases is a 2017 overhaul that gave lawmakers greater control over judicial appointments. Nawrocki vetoed a bill in February aimed at reversing those changes, arguing it would usher in a “new phase of chaos.”

Nawrocki’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The ECHR has already sided with applicants ranging from a distributor of sex-enhancing supplements to former Polish President and Nobel Peace Prize winner Lech Wałęsa.

Wałęsa had won a defamation case against a former associate who accused him of collaborating with the communist secret police, only to see that victory overturned years later by a newly created chamber of Poland’s Supreme Court.

The ECHR awarded him €30,000 in damages in a landmark 2023 ruling that prompted the suspension of similar cases. It twice extended the suspension but let it expire Monday.

]]> en “Les COP, c’est une blague” : les critiques enflent contre les sommets climatiques après l’échec à Antalya https://www.politico.eu/article/les-cop-cest-une-blague-les-critiques-enflent-contre-les-sommets-climatiques-apres-lechec-a-antalya/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 25 Nov 2026 20:07:06 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9389481 Le processus des Nations unies pour coordonner la réponse mondiale au changement climatique se fissure discrètement depuis des années. Aujourd’hui, même ses partisans historiques se rebellent ouvertement et exigent une refonte des négociations internationales.

L’élément déclencheur : l’échec retentissant des négociateurs à conclure un accord mondial dimanche. De l’Afrique à l’Europe, les représentants des pays ont exprimé leur méfiance face à un processus qui a permis aux pays riches en pétrole de passer outre les appels à inclure dans le texte final une mention sur la sortie progressive des énergies fossiles — une mesure que les scientifiques réclament depuis des années.

Les divisions se sont avérées si profondes lors des pourparlers à Antalya, en Turquie, que les gouvernements n’ont pas pu conclure d’accord de haut niveau pour la première fois depuis 2009. Cela a conduit les ministres, les négociateurs et d’autres responsables à réclamer des changements dans un processus qui, depuis des décennies, nécessite un consensus entre près de 200 pays pour avancer.

“Si nous parvenons à donner le meilleur de nous-mêmes, à nous organiser, au cours des douze prochains mois, la COP31 nous paraîtra rétrospectivement comme un moment cathartique de prise de conscience”, a positivé Rachel Kyte, envoyée spéciale du Royaume-Uni pour le climat, lors d’un entretien accordé à POLITICO, ajoutant que les pays devaient corriger le processus qui, ces dernières années, a peiné à produire des résultats.

Ceux appelant à une refonte du processus réclament une réforme du format COP, voire sa suppression pure et simple, sans que l’on ait réellement d’idées sur la manière de mettre en œuvre l’une ou l’autre de ces options. Reste que l’échec des organisateurs à négocier un accord final a libéré un flot de critiques.

Selon ses détracteurs, le processus actuel, dans lequel les pays pétroliers font obstacle aux initiatives visant à mentionner explicitement les énergies fossiles, n’est plus viable dans un monde qui se dirige à toute vitesse vers une aggravation des conditions climatiques.

“Nous avons tous été pris en otage par les producteurs de pétrole, mais aussi par les plus grands consommateurs de pétrole”, a pointé auprès de POLITICO le ministre panaméen du Climat, Juan Carlos Navarro.

La faute aux pays pétroliers, mais pas que

Ces négociations chaotiques en Turquie interviennent onze ans après que, pour la première fois, tous les pays se sont mis d’accord sur la nécessité de lutter contre le changement climatique en signant l’Accord de Paris. Depuis, des progrès poussifs ont laissé les pays à la traîne par rapport à leurs objectifs. Au point que l’ONU a annoncé le mois dernier qu’il n’y avait plus aucun espoir d’éviter un réchauffement de 1,5 °C.

L’échec de ce week-end contraste fortement avec les négociations de l’année dernière au Brésil, où les gouvernements étaient parvenus à un accord malgré les attaques à distance contre le processus du président Donald Trump, et sa décision de retirer les Etats-Unis de l’Accord de Paris.

Alors que les négociations entraient en prolongation le week-end dernier, l’Arabie saoudite et un groupe d’autres pays producteurs d’énergies fossiles se sont battus pour empêcher que les négociations ne reprennent les termes convenus il y a trois ans lors de la COP28, qui appelaient à accélérer la sortie des énergies fossiles.

“Ce que nous voyons ne doit pas devenir la norme”, insistait le 18 novembre Jiwoh Abdulai, ministre de l’Environnement et du Climat de la Sierra Leone, avant l’échec des négociations. “Il y a un manque de confiance. Je pense que l’essentiel est de trouver un mécanisme permettant de rétablir la confiance.”

Certains responsables estiment que les politiques climatiques peuvent être menées par d’autres moyens, par exemple via des accords commerciaux et des partenariats d’approvisionnement en minerais. Une grande partie de ce travail est déjà en cours, consolidant des changements concrets dans l’économie mondiale et dans la lutte contre les gaz à effet de serre.

“Les COP, c’est une blague et ce depuis des années. Elles devraient être supprimées”, a tancé mardi sur X Rohan Patel, ancien conseiller à la Maison-Blanche en matière de politique climatique et énergétique sous Barack Obama. “Au mieux, cette conférence apporte un élan moral à un problème qui ne cesse de s’aggraver et auquel nous avons tardé à nous attaquer à bien des égards. Mais en général, c’est un énorme fiasco et tout le monde le sait bien (même ceux qui y participent chaque année).”

D’autres pays ont joué un rôle dans cet échec. Les gouvernements des pays riches ont refusé d’accorder des financements aux pays pauvres pour leur permettre de s’adapter au réchauffement climatique. De grandes puissances comme la Chine sont restées en retrait. Plusieurs diplomates ont déploré en privé l’absence des négociateurs américains, qui, historiquement, ont toujours fait pression sur les récalcitrants pour qu’ils fassent des compromis.

Des participants de longue date ont estimé que les négociations se sont trop concentrées sur l’élaboration de déclarations de haut niveau, au détriment de progrès concrets pour réduire les émissions de gaz à effet de serre. D’autres ont suggéré que l’échec du week-end dernier pourrait servir à revoir le processus et à le rendre plus efficace dans un monde fragmenté.

“Je reçois des appels de partout, me disant : ‘C’est une occasion à ne pas manquer, il faut la saisir’”, a confié Rachel Kyte, l’envoyée britannique. “Donc, tout bien considéré, ça a été une décision difficile [de rejeter l’accord], mais je pense que c’était la bonne.”

Des progrès passés inaperçus

Par ailleurs, de nombreux diplomates soulignent avoir constaté des progrès discrets à Antalya, mais ils ont été éclipsés par les dernières heures catastrophiques des négociations.

L’Allemagne, la France et les Pays-Bas ont publié des feuilles de route détaillées pour abandonner le pétrole, le charbon et le gaz. Le fait que 130 pays, dont l’Union européenne, se soient opposés au texte après le retrait de la mention sur la sortie des énergies fossiles a mis en évidence une large coopération, ont soulevé certains. Plus de 80 pays ont signé un engagement lors de la COP31 visant à électrifier 35% de leur consommation finale d’énergie d’ici 2035, bien que celui-ci n’ait jamais été adopté en raison de l’échec des négociations.

En outre, les particuliers achètent de plus en plus de véhicules électriques et les pays développent rapidement leurs capacités de production d’énergies renouvelables. Cette tendance va se poursuivre, a affirmé la semaine dernière l’Agence internationale de l’énergie. Toutefois, celle-ci a également souligné que la demande d’énergie croît, ce qui signifie que la consommation de pétrole, de gaz et de charbon se poursuivra pendant des décennies.

“Le sujet, ce n’est pas des feuilles de papier. C’est décarboner réellement l’économie mondiale”, a résumé dans son podcast Christiana Figueres, qui a dirigé les négociations de l’Accord de Paris en 2015.

Chris Bowen, le ministre australien du Changement climatique et de l’Energie, qui a coprésidé la COP31 avec la Turquie, a jugé que les négociations de cette année s’étaient déroulées dans un climat particulièrement tendu. La sécurité énergétique constituait une préoccupation majeure, étant donné l’angoisse des populations face aux pénuries d’approvisionnement en carburant et à la flambée des prix due à la fermeture du détroit d’Ormuz. Les guerres au Moyen-Orient et en Europe ont encore davantage mis à rude épreuve la coopération internationale.

Les pays économiquement dépendants des énergies fossiles, comme l’Arabie saoudite et la Russie, ont adopté des positions intransigeantes face au désordre mondial. L’Union européenne, le Royaume-Uni et des dizaines d’autres pays ont considéré qu’il valait mieux rejeter un mauvais accord plutôt que de faire marche arrière.

“Il est profondément décevant qu’aucun consensus n’ait été trouvé lors de la COP31. Ce moment, après l’été que le monde vient de vivre, appelait à faire preuve d’ambition. Au lieu de cela, on nous a présenté un accord qui constitue un recul en matière de climat, et nous ne pouvions pas le soutenir”, a justifié lundi le Premier ministre britannique Andy Burnham devant la Chambre des communes.

Les négociations annuelles constituaient autrefois le mécanisme permettant de parvenir à un accord international sur les moyens de lutter contre le changement climatique. Aujourd’hui, il vaut mieux les utiliser comme une tribune pour faire pression sur les pays afin qu’ils agissent plus rapidement pour réduire leurs émissions, considère Alden Meyer, du think tank E3G.

“Je dirais que la coopération pour mener des initiatives de décarbonation sur le terrain dans tous les secteurs de l’économie revêt une importance bien plus grande que l’existence ou non d’un consensus sur une décision-cadre qui se limite au plus petit dénominateur commun”, a-t-il écrit dans un SMS.

Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Marie Thirion et Jean-Christophe Catalon.

]]> en French presidential hopeful Teddy Riner says Ukraine is ‘not our war’ https://www.politico.eu/article/french-presidential-hopeful-teddy-riner-says-ukraine-is-not-our-war/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 25 Nov 2026 16:51:22 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9390183 PARIS — Teddy Riner, the legendary judoka running for president in France, sparked controversy on Wednesday after declaring that Ukraine was not his country’s conflict.

“If I become president tomorrow, I would like to be the kind of person who brings people together, who smiles and shakes hands to put an end to this war,” Riner added about Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Riner, however, had been more closely associated with the pro-Macron camp based on early campaign statements, making his Ukraine comments more surprising. Early surveys have shown him polling at about 4%, drawing mostly from voters who opted for Macron in the last presidential election.

Center-right MEP Nathalie Loiseau, who handles foreign affairs policy for presidential candidate Edouard Philippe, seized on Riner’s remarks to attack the election rival.

“Teddy Riner’s world would be so simple: you don’t get involved in anything, you shake hands with everyone, and there’s peace and love all over the world,” she wrote on X.

Riner was speaking from the French mayors’ congress currently taking place in Paris, where he was seeking out endorsements needed to run for president.

He still has a long way to go before actually getting onto the ballot: Riner said he had obtained more than 100 signatures from local officials in support his candidacy — far from the 500 needed to confirm his candidacy under French law.

The Elysée official quoted above, who in line with the French government’s communications practices was not named, predicted that the EUCO meeting would not be conclusive and stressed that Costa’s proposal was not addressing French demands, including on raising more own resources levied by the EU directly to finance the budget.

In addition to the cuts, Macron’s office warned that Costa’s proposal offers little certainty that new-EU wide taxes would see the light any time soon, as they would have to be adopted in a separate vote after budget negotiations. ]]> en EU weist Trumps Argumente für neue Zölle zurück https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-weist-trumps-argumente-fuer-neue-zoelle-zurueck/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 25 Nov 2026 16:17:15 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro-free&p=9390546 BRÜSSEL — Die EU-Kommission hat die Begründung der US-Regierung für neue Zölle auf Waren aus Europa zurückgewiesen. Die US-Regierung war in einer Untersuchung zu dem Schluss gekommen, Europas Industrie trage zu weltweiten Überkapazitäten bei und drücke damit künstlich die Preise. Washington will deshalb einen neuen, wenn auch nicht zwingend zusätzlichen Zoll von 15 Prozent auf EU-Importe verhängen.

„Wir werden die Ergebnisse prüfen. Gleichzeitig weisen wir die These, dass Europa eine Quelle struktureller Überkapazitäten sei, entschieden zurück. Im Gegenteil: Europa gehört zu den Regionen, die am stärksten von Überkapazitäten betroffen sind“, erklärte Kommissionssprecher Olof Gill am Mittwoch.

„Die EU und die USA teilen die echte Sorge über globale Überkapazitäten, die größtenteils staatlich gefördert werden und sich auf Drittländer konzentrieren. Wir bedauern das Fehlen gemeinsamer Maßnahmen“, fügte er hinzu.

Das Büro des US-Handelsbeauftragten unter der Leitung von Jamieson Greer hatte festgestellt, dass 14 Handelspartner, darunter die EU, China und Japan, Preise künstlich gedrückt hatten, indem sie die Märkte mit Industriegütern überschwemmten. Die Entscheidung folgte auf eine im März eingeleitete Untersuchung nach Abschnitt 301 des US-Handelsgesetzes von 1974

Greer schlug einen Zollsatz von 15 Prozent für die EU vor. Er entspricht der Obergrenze, die im Juli 2025 im EU-US-Handelsabkommen von Turnberry vereinbart wurde.

Greer wird voraussichtlich am Montag per Video an einem Treffen der europäischen Handelsminister teilnehmen. Die EU-Minister dürften dabei mangelnde Fortschritte bei der Senkung der Zölle auf EU-Produkte mit Stahlanteilen zur Sprache bringen. Für einige davon gelten nach wie vor US-Zölle bis zu 50 Prozent.

Die Untersuchung gemäß Abschnitt 301 die zweite abgeschlossene Handelsuntersuchung der USA gegen die EU seit dem Frühjahr. Die US-Regierung hatte bereits einen Zollsatz von 10 Prozent gegen die EU verhängt, weil die EU die Einfuhr von Waren nicht verbiete, die unter Einsatz von Zwangsarbeit hergestellt wurden. Es werde aber nur der höhere der beiden Zollsätze gelten, anstatt dass beide addiert würden, erklärte ein hochrangiger US-Beamter. Außerdem werde die Turnberry-Grenze von 15 Prozent eingehalten.

Der Vorsitzende des Handelsausschusses des Europäischen Parlaments, Bernd Lange, bezeichnete die Schlussfolgerungen des USTR-Berichts als „absurd“.

„Wer nach den Zwischenwahlen ruhigere Zeiten erwartet hatte, hat sich getäuscht. Das hatte ohnehin kaum jemand ernsthaft erwartet“, erklärte Lange. Bei der Wahl vom 3. November hatten die Demokraten im Senat und im Repräsentantenhaus deutliche Mehrheiten errungen.

„Weder das Urteil des Obersten Gerichtshofs noch das Votum der Wähler haben Donald Trump vom Kurs abgebracht. Wenn ein Gericht die Rechtsgrundlage für seine Zölle aufhebt, sucht er sich eine neue. Sein Ziel bleibt dasselbe. Er nutzt Zölle, um Druck auf seine Handelspartner auszuüben und ihnen immer mehr Zugeständnisse abzuringen“, so Lange.

Der Artikel erschien bei POLITICO zuerst auf Englisch.

]]> de UK will not offer equal tuition fees for EU students, says Burnham https://www.politico.eu/article/uk-will-not-offer-equal-tuition-fees-for-eu-students-says-andy-burnham/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 25 Nov 2026 16:04:33 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9389808 LONDON — Andy Burnham on Wednesday appeared to rule out students from the European Union being allowed to pay the equivalent of “home fees” while studying at British universities.

During Prime Minister’s Questions, the Labour Party leader suggested equal fees “won’t be put on the table” in negotiations when pushed by leader of the opposition Kemi Badenoch to rule such an agreement out. EU students are currently charged considerably more than domestic students.

In the House of Commons, Burnham told MPs the European negotiating position “is not the British negotiating position, this has not been put on the table.”

The issue of tuition fees has become politically fraught since Friday, when contradictory briefings from London and Brussels left it unclear if the agreements reached at the U.K.-EU summit on food, emissions and youth mobility were contingent on a deal for students.

Burnham insisted that the university deal was not linked to the other agreements. “The deal on tuition fees is not done,” he said. “It’s on a separate piece of paper, a separate deal.”

Under the current scheme, EU students pay international fees — which can sometimes be £20,000 higher than the rate British students pay.

Last week, two EU diplomats, granted anonymity to discuss the plans, told POLITICO London had so far offered fees of £12,000.

In a joint statement released Friday, EU and U.K. leaders said they would “work towards” an agreement on tuition fees. “We will conclude the negotiations within six months from the date of the summit,” they added.

Universities have warned that giving EU students a better deal on fees could impact the financial health of higher education institutions — many of which are already facing a cash crisis.

A statement from the Russell Group — which includes some of the U.K’s top universities — said that any reduction in EU student fees “would put pressure on U.K. student places and take more money out of U.K. higher education, without necessarily achieving the ambition of growing opportunities for EU students to study in the U.K.”

A No.10 spokesperson would not say on Wednesday whether implementation dates for the other agreements would be met without striking a deal on tuition fees.

“We’re moving quickly to ensure the benefits of these deals as soon as possible,” they said.

A spokesperson had said Monday that they were “confident” implementation dates would not change “even if we don’t reach an agreement on the tuition fees issue within six months.”

]]> en EU rejects Trump’s case for new tariffs https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-rejects-donald-trump-case-for-new-tariffs/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 25 Nov 2026 15:48:14 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9390069 BRUSSELS — The European Commission on Wednesday rejected Washington’s claim that Europe is fueling global industrial overcapacity, after the Trump administration proposed a 15% tariff on the 27-country bloc.

“We will study the findings. At the same time we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity,” Olof Gill, the Commission’s deputy chief spokesperson, said in a statement. 

“The EU and the U.S. share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” he added. 

The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, led by Jamieson Greer, found that 14 trading partners, including the European Union, China and Japan, had artificially deflated prices by flooding markets with manufactured goods. The decision follows a trade investigation launched in March.

Greer on Wednesday proposed a 15% tariff on the European Union, in line with the ceiling agreed in the transatlantic trade truce struck in July 2025 between U.S. President Donald Trump and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

Greer, who is expected to dial in next Monday to a meeting of European trade ministers, can expect pushback on the excess capacity probe. EU ministers are also expected to bring up the lack of progress on lowering tariffs on EU products containing steel — some of which still face U.S. duties of as high as 50%.

The overcapacity investigation, launched under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, is the second of two trade probes initiated in the spring as part of the Trump administration’s mission to rebuild its tariff wall. 

After the “reciprocal” duties Trump imposed in 2025 were invalidated earlier this year by the U.S. Supreme Court, the administration imposed a 10% tariff on the European Union, citing concerns that Brussels had failed to ban the import of goods made using forced labor. The higher of the two tariff rates will apply, rather than the two being added together, a senior U.S. official said. 

The official added that the proposed duties would likely take effect in January at the earliest, after USTR holds hearings and receives public comments.

The chair of the European Parliament’s trade committee, Bernd Lange, lambasted the conclusions of the USTR report as “absurd.”

“Anyone who expected calmer waters after the midterm elections was mistaken. Few seriously expected that in the first place,” Lange said in a statement, referring to a Nov. 3 vote that returned firm majorities for the Democrats in the Senate and the House of Representatives.

“Neither the Supreme Court ruling nor the verdict of the voters has swayed Donald Trump. When a court strikes down the legal basis for his tariffs, he looks for another. His aim remains the same. He uses tariffs to put pressure on trading partners and wring ever more concessions out of them.”

]]> en Metsola reelection talks in trouble after EU conservatives vote with far right again https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-parliaments-socialists-and-liberals-halt-talks-with-epp/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 25 Nov 2026 14:48:51 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9389814 STRASBOURG — Negotiations between EU Parliament’s three main centrist parties that were intended to pave the way for the reelection of President Roberta Metsola are on hold after the European People’s Party again teamed up with far-right forces on green legislation.

The Socialists & Democrats and Renew have been working for two weeks to lock the EPP into a coalition agreement, after the center-right party repeatedly voted through key migration and climate legislation with the far right over the past two years.

The deal is also meant to break the deadlock between the EPP, which wants Metsola to have a third term, and the S&D, which insists it’s their turn to have the top Parliament job. Such a deal would give the Socialists written political commitments in exchange for backing Metsola’s reelection.

Wednesday’s move to freeze talks, confirmed by Renew chair Valérie Hayer’s spokesperson, is unlikely to derail talks for long, as the three groups need to work together to pass laws proposed by Ursula von der Leyen’s Commission and agreed among EU countries. A final deal was expected in two weeks following a meeting between the leaders of the three groups that took place on Tuesday, according two people familiar with the negotiations, granted anonymity to speak freely, as were others in this piece.

Before continuing work on four thematic coalition clusters discussing specific policy files, the S&D and Renew are asking the EPP to commit to adding “strong safeguards in the agreement to prevent, once and for all, this kind of behavior” before returning to the negotiating table, said a third person familiar with the negotiations. A fourth person said the EPP must commit to adding “strong” wording in the agreement committing to a centrist coalition before full talks resume.

But the EPP is unlikely to budge — as it didn’t on the package on environmental requirements for businesses on Wednesday, when it voted with the far right. “There is no exclusivity” on working with the EPP, its leader, Manfred Weber, said at a press conference on Tuesday. 

Environmental deal collapses

After reaching a centrist agreement on the green laws following weeks of talks, the deal fell apart when the EPP decided to support an amendment put forward by the right-wing European Conservatives & Reformists, which called on the Commission to reopen the bloc’s laws protecting wildlife and natural parks. The Socialists said they could not accept this amendment.

It was Weber himself who pushed the EPP to back the amendment despite the Socialists’ opposition, arguing that reopening the laws was part of the conservatives’ political program and warning against falling into the left’s “traps,” according to an internal note from a group meeting on Monday. That was despite Radan Kanev, the EPP’s lead negotiator on the file, urging lawmakers at the same meeting to abstain to preserve the deal with the S&D and Renew.

Weber is walking a tightrope between keeping the EPP anchored in the center while appeasing those internally itching to move further right to deliver on the party’s program. In October, he pushed through a centrist deal on a car package, even though negotiators were ready to team up with the right to weaken carmakers’ CO2 targets further, two EPP officials said.

Spokespeople for Weber and S&D group leader Iratxe García declined to comment.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Wed, 25 Nov 2026 22:01:47 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.5 With no summit deal expected, it is clear the EU budget falls short on ambition – but does it matter? https://euobserver.com/251633/with-no-summit-deal-expected-it-is-clear-the-eu-budget-falls-short-on-ambition-but-does-it-matter/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251633 After months of haggling and negotiation the next seven year EU budget looks devoid of ambition and purpose.]]> Of all the EU’s policy battles, nothing causes more ink to be spilled, is given more reverence and yet is unimportant as the EU budget. There – I’ve said it. 

The income guarantees in the EU budget offer vital financial life-support to millions of European farmers but this week’s budget summit in Brussels, which follows months of painstaking negotiations, will see EU leaders spend two days haggling over the difference of about €30-40bn.  And few expect any white smoke to emerge. 

Read more

Less EU money for farmers and regions, but a growing Ukraine bill: Leaders meet to square trillion-euro circles at special summit

EU budget negotiations have followed a similar pattern for a generation; the EU commission proposes plans to significantly increase spending; the European Parliament demands more still and member states radically pare down the spending plan. The end result is typically a small increase, close to the rate of inflation, with which nobody is happy. 

That pattern – or exercise in futility – is set to play out again this week.

]]> [Exclusive] Details leaked of EU plan to cancel Russian sports in Europe, including Trump Jr.’s boxing pal https://euobserver.com/251647/exclusive-details-leaked-of-eu-plan-to-cancel-russian-sports-in-europe-including-trump-jr-s-boxing-pal/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 17:11:25 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251647 "Russia increasingly uses the fields of sports and culture as ... avenues for propaganda to legitimise its military aggression," said the draft EU sanctions text.]]> Russia is being fully cancelled from European sports, in a cultural counter-offensive that also strikes at the US president’s family, and comes with added financial stings in the tail for Moscow.

“Russia increasingly uses the fields of sports and culture as … avenues for propaganda to legitimise its military aggression, exert influence within the Union and undermine European Union democratic values,” said the EU’s draft 22nd sanctions on Russia, an internal document seen by EUobserver on Wednesday (25 November).

“In addition, Russia’s war of aggression continues to irreversibly damage the cultural heritage of Ukraine,” added the text.

It banned “athletes or sports professionals who compete on behalf of … the Russian Federation to participate at sporting events or competitions on the territory of the Union”.

Russian fans in EU stadiums would still be free to wave their flags and sing national songs to cheer on Russian athletes, who could compete “under a neutral status”.

But it will be forbidden for “organisers, promoters, or athletes and sports professionals to display or present official symbols of the Russian Federation, including flags, emblems, colours, anthems,” said the draft text.

Russian government officials will not be allowed into venues in their formal capacities.

Read more

Nathan Cofnas is just the latest far-right ‘snowflake’ to pretend he’s being martyred in Europe

“It shall be prohibited to allow Russian nationals to hold any posts in the governing bodies of international or … national sports governing bodies established in a member state”, it added.

And there will be “restrictions acceptance of financing or other benefits from the Russian State or its proxies by Union sporting and cultural associations or entities,” it also said.

Switzerland is home to some 70 international sports federations and normally aligns itself with EU sanctions, but the Swiss foreign ministry did not reply in time when asked if Bern would mirror the sports ban.

The International Olympic Committee, in Lausanne, which voted in July to let back Russian athletes into world sports, also did not reply.

But, for its part, the EU will also strike a blow against Donald Trump Jr. (the thin-skinned US president’s son) by singling out a Russian billionaire who bankrolled Trump Jr.’s lavish Caribbean wedding in May and went with him to shoot endangered sheep in Mongolia in August – Umar Kremlev.

Kremlev, who heads the International Boxing Association (IBA) in Lausanne, Switzerland, and who made his fortune in car dealing and state lotteries in Russia, will go under an EU visa-ban and asset-freeze, as the only internationally known figure out of the 80 new individuals and 81 entities being blacklisted.

The EU mentioned the fact Russian president Vladimir Putin personally gave him the Order of Friendship medal this year as one reason to scalp Kremlev, while adding that he was “supporting and implementing actions and
policies which undermine or threaten the territorial integrity,
sovereignty and independence of Ukraine.”

The others were mostly minor names in Russia’s defence and oil industries, except for Alexander Stuglev, the head of Roscongress, which runs the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum, an annual Russian business beauty parade, aimed at wooing Western investors and influencers.

Kremlev’s IBA did not reply to EUobserver when asked if he would step down after being blacklisted, but Russia’s former head of the International Chess Federation in Switzerland, Arkady Dvorkovich, did give up his post after being listed by the EU in the 21st round in July.

Read more

Weird guests and Ukraine drones make ‘Putin’s Davos’ a PR disaster, despite return of US businessmen

The final sanctions might still change and Slovakia’s pro-Russian prime minister Robert Fico, as well as Bulgaria’s prime minister Rumen Radev, have, in the past, vetoed EU culture sanctions, for instance against Russian Orthodox Church Patriarch Kirill.

But they will both feel under pressure in Brussels on Thursday to agree the Russia measures, when they come to an EU budget summit, in which Germany, for one, has threatened to withhold “cohesion funding”, which poor Bulgarian and Slovak regions need, unless they get behind Ukraine.

The 22nd round also comes amid blossoming US-brokered peace talks between Russia and Ukraine, in which Italian foreign minister Antonio Tajani said on 16 November that the EU could use sanctions relief as leverage to force Moscow to listen to its views.

The draft 22nd round of Russia sanctions contains nothing on wealthy Russian tourists, who still flock to France, Italy, and Spain in growing numbers.

]]> MEPs want billions more to tackle migration in next seven-year EU budget https://euobserver.com/251594/meps-want-billions-more-to-tackle-migration-in-next-seven-year-eu-budget/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 16:22:30 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251594 MEPs have demanded more than €3bn in additional funding for three key migration and home affairs programmes in the EU's next seven year budget.]]> As negotiators clash over the future of the EU’s €1.8 trillion budget, MEPs are demanding more cash for migration, integration and the shoring up of external borders.

MEPs spearheading three home affairs files and their respective budgets on Wednesday (25 November) presented their arguments for the EU’s next seven year budget for 2028 to 2034.

Their files cover integration, borders and internal security.

The commission earmarked a total of €34.2bn for all three, a ring-fenced minimum. MEPs are demanding an 11 percent increase.

Read more

Less EU money for farmers and regions, but a growing Ukraine bill: Leaders meet to square trillion-euro circles at special summit

Karlo Ressler, a centre-right MEP from Croatia with the European People’s Party (EPP) told reporters in Strasbourg that funding “border infrastructure” was vital.

Ressler, along with Portuguese socialist Ana Catarina Mendes and Belgium’s Assita Kanko of the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR), were presenting their arguments ahead of negotiations with EU governments.

Ressler wants €17.12bn for borders, up from the commission’s proposed €15.3bn.

The money, he said, is needed to fund the development, construction, adaptation, maintenance and modernisation of infrastructure and facilities.

Although the terminology is vague, it doesn’t explicitly cite border walls and fences. Funding walls is controversial given the historical precedents Europe faced in Germany in the aftermath of the Second World War.

Instead, he specifies the need for equipment at border crossing points and along external borders, including fixed, mobile and deployable assets required for border checks, and surveillance operations.

Ressler also highlighted the need for funding to support migration projects abroad to create “stronger operational cooperation beyond the EU’s territory.”

Far right unhappy

The far-right Patriots for Europe Group were not happy.

Fabrice Leggeri, a French far-right MEP who once led the EU’s border force Frontex, faulted Ressler for explicitly including search and rescue but not border fences.

Portugal’s Ana Catarina Mendes focused on integration (as well as asylum and migration) and is hoping to increase the budget to €13.31bn from the commission’s €12bn.

Mendes says at least 15 percent of that sum should go towards legal migration, integration and social inclusion.

“Integration can’t simply be seen as an expense; it’s an investment in social cohesion, the economy, and the future of our societies,” she said.

Meanwhile, Belgium’s conservative Assita Kanko dealt with internal security.

She wants its budget to increase to €7.61bn, up from the commission’s €6.84bn.

Kanko highlighted the need to finance projects to counter instrumentalisation, a catch-all phrase used to describe the ways that hostile states use migrants to destabilise Europe.

Read more

Europe’s rights court clears way to return more asylum seekers to Belarus, after pressure from nine governments

“At the same time, this proposal aims to grant member states more flexibility,” she said.

“The new fund will run until 2034, after all, and a period during which the security landscape could well undergo significant change,” she said, highlighting hybrid threats.

Numbers aside, the boost in budget lines proposed by the commission points to clear political priorities when it comes to reducing irregular migration.

The commission has set out plans to triple its migration budget to €81bn between 2028 and 34. And the three files covered by the MEPs have also increased dramatically.

When compared to the current seven year budget, the figures dealing with integration got a 64 percent boost, the budget dealing with borders a 247 percent boost, while internal security saw its offering climb by 399 percent.

An internal negotiating spreadsheet highlighting the differences, seen by EUobserver, shows that those figures have so far not been disputed or challenged by the Irish EU presidency.

    It cannot be assumed that Fico lacks the means to verify the real situation in Lviv, so the most likely explanation is that he is knowingly lying.     ]]>         EU commission proposes €50bn tech fund to buy into AI, quantum and other strategic companies https://euobserver.com/251514/eu-commission-proposes-e50bn-tech-fund-to-buy-into-ai-quantum-and-other-strategic-companies/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 14:15:02 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251514 The EU Commission has presented plans to launch a €50bn tech sovereignty fund to take stakes in strategic companies to prevent them leaving to the US or China. ]]> The European Commission on Wednesday (25 November) revealed the first details of a future fund with a target size of €50bn designed to take direct stakes in strategic companies so that they remain in Europe.

    “We are now creating the legal basis so that we can set up such a fund,” said Henna Virkkunen, the EU’s tech sovereignty chief.

    She called the fund’s size a “target” and a “sufficient starting point” which is meant to “leverage” further investments worth €400-500bn, she said. 

    Some member states already have smaller sovereign funds of their own. 

    But investment needs in critical technologies such as artificial intelligence, quantum computing or other ‘deep tech’ sectors, “often need investments of hundreds of millions of euros,” she said.

    “We have to really pool our resources in Europe,” she said, adding that the EU does not have that kind of equity fund at European level.

The Brussels executive is expected to propose a cage phase-out plan in December.]]> By delaying its response to requests for a ban on cages for farmed animals, the EU Commission failed to meet its legal obligations, the EU court has found.

    In the first ruling of its kind, the European Court of Justice decided on Wednesday (25 November) that insufficient action was taken after 1.4 million people signed a European Citizens’ Initiative petition to ban cages for farmed animals.

    In its judgment, the General Court in Luxembourg upheld the action of a citizens’ committee seeking a declaration that the commission failed to act.

    The commission is legally obliged to respond to petitions once they reach 1m or more signatures. In 2021, it responded positively to ‘End the Cage Age’ after MEPs also voted to endorse the initiative.

    But the Brussels executive is yet to propose the animal rights legislation that the petition requested.

    Read more

    Poll shows public revulsion on caged hens ahead of EU-ban deadline

    ‘Historic victory for animals’

    The court decision was “a historic victory for animals and for democracy in Europe”, said Annamaria Pisapia, a spokesperson for the petitioners.

    ]]>         A Russian plan to federalise Moldova could give it a window to control access to EU membership https://euobserver.com/251069/a-russian-plan-to-federalise-moldova-could-give-it-a-window-to-control-access-to-eu-membership/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 12:45:15 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251069 A reported Russian plan to federalise Moldova would hand the Kremlin a lever over who joins the EU. Europe should rule it out before it reaches the table.]]> Moscow’s strategy in its negotiations with Ukraine is no secret. The war’s resolution is no longer the sole subject of bilateral talks, but rather one item in a long list of maximalist demands. Russia now demands a new “security architecture” for all of Europe, with the war’s end a secondary priority. 

    It is not hard to compare this stance with Russia’s December 2021 ultimatum, demanding that Nato members commit to no further enlargement of the alliance and a ban on Nato activity in Eastern Europe. Moldova, yet again, finds itself directly at the centre of Russia’s confrontation with the West. 

    In late November 2003, Vladimir Putin was preparing to fly to Chișinău to witness the signing of the Kozak Memorandum, a Russian plan to turn Moldova into an asymmetric federation in which the breakaway region of Transnistria would hold a blocking vote over national decisions. The plan collapsed the night before.

    Under heavy Western pressure, Moldova’s leadership withdrew its consent, and Putin never boarded the plane.

    Twenty-three years later, the same idea appears to be back. This time, the idea is subsumed within the negotiations over Ukraine. Europe risks watching from the corridor.

    Read more

    War of propaganda: Russia calls Ukraine a ‘burden’ and uses Moldova as a ‘testing ground’ to sabotage EU enlargement

    Russian outlet Eho, citing sources close to the talks, reported this week that Moscow is seeking to restructure Moldova as a federation of Moldova, Transnistria and Gagauzia, with independence referendums in the two regions should Moldova join the European Union.

    The proposal would reportedly also include the withdrawal of Russian troops from Transnistria in exchange for a Moldovan commitment not to join any military alliance. The report is unconfirmed. But its logic fits Russian policy so closely that European capitals cannot afford to dismiss it.

    Read more

    [Interview] Moldova races for EU membership by 2030: ‘We owe this chance to Ukrainians’, minister says

    A veto over enlargement

    The most dangerous element is the referendum clause, because it targets the EU itself. Moldova’s 1994 law on Gagauzia already grants the region a right to external self-determination, if Moldova’s status as an independent state changes.

    The reported proposal would attach an explicit secession trigger to EU membership.

    If incorporated into a settlement, this provision would attach the threat of territorial fragmentation to Moldova’s European integration. The referendum need never take place for that threat to shape accession.

    Tajikistan was until now the only country in Central Asia to have ratified the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the ICC. And it’s not the only country withdrawing. No fewer than six other countries have notified the UN of their intention to withdraw this year: Niger, Burkina Faso, Mali, Venezuela, Chad and Nauru.

    Another blow to the court came last week, when Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping issued a joint declaration warning the court not to abuse its jurisdiction.

    Here’s a quick reminder of what the ICC is, and what it isn’t. The ICC was established in 2002. Its job is to investigate and prosecute individuals accused of four of the most serious international crimes: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression.

    The ICC is a court of last resort. It is supposed to step in only when national authorities are unwilling or genuinely unable to investigate and prosecute these crimes themselves.

    Read more

    The clock is ticking: Europe is running out of time to save the International Criminal Court 

    That’s how it came to issue an arrest warrant against Russian president Vladimir Putin in March 2023 over the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children from occupied territories to Russia.

    In November 2024, the court issued arrest warrants against Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant. They are accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, including using starvation as a method of warfare.

    Those warrants were made possible by the fact that the ICC can investigate crimes committed on the territory of a member state, even when the alleged perpetrators come from a country that has never accepted its authority.

    It can also exercise jurisdiction when the accused is a national of a member state, or when the UN Security Council refers a situation to it.

    Now, Washington wants to challenge that principle and, more broadly, dismantle the ICC.

    The US is seeking to prevent the ICC from exercising jurisdiction over individuals from countries that are not members of the court, even when the alleged crimes were committed on the territory of a member state.

    Such a change would fundamentally alter the court’s reach. On top of that, the Trump administration is also putting pressure on the ICC and its member states.

    According to Politico, US diplomats have been urging NATO allies to withdraw from the Rome Statute and immediately stop providing material support to the court.

    Read more

    We cannot say whether the seven countries that have notified their withdrawal this year have done so because of US pressure. But the timing is noteworthy, particularly in the cases of Venezuela, Chad, Nauru and Tajikistan.

    These sanctions have concrete consequences: restrictions on financial transactions, frozen assets, and bans on entering the United States, among other things.

    According to MEP Chloé Ridel, these sanctions are already affecting the ICC’s work: the prosecutor’s activities have slowed down, and some people have been sidelined from certain cases.

    The court still has 125 member states, and the withdrawal process takes time. But its ability to function depends heavily on international cooperation, financial resources and political support.

    ]]>         Some 720,000 Russian soldiers killed in the war, in leaked data deemed authentic by the independent Mediazona news website (Ukraine Battlefield update, day 1,734) https://euobserver.com/251050/some-720000-russian-soldiers-killed-in-the-war-in-leaked-data-deemed-authentic-by-the-independent-mediazona-news-website-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1734/ Tue, 24 Nov 2026 16:46:06 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251050 The newly authenticated death rolls show a war hollowing out Russia’s working-age male population, stripping poor regions of fathers and breadwinners at a pace that already eclipses all Soviet conflicts since 1945. ]]>
  • Mediazona has verified data from a leak from Russia’s statistical agency — it is authentic.
  • It is certain that at least 490,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the war. The actual figure, however, is estimated at 720,000 dead.
  • The data confirm that the age of soldiers killed is increasing, as is the fact that they come from poor regions. The highest number died near Bakhmut and Pokrovsk.
  • Recruitment apparently cannot keep pace with current losses: this year, Russia signed up 10 percent fewer men than last year.
  • Map of the day: Dobropillia.
  • Videos of the day: an Abrams tank adapted for modern warfare; a strike on central Zaporizhzhia; Russians built scaffolding around facilities at a refinery in Perm; it apparently did not help.

    • Two weeks ago, we wrote about data that Belarusian and Ukrainian hackers had stolen from Russia’s statistical agency, Rosstat. The data concerned deceased Russian citizens from 2021 to the end of August 2026.

    From these data, both groups concluded that between 400,000 and 450,000 Russians had been killed in the war. It was still not clear, however, whether the data were authentic — Russian sources had previously also published similar leaks claiming enormous, and therefore implausible, Ukrainian losses.

    However, the hacker groups Cyber Partisan and Silent Crow provided the data to various media outlets. They are now freely accessible to the public (the files total 365 gigabytes).

    It was awaited what the Russian independent website Mediazona, which has long searched for and catalogued the deaths of Russian soldiers through obituaries, official documents and other sources, would say about the data.

    On Monday evening, the Russian website published its analysis of the data.

    Mediazona’s journalists have no doubt that the Rosstat leak contains authentic data on real people who died in the war. They compared it with their own data. They found 95 percent of “their” soldiers in Rosstat’s records.

    “We are convinced that these data are authentic: they were verified using a list of the names of the deceased, including records not previously published, the register of inheritance proceedings, other leaked records from civil registry offices, the texts of court rulings from publicly available sources, and data previously published by Rosstat itself,” Mediazona wrote.

    The analysis of these data suggests that the total number of Russian soldiers killed is even higher than previously estimated.

Its findings also show that some doctors upload sensitive patient data to commercial AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini without approval, and that hospitals struggle to comply with overlapping EU rules on privacy and AI.]]> Hospitals depend on AI they do not control, while EU-funded health startups rarely reach public hospitals in Europe, a report published on Tuesday (24 November) reveals.

    Its findings also show that doctors facing burnout often upload sensitive patient data to commercial AI chatbots without approval, and that hospitals struggle to comply with overlapping EU rules on privacy and AI.

    The EU previously identified healthcare as one of 10 strategic sectors to boost European competitiveness. “I wanted to find out if the EU’s ambitions around scaling health AI and developing truly sovereign European health AI tools really hold up in practice,” lead researcher Júlia Keserű told EUobserver in an interview. 

    Her analysis was run in partnership with Liberties, a human rights watchdog, and was supported by The Collaborative for AI in the Public Interest, a philanthropic project by eBay’s founder.

    The research included interviews with more than 50 hospital workers, scholars and patient advocates, whose insights exposed the struggle of the health sector to comply with EU rules on data privacy and artificial intelligence.

    “There are too many rules and they are too complicated,” Keserű said, explaining that hospitals struggle to comply with rules that are often overlapping and contradictory.

    And while the privacy rights researcher calls for “harmonisation” of rules, she warned that “if simplification means cutting baseline protections for patients, it creates new risks.”

    ‘Careless’ use of AI by stressed doctors

    Among the concerns raised by Keserű’s interviewees, the most prominent was the use of ‘shadow AI’, where clinicians paste potentially sensitive patient data into commercial generative AI tools such as ChatGPT or Gemini without approval from their employers.

Opposition leaders accuse them of brazenly rewriting the rules to shut out hostile voters before the next election. ]]> Slovakia’s parliament voted on Tuesday (24 November) on a proposal that would abolish voting by post for its citizens living abroad in parliamentary elections, replacing it with in-person voting at Slovak embassies and consulates.

    In the 2023 elections, almost 59,000 citizens voted by mail, with the current opposition party emerging as the clear winner among them, receiving 62 percent of the votes.

    “Representatives of this coalition had no problem with postal voting for 20 years, until voters made them pay for it in the last election,” Ľudovít Ódor, Slovak MEP for Renew Europe and former prime minister, told EUobserver.

    “Slovaks living abroad are often critical of the current government,” Martin Hojsík, vice-president of the European Parliament and Slovak MEP, told EUobserver. “Which is precisely why this proposal raises serious questions.”

    “It is hard to escape the impression that the governing coalition is not concerned with election security, but rather with who will be allowed to participate in them,” he added.

    The proposal has become controversial not only because of its practical implications for Slovaks living abroad, but also because of the way it has been brought back onto parliament’s agenda – after already failing twice.

    The bill, introduced by prime minister Robert Fico’s Smer-SSD party, had already been removed from the agenda on 16 September and again on 11 November, after neither its sponsors nor the designated rapporteur attended the scheduled debates. Under parliamentary rules, the second failure should have meant that the proposal could not be discussed again for six months.

    “If this amendment is indeed passed, we will take the matter to the Constitutional Court,” Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová, Slovak MEP for Renew Europe, told EUobserver.

    Party-political motives

    As the organisation of elections remains primarily a national competence, EU member states retain discretion over how their citizens exercise their voting rights.

    For Slovak MEPs, it is interesting to see how political parties use these regulations to alter the conditions of political competition and potentially limit the ability of certain groups of citizens to have a say in the direction their country takes.

    “It is clear that this is a politically motivated move,” Miriam Lexmann, a Slovak MEP from the European People’s Party (EPP), told EUobserver.

    Read more

    ‘Manual for autocrats’: how Fico’s rule-of-law breaches put Slovakia in EU sanctions crosshairs

    It is not a new phenomena. For US president Donald Trump, mail-in ballots represent a “massive voter fraud”, he claimed. And Fico’s coalition has also echoed this argument.

    “Trump has claimed that the most recent US elections were manipulated because of postal voting. But there is absolutely no evidence to support these allegations,” Rasťo Kužel executive director at Memo98, international organisation in the field of media and elections, told EUobserver.

    Many other EU democracies such as Germany use postal voting.

    For Kužel, it is a way of dividing the population.

    In this case, “Smer is positioning itself against people who live abroad. This is primarily about further polarising society.”

The ruling came after nine EU states complained about the Strasbourg-based court. ]]> The European Court of Human Rights has ruled EU states can return asylum seekers to Belarus when Minsk exploits them to destabilise neighbouring countries such as Poland, Lithuania and Latvia.

    The Tuesday (24 November) judgement spanned several separate cases involving Poland, Lithuania and Latvia at a time when Belarus was rounding up people and pushing them across its border, triggering stand-offs with authorities and a tightening of asylum rights.

    Read more

    As people die in the forests, Europe asks its human-rights court to bless pushbacks to Belarus

    While each case had their own individual particularities, ruling in favour of some and against others, the court now allows national authorities to return able-bodied adults to a hostile state if they are unable to prove they face an immediate danger. Small children and the disabled are exempt.

    The distinction is important because it only applies in the context of instrumentalisation, a catch-all phrase used to describe the orchestrated attempts by a government or state to destabilise an EU country.

    Some have accused Morocco of similar tactics, when over 70,000 people suddenly arrived in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in late July. Turkey has also been similarly accused previously, when thousands arrived in Greece in 2020, laying the framework for a new EU asylum law that is supposed to respond to such scenarios.

    Tuesday’s verdict is likely to complicate the future efforts of those seeking asylum in Europe, as well as weigh in on 30 similar pending cases at the Strasbourg-court.

    It also opens the door for the European Commission to propose new policy later this year to help curb asylum whenever people are being instrumentalised in cases similar to Ceuta.

    Read more

    Poland’s pushback drive and EU asylum ‘emergency’ plan put rights ‘on a cliff edge’, warns Europe’s top rights chief

    Tuesday’s verdict most likely affects young males and other adults.

    Mattias Guyomar, the court’s president, says their removal would not violate article three of the European Convention of Human Rights, which bans torture and inhumane treatment.

    “Treating human beings as instruments is an affront to the values of the convention,” he said.

    “The reality of this phenomenon was not in doubt; it was well-documented and also publicly admitted to by Belarus,” he added, noting the court is bound to protect the integrity of the convention.

      <title>Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/25/trump-new-china-tariffs-europe</link>
      <description><p>Administration is suggesting an added 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total to about 40%</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/25/donald-trump-jensen-huang-nvidia-pardon-senate-hearing-iowa-abdul-el-sayed-latest-news-updates">US politics live – latest updates</a></p></li></ul><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a> is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the European Union, that would go into effect early next year, the office of the US trade representative said on Wednesday.</p><p>The administration is <a href="https://ustr.gov/about/policy-offices/press-office/press-releases/2026/november/ustr-makes-determinations-and-proposes-actions-14-section-301-investigations-relating-structural">proposing</a> an additional 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total tax to about 40%. Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/25/trump-new-china-tariffs-europe">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>After chaos at airlines, banks and companies from Microsoft to Apple, people have become convinced the world’s systems are under attack</p><p>Nicole Reindorf’s American Airlines flight was ready for takeoff in Phoenix when the pilot came on the intercom and announced what was to become the longest nationwide aviation shutdown since <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/september11">9/11</a>.</p><p>Reindorf, 70, had seen the headlines hours before about a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/live/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage-down-today-live-update-outlook-teams-365-when-fixed-latest-status-cause-news">global Microsoft outage</a>. She immediately suspected the two were linked in some way by AI-related threats – and that she would not get to the wedding of her best friend’s son in California.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/22/hacks-ai-internet-outages-airlines-banks-microsoft-apple">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/trump-nvidia-gilded-age</link>
      <description><p>Oligarchs believe they’re untouchable – the blue wave offers hope that the rampant corruption of the Trump era may soon be over</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/nvidia-staff-what-do-you-think-jensen-huang-return-chief-executive">Nvidia staff: what do you think of Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive?</a></p></li></ul><p>One can imagine high-fives all around Nvidia’s boardroom after the board <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/23/jensen-huang-reinstated-as-nvidia-chief-executive">reinstated</a> Jensen Huang to the CEO suite. The market gave the move a fat thumbs-up, boosting Nvidia’s share price by about a third. Shareholders, whose interests the board is meant to represent, are surely happy.</p><p>But like Fifa’s controversial decision to defer the one-match suspension of US forward <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/jul/06/folarin-balogun-red-card-reversal-trump-calls-fifa-explainer">Folarin Balogun</a> after receiving a red card for a foul on Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Tarik Muharemović during the World Cup over the summer, Huang’s absolution might backfire.</p><p>Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter <a href="https://eduardoelreportero.substack.com/">Being There</a> on Substack</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/trump-nvidia-gilded-age">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/nov/23/thanksgiving-air-travel-us-explainer</link>
      <description><p>Amid air chaos, travelers will have to navigate an outdated system (and complex company policies if it all goes wrong)</p><p>Millions of people are planning to fly in the US over the Thanksgiving holiday, just two weeks after the US Federal Aviation Administration’s 13 November <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/13/faa-ground-stop-flights-explained">ground stop</a> halted all flights nationwide for the first time since 9/11 (aside from a brief halt in 2023).</p><p>In the chaos that ensued, some travelers embarked on <a href="https://www.reddit.com/r/royalcaribbean/comments/1xvkopq/comment/19smxjywidlcw/?context=3">overnight drives</a> to catch cruise ships and <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/women-stranded-faa-ground-stop-buy-ford-bronco-27-hour-road-trip-rcna609629">bought new cars</a> to make business meetings. Many had to simply cancel their plans and incur the costs that came with it. More than 18,000 flights were cancelled at a potential cost to travelers of $1.9bn in lost time and related expenses, <a href="https://www.andersoneconomicgroup.com/analysis-nationwide-ground-stop-cost-travelers-nearly-2-billion/">Anderson Economic Group estimates</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/nov/23/thanksgiving-air-travel-us-explainer">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comWed, 25 Nov 2026 23:57:25 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Dealz parent Poundland enters administration heightening threat to Irish jobs ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/25/dealz-parent-poundland-enters-administration-heightening-threat-to-irish-jobs/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/25/dealz-parent-poundland-enters-administration-heightening-threat-to-irish-jobs/Wed, 25 Nov 2026 20:42:00 +0000The threat to the jobs of up to 1,150 employees of the discount retail chain Dealz grew substantially on Wednesday when its British parent company Poundland entered administration in the UK.

The administrators appointed, AlixPartners, said the stores would remain open and continue trading while efforts continue to secure a buyer for the business, but in its statement it called on retailers with job vacancies to get in touch. The chain has about 40 stores in the Republic.

The chain previously employed about 3,000 staff in 70 stores, but a spokesperson said the numbers had reduced substantially after store closures and job cuts.

Trade union Mandate has called on the Government and, in particular, Minister of State for Retail Alan Dillon to contact the administrators “to ensure that everything possible is done to save these jobs”.

The threat to them “this close to Christmas is very worrying for the workers concerned and follows on the closure of so many other big ‘bricks and mortar’ retailers in Ireland like Argos, Debenhams and Clerys,” the union’s assistant general secretary, Jim Fuery, said.

Labour’s finance spokesperson, Ged Nash, said the workers should be provided with immediate clarity on what the administration process means for them.

In its statement, the company’s ultimate owners, US firm Gordon Brothers, said the decision came after a three-month process intended to find a buyer for the business had failed.

“Commercial negotiations with interested parties for both the whole of the company and with established retailers interested in acquiring substantial portions of the business will now continue, led by the administrators, and conclude through the administration process.”

The firm said it had invested substantially in the business and cut operating costs since buying it for £1 (€1.19) in July of last year but its role has been disputed and it has been reported it took substantial management fees out of the company over the 16 months of its ownership.

More than 1,000 people failed to take up public sector job offers over 18 months

A number of parties had been in negotiations about taking the chain over as a going concern with family owned Northern Irish firm, Martin Property Group, reported to be working with the retailers’ existing management, had been involved in negotiations until earlier this week.

It is understood the terms of the repayment of a loan made by Gordon Brothers to the chain had been a stumbling block early on. The Boston-based company said it had received interest from other established retailers in relation to parts of the business and specific locations.

The break-up of the business in this way, now far more likely in the wake of Wednesday’s announcement, would be expected to result in many stores being closed and the loss of a substantial number of jobs.

The AlixPartners statement made no reference to the Irish Dealz chain part of the business or its employees, however, and the firm did not respond to requests for information on how the process would unfold here.

]]>Eric Luke<![CDATA[US stocks sell-off deepens as AI trade cracks]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/25/us-stocks-sell-off-deepens-as-ai-trade-cracks/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/25/us-stocks-sell-off-deepens-as-ai-trade-cracks/Wed, 25 Nov 2026 15:31:47 +0000Wall Street’s sell-off of artificial intelligence (AI) shares sent global markets sliding on Wednesday, pushing the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 index down 3 per cent a little after midday New York time.

Similar pullbacks on the other side of the Atlantic shook fellow semiconductor providers, with investors seeking stability in consumer products, while a brief respite in oil prices helped energy companies hold their nerve.

DUBLIN

The Iseq All-Share index fell 2.08 per cent to close at 14,120.63, in large part due to trades turning away from the banking sectors and Kingspan struggling to keep pace.

AIB saw its share price fall 4.28 per cent to €10.50 by close, with Bank of Ireland faring only slightly better, but still down 4.13 per cent to €17.66 a share. PTSB, however, saw a 0.34 per boost to close at €2.98, while the High Court decision on its proposed takeover by Austrian lender Bawag looms in the mind of many shareholders.

Building materials specialist Kingspan, typically an Iseq heavyweight, fell 3.60 per cent to €87.10 as the data centre building boom proved a less safe bet than previously believed. Nutrition giant Kerry Group, however, continued its share price climb with a modest 0.48 per cent increase to €104.20 a share.

Nvidia’s Jensen Huang apologises to staff: ‘I made some terrible mistakes’

LONDON

The London Stock Exchange closed in the red as the city’s two leading indices struggled to recover from the impact of a falling financial sector and stalling energy industry.

The blue-chip FTSE 100 closed 0.38 per cent down, while its mid-cap equivalent, the FTSE 250, fell further, down 0.93 per cent by close.

British banks struggled to hold on to investors’ confidence as leading retail institutions fell into decline, with Barclays down 2.53 per cent and Lloyds Bank dropping 1.39 per cent.

Energy giants Shell and BP saw little change in share price, but grew 0.10 per cent and 0.15 per cent respectively by close, signalling a small return of growth to the sector largely dependent on Middle Eastern oil supplies.

EUROPE

Market indices across the Continent broadly declined following similar falloffs in technology shares seen on the other side of the Atlantic, but deepened by further decreases in the European financial and industrial sectors.

The blue-chip Stoxx 50 closed 1.87 per cent down, while its mid-cap equivalent Stoxx 600 fared slightly better, although still in the red with a 0.93 per cent decline by close of markets.

Semiconductor company ASML Holdings dropped 5.79 per cent, while Infineon fell further with a 6.80 decrease in share price. Meanwhile, many leading banks saw similar misfortunes: Spain’s Santander down 3.96, France’s BNP Paribas falling 2.03 per cent and Germany’s Deutsche Bank decreasing 2.78 per cent.

Consumer products, however, fared better as investors sought security, with nutrition giant Nestlé up 1.01 per cent and British American Tobacco jumping 2.04 per cent by close.

NEW YORK

Early trades on Wall Street turned away from technology shares, as questions about the AI stock boom continue to trigger a collapse of investor confidence not helped by looming inflation data to be released by the US Federal Reserve later on Wednesday.

The city’s leading market indices all fell before midday New York time: the S&P dropping around 2.5 per cent, the Dow Jones Industrial Average dipping circa 1.5 per cent and the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 sinking 3 per cent.

Shares in chipmaker Nvidia, which soared on Monday following the shock reinstatement of Jensen Huang as its chief executive, rescinded as much as nine per cent by midday. Rival chipmaker Broadcom lost seven per cent, while Micron was down 11 per cent.

US president Donald Trump on Wednesday unveiled a number of new tariffs on significant trading partners, including the EU, China, Japan and South Korea.

This instability briefly pushed the Nasdaq back into a bear market, defined as a fall of 20 per cent from a recent high. – Additional reporting: The Financial Times and Bloomberg.

]]>Bloomberg<![CDATA[Staff win €23,000 for rights breaches after dismissals by Conor Murray’s hospitality firm]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/25/staff-win-23000-for-rights-breaches-after-dismissals-by-rugby-stars-hospitality-firm/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/25/staff-win-23000-for-rights-breaches-after-dismissals-by-rugby-stars-hospitality-firm/Wed, 25 Nov 2026 18:19:33 +0000Three workers left jobless when a hospitality firm co-owned by former rugby international Conor Murray closed down its operation at a west Clare gastropub have secured rulings worth over €23,000 for employment rights breaches.

Manager Catherine Jones and chefs Kamil Bozek and Kamil Baran had pursued complaints at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) against their former employer, CMK Hospitality, trading as Morrissey’s of Doonbeg.

The workers stated in their complaints that they each got a text at 6pm on Sunday, November 9th, 2025 from operations manager Bryan Gill, informing them that Morrissey’s “would be closing after that night”.

Jones gave evidence that she was directed to inform the rest of the staff and was told notification letters would be issued the following day, it was submitted.

It was the following Thursday when the letters came, she said, with hers stating that it was “no longer sustainable” to continue trading into 2026.

Jones showed the tribunal email correspondence with the operations manager, Gill. In these, Gill suggested the company might have work available in Limerick and Tullamore, the tribunal noted.

Jones said neither were feasible given the travel time involved, as the Limerick site was an hour and a quarter’s drive from Doonbeg and the Tullamore site was two hours and 40 minutes away.

Jones, Bozek and Baran each sent the official form seeking redundancy payments on December 4th, 2025, all of which were returned as “undelivered” by An Post a fortnight later, it was submitted.

When Jones followed up with Gill about the redundancies on December 15th, 2025, Gill said he was leaving the business and referred her to a human resources manager, Fionna Gallagher, it was submitted.

European loan of €119m to help build major housing development in Dublin

There was no reply to Jones’s emails to Gallagher on the matter other than an “out of office” response, she said.

The tribunal noted “no attendance by or on behalf of the respondent” at a hearing last month.

In decisions published on Wednesday, adjudicator Ewa Sobanska found the company had failed to give any of the three workers notice of the termination of their employment, or to pay them in lieu of notice.

She awarded two weeks’ wages to each of the complainants.

Sobanska also directed the payment of €2,163.45 to Bozek for the firm’s failure to pay out the value of unused annual leave at termination of employment, and awarded him €1,000 in compensation for this breach of the Organisation of Working Time Act 1997.

The adjudicator also awarded all three of the workers their statutory redundancy under the Redundancy Payments Act 1967.

Fundamental shift required in how foreign languages are taught, learned and assessed

That means redundancy payments totalling over €15,000 are also due to the workers, subject to confirmation of their PRSI contributions during the employment, and brings the total sum owed by the company to its former staff to over €23,000.

Murray, who retired after Ireland’s Six Nations campaign last year, holds a 22.5 per cent share of the company, according to company filings.

Larger stakes are held by fellow directors Alan Clancy and Robert Kearns, according to company filings.

The establishment is reportedly under new ownership.

]]>©INPHO/Ben Brady ©INPHO/Ben Brady<![CDATA[Heathrow seeks to pass on £300m third runway planning costs to passengers]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/25/heathrow-seeks-to-pass-on-300m-third-runway-planning-costs-to-passengers/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/25/heathrow-seeks-to-pass-on-300m-third-runway-planning-costs-to-passengers/Wed, 25 Nov 2026 12:08:06 +0000Heathrow airport wants to spend more than £300 million (€358 million) in the first half of 2027 on a planning application to build a third runway, almost doubling the costs it has spent so far on the project.

The airport is seeking permission from the UK regulator, the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA), to claw back the money through higher passenger charges for the next 20 years.

In total, Heathrow planned to spend up to £304 million in the first half of 2027 on its application, the CAA said on Wednesday. A rival proposal for a new runway, by hotelier Surinder Arora’s Heathrow West group, intends to spend only £35 million on its application in the same period.

If the combined costs of both applications are reimbursed and passed on to passengers, the average fare would rise by about 70 pence from Heathrow, which is already one of the most expensive airports in the world.

Aer Lingus is one of the biggest operators of flights to Heathrow each day, with between 19 and 21 flights a day, depending on the time of year, from Dublin, Cork, Shannon and Knock airports.

In a statement, IAG, the parent company of Aer Lingus, British Airways and other airlines, said: “Competition is good for consumers, but expansion can only succeed if it remains affordable for passengers and airlines. The focus now on Heathrow expansion should be on ensuring any proposals deliver increased capacity and connectivity while keeping costs firmly under control.”

The CAA on Wednesday launched a consultation on whether to allow all or some of the costs to be recouped through ticket prices. An increase in spending had been expected as both groups move closer to lodging formal planning applications, which they intend to file by the end of next year.

The CAA’s consumer director Tim Johnson said the regulator aimed to strike “a balance where the conditions for credible expansion proposals can come forward, but only where there is clear evidence that costs are efficient, appropriately justified and deliver value”.

The long-mooted project has been beset by delays and buffeted by political changes, including the replacement of supporter Keir Starmer as UK prime minister by Andy Burnham, who has been sceptical of the runway in the past.

Ryanair quietly changes seating policy for passengers who do not pre-book seat

Heathrow has spent about £320 million in the past two years readying its application, although it has said it will not begin formal work on planning approval unless it gets a green light from Burnham.

The airport’s chief executive has warned that it needs the go-ahead before the new year or its international investors will reassess the viability of the scheme.

“The planning system is complex and costly and while we’ve lobbied for change, we must work within today’s system,” Heathrow said.

It added that, while the expansion “will deliver jobs and growth for the whole country, we know the project must be affordable and are working hard with airlines to reduce costs”.
