Donald Trump has unveiled plans for new tariffs on the US’s major trading partners, including the European Union, doubling down on his signature economic policy despite steep Republican losses in the midterm elections.

US officials are proposing tariffs of up to 20 per cent on specific lists of goods from more than a dozen trading partners, with China and Vietnam facing the highest rate, and the EU being subject to 15 per cent.

The European Commission, which leads on trade policy for the EU bloc, said it expected new tariffs from the Trump administration to keep the total levy charged on EU goods capped at the 15 per cent rate agreed last year.

The 15 per cent “ceiling” on tariffs applied to trade from EU states into the US was “all-inclusive”, the commission’s trade spokesman Olof Gill said on Wednesday.

“We expect any measure from this investigation to respect it in full, including when combined with existing duties.”

The EU’s powerful executive arm rejected any suggestion Europe was a source of structural overcapacity, a concept in trade policy that describes a scenario where a country produces far more than its domestic market can consume, fuelling a need to export goods and products elsewhere, often at artificially low prices that undercut manufacturers in other markets.

“To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity. The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” Gill said.

Most of the new levies, which come after the US president’s “liberation day” tariffs were ruled unlawful earlier this year, will match the rates agreed in trade deals struck since he unleashed his trade war.

China had agreed a 10 per cent reciprocal tariff rate with the US earlier this year, on top of a 10 per cent levy that related to fentanyl. The new proposal for a matching 20 per cent rate could be doubled if US officials believe Beijing has stopped abiding by the terms of its previous trade truce with the US.

A previous attempt was made to stand up tariffs by arguing European countries and other global trading partners had failed to stamp out forced labour in their economic supply chains.

“The outcome today does not put any new tariffs in place … For now, the current tariff of 10 per cent on goods from the EU remains in place, unless otherwise exempted,” Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade Helen McEntee said in a statement.

Separately, documentation published by the US administration showed progress was being made to exempt Irish whiskey from tariffs, she said.

Trump made an off-the-cuff promise to lift import duties charged on Irish whiskey when attending the Irish Open golf tournament held at his Doonbeg course in Co Clare, in September.

Irish whiskey was on a list of goods to be exempt from proposed tariffs published on Wednesday, which McEntee said was a “positive” sign.

“While this is not expected to be effective until the end of January 2027 at the earliest, I welcome this much-anticipated and important development for this key Irish exporting sector,” the Fine Gael minister said.

The latest wave of tariffs comes as Trump continues to push his trade strategy, even after voters punished Republicans in November’s midterm elections over rising prices, driven by tariffs and the war in Iran.

The US president’s top trade negotiator, Jamieson Greer, has been formally investigating a list of economies, including those of China, the EU, Japan and South Korea, over whether they give their own companies unfair subsidies.

Greer and other US officials have argued that government subsidies unfairly benefit foreign companies and harm US business, while also leading some countries to send artificially cheap goods to the US.

Earlier this summer, US officials applied 10 to 12.5 per cent blanket tariffs to trading partners to retaliate for failures to tackle forced labour practices. The new tariffs will not be added to those levies. A US official said countries would pay the higher of the two tariffs.

The proposed new duties will affect 14 US trading partners, including China, Japan, South Korea, the EU, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, Vietnam, Bangladesh and Cambodia.

Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Bangladesh all received proposed tariffs of 18 per cent.

Taiwan, Korea and Japan will be hit with 15 per cent, and Singapore with 10 per cent.

Mexico and Norway were included in the probe, but reports on the two countries were not released this week.

A US official on Tuesday said for most countries investigated, USTR found that a “higher rate is warranted”, but it would be “willing to apply a lower tariff rate”.

The US official said Trump and Xi had a “great meeting” in the southern Chinese city and that he did not expect countries affected by the new proposed tariffs, including China, to retaliate against the measure.

US and Chinese negotiators extended their trade war truce by two months until January, rather than the much longer extension that Beijing had requested.

In advance of the Christmas party season, we asked experts what happens if things go wrong. Who is liable?

Can employees face consequences, including dismissal, for any wrongful actions at such an affair?

The simple answer is yes.

Employees appreciate the chance to let their hair down and connect with colleagues outside of their usual working environment, says Moira Grassick, chief operating officer at employment law and HR firm Peninsula Ireland. “We’ve all heard the nightmare tales of Christmas parties gone wrong, and it’s important for employers to mitigate risks where they can.

Aer cardholders could claim two free Aer Lingus flights and earn “Avios”, a loyalty currency used by several major airlines, at an accelerated pace.

Spend your gift vouchers as soon as you get them – there’s no point in waiting

The move follows criticisms about the difficulty in redeeming the Aer Lingus flight freebie.

Getting a free airfare for simply tapping your card feels like a good deal. But choosing a card for its travel rewards alone will be a false economy if the card membership fees, transaction charges, interest and the hassle of claiming your benefits outweigh the perks.

Credit cards in particular are an expensive form of borrowing. They make most sense if you can pay what you owe in full and on time. Setting up a direct debit to clear the full balance will prevent costly interest charges.

So spend within the lines, watch for fees and check for ease of booking and that the travel rewards offered by your card provider may be actual rewards.

Aer card

The recently discontinued Aer credit card, offered by Bank of Ireland in partnership with Aer Lingus, was all about the travel perks. Examining what was good and bad about this card is instructive.

The sales pitch was that once you hit spending of €5,000 or more in a “reward year” – so in the 12-month period starting from the date the credit card account was opened, you got two free return tickets on an Aer Lingus ticketed and operated service from Dublin, Cork, Shannon or Belfast to Europe.

There were other sweeteners, too: cardholders would automatically get two Aer Lingus “fast track” passes to get you through Dublin and Shannon Airport security, though fast track wasn’t available Cork.

You’d get two free Aer Lingus Lounge passes and two priority boarding passes every year, too. You also got multi-trip travel insurance for a family of four, including winter sports cover.

Bank of Ireland valued these sweeteners at “over €400 a year”.

So if you were going to spend €5,000 in the year anyway, your finances were robust and you trusted yourself to pay down your credit card balance when it fell due without incurring punitive interest, then you might have thought: “Why not?”

Did these perks add up?

First, there was a fee for the credit card of €6.50 a month and there’s the annual government stamp duty on all credit cards of €30. So whatever perks you were going to get should be worth more than €108 a year you were spending simply to have the credit card.

The free multi-trip travel insurance was a nice touch, but if you had private health insurance, this cover may already be included in your premium, or could be added for a small fee, making this perk redundant.

The Aer Lingus lounge has free sandwiches, snacks, coffees and juices. With food in the main airport costing an arm and a leg, this was arguably a useful perk. But the two passes could make some tough choices on a family holiday as children aged over two needed their own pass.

What about the free flights?

Two free return Aer Lingus flights to Europe for two people could definitely take the sting out of the cost of a summer holiday, a midterm break trip, a city break with friends or a Six Nations rugby weekend.

Except you were unlikely to be able to cash in your two Aer card free flights then.

Availability was restricted during peak travel periods, including but not limited to bank holidays, school holidays and sporting events, Aer Lingus said. They are particularly restricted on weekends, during school summer holidays, over Christmas and Easter and Irish bank holiday weekends.

So it’s possible your free return flight to Europe wasn’t going to be one you had planned to take anyway, but rather an extra one you ended up taking at a random time simply because it was free.

The reward flight included a free 10kg carry-on bag, but you still had to pay taxes, fees and charges on the flights. Users say these typically come to about €70 for two return flights.

Aer Lingus says there were just two Aer credit card seats available to book on each eligible flight.

But you couldn’t actually book your free flights through aerlingus.com – you couldn’t directly book at all. Instead, you submit a “request” to a separate credit card portal, specifying all your passenger information and a few different preferred dates.

Once you completed the form, you got a “case number” and an Aer Lingus agent contacted you about your case. So it was not as easy as booking a free flight of your choice.

Reddit users have plenty to say about this. Some describe the free flight request process as a “nightmare” and an “endless loop”.

Some users report it taking three or more attempts, submitting different possible travel dates and several weeks to get flights approved.

You had 12 months from the date you reached €5,000 in eligible spending to request the two free return fares otherwise you lost them. You could find yourself on a flight to Warsaw in November in a bid to use the only available freebie before your perk expired.

Book early and you were more likely to get your preferred destination and travel dates, Aer Lingus said.

Existing Aer credit cardholders can continue to try to book their free return flight through the portal in the usual way until November 30th, 2027, Aer Lingus says. But while you can fly until October 31st, 2028, your two free lounge and fast track passes expire a year earlier.

The card’s withdrawal is likely to generate a clamour of attempted bookings. As the existing quota of just two reward seats per eligible European flight remains, claiming your free flight could become harder still.

What’s the point?

Revolut customers can earn RevPoints. These can be converted one to one for “Avios” and redeemed in full or part payment towards flights with partner airlines, including Aer Lingus, British Airways and KLM.

RevPoints can be earned on eligible credit and debit card purchases at a rate linked to your Revolut plan – of which there are five.

For example, those using Revolut’s “Standard” plan debit card, which is free, earn one RevPoint for every €10 spent.

Gillian Harvey, her husband Mick and children Chloe and Sophie are big world travellers, having visited 38 countries.

“We are always looking at ways to save money on trips and get a little bit extra back from the spending we would be doing anyway,” Harvey says.

She tries to collect Avios points on everyday spending, putting these towards flights.

Harvey does that by spending on her Aer card and Revolut card and by converting her Tesco Clubcard points to Avios.

She watches out for promotions that enable 20 per cent more Avios points when converting.

Avios points helped towards a family trip to Florida this year.

“We use our Aer Lingus credit card for everyday spending, pay it off straight away and build up Avios towards flights,” says Harvey, who runs the Instagram account @wherearewegoingtomorrowtravel.

“We always make sure to pay the credit card balance in full, so we’re not paying any interest.

“The two free flights with the Aer card are a lovely added perk, but I wouldn’t choose the card solely for those, given the restrictions on availability.”

She is a member of the Aer Lingus AerClub loyalty programme, which is free. It runs the AerClub eStore, an online shopping portal where members can earn Avios by shopping with participating brands. Avios can be earned using any accepted card.

“You can earn points through retailers like Arnotts, Brown Thomas, Lifestyle Sports – it’s worth checking before you buy anything,” Harvey says.

“One thing I’ve learned is you need to go through the AerClub website first and click on the retailer you want to shop with for the points to track.

“It’s great around Christmas – when picking up gifts for others we are also earning points towards our next trip.”

She also recommends making sure everyone in the family has their own AerClub account and adding their membership numbers when booking flights to maximise points.

When the Aer card is discontinued next year, cardholders’ Avios will remain linked to their AerClub account, Aer Lingus says.

Which plan?

Revolut customers earn RevPoints at a rate linked to their Revolut plan.

For example, those using Revolut’s Standard plan debit card, which is free, earn one RevPoint for every €10 spent.

The Revolut Premium plan, which costs €9.99 a month, offers one RevPoint for every €4 on regular spending using a Revolut Premium debit card. This is the same Avios points-earning ratio as the Aer Lingus credit card.

Use the Revolut Premium credit card for the purchase instead and you get half a point more.

The annual percentage rate for Revolut credit cards is 17.99 per cent.

Revolut Metal and Revolut Ultra plans are a faster way to accumulate points towards airfares – but membership paid monthly costs €17.99 a month and €55 respectively, though €55 is an introductory offer.

With a Revolut Metal credit card, you will earn one RevPoint for every €1 spent. With an Ultra credit card, you will earn one and half RevPoints per €1 spent.

Premium, Metal and Ultra plans include travel insurance, with Ultra having broader car hire excess and cancellation cover.

With Ultra, you get unlimited complimentary airport lounge access at 1,600 airport lounges worldwide and unlimited fast track through security where it’s possible.

There are no currency exchange fees with these three Revolut plans. The Aer card for example charges 2.25 per cent of the transaction value for purchases in non-euro currencies.

Some of the higher-end Revolut plans bundle in lots of other things into membership, but here we are looking at travel perks.

Spend €5,000 on a Revolut Metal credit card and you’ll earn 5,000 RevPoints or Avios.

This number of points could, for example, get you a one-way flight with Aer Lingus to somewhere like London, Paris or Amsterdam.

Keep your credit card balance paid in full to avoid interest and charges and the reward flight will cost you the €30 stamp duty and the €17.99 a month in Revolut membership fees.

You can book an Avios reward flight through your airline loyalty account, such as AerClub, British Airways Club or Qatar Airways Privilege Club. You pay with Avios plus cash for taxes, fees and carrier charges.

When choosing a credit card don’t be blinded by the points. Weigh up the cost of the card, your capacity to keep the balance paid and how accessible the rewards really are.

If the scheme means spending more to earn a freebie, then it isn’t really free.

]]>Alan Betson<![CDATA[The economics of the AI boom are actually quite old-fashioned]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/11/21/david-mcwilliams-the-economics-of-the-ai-boom-are-actually-quite-old-fashioned/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/11/21/david-mcwilliams-the-economics-of-the-ai-boom-are-actually-quite-old-fashioned/Sat, 21 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000This week saw the largest share offering the world has ever seen. Anthropic, the AI company that makes Claude, floated on the US stock market with an initial value of just over $1 trillion – a thousand billion dollars. Founded only six years ago, it is today the 10th most valuable corporation in the US.

With the share offering coming a week after the Jensen Huang scandal, it seems that the world is captured by some AI story or another. Even global politics is in thrall to this new technology. On Thursday, when Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin sat together, it was clear that the new cold war was as much about tech as arms. We are looking at an industrial transformation on the scale of the move to oil and gas in the early 20th century. It will change the world, but that doesn’t mean everyone can profit from it.

Despite all the money flooding into what is known as “the AI trade”, there seems to be precious little understanding of the economics underpinning the AI boom. Where is the money going, why is everything so expensive and what are the risks that it collapses following one big speculative mania?

When so few people have the answers, it makes sense to ask the questions.

The AI story is portrayed as a high-end technology story, but when you drill down a bit, the economics of AI seem close to old-fashioned heavy industry. It involves pouring concrete, connecting power grids and buying manufactured microchips at a large scale. The lion’s share of the money goes on imported hardware. Very little of the spending is creating new tech jobs. And a growing share of the AI buildout – estimated to be $1 trillion this year – is being financed with borrowings that will need to be paid back sooner or later.

Who is profiting at the moment, who is paying, and how long can it last?

Most of the profits are being made by chipmakers largely based in Asia. Most of the cost is borne by the companies in the US doing all the borrowing, those building or renting the data centres. In addition, as almost everything uses chips – your phone, your car and your fridge – we are all paying through higher costs in our data-driven economy. The amount of new debt means the AI boom is dependent on the rate of interest, the patience of lenders and the tolerance of local communities for data centres, which were a big issue in the US midterms, as was a general dislike of the tech titans who dominate the AI world.

A data centre needs four things: chips, land, water and electricity. Building a new facility can take about two years. There’s a lot of concrete to pour. The amount of money, water and electricity required is enormous. Consider a 1 gigawatt (GW) campus of data centres. Granted, this is a huge data centre but it gives us an idea of the scale of the industrial transformation in front of us. One GW of electricity roughly corresponds to the output of a nuclear power plant or the annual electricity for some 650,000 houses – bigger than Dublin. About 10.5 billion gallons of water are needed to cool the machines, about enough for 100,000 households, and it needs around 700-1,100 acres of space, about half the total size of Phoenix Park. Are you beginning to grasp the scale?

There is little indication we have a plan for what to do if the AI bubble bursts

Most data centres are not this big, running on the megawatt rather than gigawatt scale, closer to 100-250MW of energy, but the demands of AI mean this figure is trending relentlessly upwards, which makes it worthwhile to look at the jumbo data centre.

A 1GW data centre costs about $50 billion – roughly $15 billion for the facility and $35 billion for the compute to power it. Chips make up roughly 70 per cent of the total cost. Because chips dominate the cost, the profits flow to whoever makes them. Nvidia and the amorous Jensen Huang may well design these chips, but they do not manufacture them. Rather, the likes of SK Hynix, TSMC and others do, with Korea, Taiwan and Japan controlling manufacturing. Others will want to get in on the game.

AI fever is producing some strange symptoms

The hyperscalers, companies such as Google and Meta, are designing their own chips, elbowing in on Nvidia’s turf. Geo-strategically, rival suppliers, particularly in China, will emerge. Greater supply of chips will bring down the cost and as the cost of chips falls, the price of using AI will fall. The dilemma for companies such as Anthropic is that if the price of using it falls, its revenues will fall, undermining its new position as the 10th most valuable company in the US.

Not only is the industrial model changing rapidly, with new competitors emerging at every stage of the supply chain, but maybe – more critically – the financing of the AI transformation has changed from cash flow to debt and equity. The hyperscalers, such as Google, used to finance their AI businesses from their large cash flow but, as the costs have risen, even a big company such as Google has had to start borrowing money.

About 10 per cent of all global investment-grade bonds are already related to AI, possibly rising to 16–19 per cent by next year. The AI borrower is in a highly competitive market. For example, the US government bond yields roughly 5 per cent with essentially no risk, so every data centre bond competes with sovereign debt.

Moreover, central banks that are trying to bear down on inflation are raising interest rates, pushing up rates everywhere. Markets are already getting nervous. Hyperscalers with other subscription businesses can borrow cheaply, but others such as Oracle are paying the widest spread. There is also another group of AI-related businesses called neo-clouds that offer cheaper data centre services than Google, Meta, Amazon or Microsoft. You might have heard of names such as CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda and Crusoe. They are paying much higher interest to get money and are most exposed to any change in interest rates or market sentiment.

Over the past few weeks, the huge amounts of money involved have put the wind up financial markets. Can the AI companies such as Anthropic that have yet to make a profit generate money to validate their huge valuations? Will the hyperscalers continue to bankroll our datacentres? Will banks start to call in loans? And can all this credit continue to flow into a sector that is spending so much but – at least so far – is earning so little?

We’ve seen boom and bust before. Will this be the biggest one?

]]>imaginima<![CDATA[Tax-free lump-sum loophole for workers is set to close in Finance Act]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/24/tax-free-lump-sum-loophole-set-to-close-in-finance-act/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/24/tax-free-lump-sum-loophole-set-to-close-in-finance-act/Tue, 24 Nov 2026 05:28:00 +0000It has long been the case that workers can benefit from a tax-free lump sum of up to €200,000 throughout their lifetime, and across redundancy payouts and various pension vehicles.

However, a loophole has been in place, which meant some people, either inadvertently or deliberately, have been able to benefit from the tax advantages during both redundancy and retirement.

Now the Government is working on closing this mismatch in the upcoming Finance Act. What will it mean for tax-free lump sums going forward? And how should people plan for a lump sum at retirement?

Finance Bill update

The tax-free lump sum does not have to be received just the once, it can be paid out several times – in a termination payment, different pension pots, etc – but they must reference each other up to the limit of €200,000.

If you opt to avail of it (or some of it) in a termination payment, then you must sign a waiver indicating that you have already availed of it.

However, this waiver is only tied to that current employment – and so if someone was to leave a job, use the lump sum to reduce the amount of tax payable on their redundancy payment, and transfer their pension to a PRSA, then they could once more avail of the lump sum at retirement, because they would no longer be claiming in relation to that old employment, as PRSAs aren’t covered by the waiver.

This situation has been in place since 2002, when PRSAs were created.

“As a result you had a slightly unusual result whereby occupational pension schemes were included when you were calculating pension lump sums that one might receive. But PRSAs were excluded,” says Munro O’Dwyer, a partner with PwC.

It may not have been a big cohort that availed of it. First of all, you would have had to receive a termination payment and the figures would need to have been substantial enough to make use of possible double lump sum.

And many may not realise the impact of having some pension funds in a PRSA.

“People who had previously waived their right to a pension lump sum have inadvertently benefited from this loophole,” says Jim Connolly, head of pensions with Goodbody.

But it’s likely that others may have deliberately availed of it.

“Where it gets a lot more grey is where people took an action to position themselves in PRSAs, to take advantage of this mismatch,” says O’Dwyer.

Given the mismatch – and the possibility for people to avail of it in excess of the lifetime limit – in this year’s Finance Bill there has been a move to close this, by extending the waiver to “the broader suite of modern pension products that are now available”. These include PRSAs, MyFutureFund, pan-European pension products, as well as foreign pension plans.

In that way, the tax relief on offer should be the same to all – regardless of the pension product in place.

Pension or the new investment account: where should your spare cash go?

It is expected that the change will take place from January 1st, 2027, pending enactment of the Finance Bill. So, if you’re calculating something from January 1st, 2027, O’Dwyer says PRSAs will be in scope.

“What’s less clear is for waivers signed historically,” he says.

But the Finance Bill may yet be changed before it is enacted.

How is my lump sum calculated?

If you haven’t accessed some of your lump sum in a redundancy payment – or at least did so prior to the Finance Bill amendment – the maximum tax-free amount at retirement depends on one of two calculations.

Firstly, if it’s a PRSA, it will always be based on 25 per cent of the fund, up to €200,000. A retirement fund of €100,000 would mean a tax-free lump sum of €25,000; a €300,000 fund would mean a tax-free lump sum of €75,000; a €500,000 fund would get €125,000; and €1 million, €200,000 (plus €50,000 to be taxed).

A favourable rate of tax, at 20 per cent, applies on the next tranche of between €200,000 and €500,000. Above that you’ll face your marginal rate of tax. The balance of the fund can then be put into either an annuity or an approved retirement fund (ARF).

This rule also applies to occupational schemes, but there is another way of calculating the tax-free element: the salary and service formula. This depends on how long you’ve worked with your current employer, and your final pensionable salary. If you are eligible this can be 1.5 times your final salary – so can exceed the other calculation. Someone with a pension fund of €150,000 for example, would get only €37,500 based on the 25 per cent calculation but could get the full amount if they had a salary of €100,000.

But it’s not just about how much you earn when you retire, according to Connolly. Revenue applies a “final remuneration” approach to calculating this figure, which means that you can look back over salary history up to 10 years – and take the best average.

The kicker with the salary and service calculation, however, is that you have to buy an annuity with your fund (apart from your additional voluntary contributions or AVCs as they are better known).

If you have a bumper pension pot, and will easily meet the €200,000 tax-free limit, then how you calculate this lump sum won’t matter. What’s more of a concern is how you draw down your pension income via an ARF or annuity.

“For a higher earner it’s not going to cause much of a complication,” says O’Dwyer.

If, however, your fund won’t hit the limit then it needs more attention.

“If you’ve a million euro in your fund – it’s simple, you get €200,000. The challenge is if you’ve €150,000,” says O’Dwyer, noting that someone might want to maximise their tax-free amount via a salary and service calculation – but may not want to buy an annuity.

Pension millionaires to benefit from higher tax relief over coming years

There could be an argument then, to remove the annuity requirement from the salary and service option.

“In some respect, having different options is fine, but prescribing what you do with the balance is where the issue comes in,” O’Dwyer says.

What if I’m in a defined-benefit pension scheme?

According to Connolly, lump-sum planning for those in defined-benefit (DB) schemes can be tricky, as to take a tax-free lump-sum of 1.5 times final salary will reduce the pension payments. This is known as commutation. Those with such a pension plan also have an option of taking 25 per cent of the pension fund if they get a transfer value and move the fund.

But those in DB plans don’t always have the full information to make the best decision. “Trustees generally don’t make them aware they have the option of a transfer value,” says Connolly, noting there can be a “massive difference” between the two ways of calculating the lump sum.

Moreover, someone with a serious illness, for example, may be better to get the transfer value, rather than have their pension paid out in an annuity.

While there is no regulatory requirement to offer a retiree a transfer value, Connolly argues there is a fiduciary one to act in the best interest of members of the DB scheme.

How to plan for your lump sum

“I would have an eye on my lump-sum entitlements from age 50 onwards,” says Connolly.

The age 50 is a pertinent one, as this is the age you may be able to access certain pension pots, such as those from older employments – you don’t have to draw down all your pots at the same time.

“You can have as many retirements as you’ve had jobs,” says Connolly, and you can take 25 per cent each time you draw a pot down – up to the lifetime limit of €200,000.

But there is a complication. If you use salary and service to calculate your lump sum, and only have 20 years’ service, you’ll need to use the uplift approach to get 1.5 times final salary.

But this enhanced scale means “you do have to reference retained benefits” from other pension pots, O’Dwyer says.

The survey of 1,000 employees, conducted for HR consultants SD Worx, found that 47 per cent of respondents believe they will not be able to retire when they would have intended and 48 per cent believe they will have to work beyond what has been the traditional retirement age in many sectors, 65.

Thirty-five per cent of those questioned, rising to 41 per cent among those aged 55 or over, say they would like to work beyond 65 but the average age respondents suggested they would ideally stop working at was 61.

Just over 60 per cent, however, believe they will have to work beyond their desired retirement age for financial reasons with 66 per cent of women expecting to have to do so compared with 58 per cent of men.

Older employees remain “highly engaged with their work,” the research suggests with four in five (80 per cent) of those aged 55 and over saying they have the energy to do their job well and 82 per cent believing their work has purpose or matters. Both measures are higher among over-55s than among younger employees.

Just 43 per cent of employees aged 55 and over feel their organisation supports them in planning for retirement, however, while just 36 per cent of the same group suggest their employers adjust or adapt work or tasks when needed.

Two-thirds of workers fear their pension won’t be big enough to fund their retirement

Under the Employment (Contractual Retirement Ages) Act 2025, those with a contractual retirement age below 66 can now notify their employer that they wish to stay in work until the State pension age, but the number of people working beyond 65 has already quadrupled to more than 133,000 over the past 25 years with housing and changing family circumstances repeatedly cited as key factors.

“The gap between when people would like to retire and the reality of when they expect to stop working raises important questions for employers,” said Eimear Byrne, managing director at SD Worx Ireland.

“Living longer can mean a retirement that’s almost as long as the average person’s working life. While that is, of course, good news, it does mean that many of us will be working longer out of financial necessity.

“Businesses must think about how they prepare for an ageing workforce and support employees whose retirement plans may change. This means planning ahead, having open conversations about future working arrangements and considering how roles, hours or responsibilities might adapt over time,” she said.

The City of London’s new lord mayor, Bronek Masojada, told The Irish Times in Dublin that the UK-EU deal agreed last week was a good start for both sides to build upon in terms of a closer trading relationship. Joe Brennan met Masojada.

Almost half of employees in Ireland believe they will have to work beyond 65 with more than 60 per cent fearing they will not have enough to live comfortably in retirement, new research suggests. Emmet Malone reports.

Profits at the company behind Yuno Energy and Prepaypower climbed more than 23 per cent to €5.3 million, according to its latest accounts. Barry O’Halloran has the details.

Software company Workhuman saw operating profit fall 7 per cent last year, as revenue declined. But it plans to invest more than $60 million in research, development and innovation next year as it seeks to expand its workforce intelligence platform. Ciara O’Brien reports.

Pepper Advantage Ireland, the mortgage services provider, has seen its assets under management decline by 27 per cent in the past three years, driven by borrowers paying down debt following a wave of loan portfolio sales after the 2008 financial crash. Joe Brennan goes through the numbers.

Profits at Irish-headquartered healthcare technology company Lanas rose last year as revenue remained stable and the company trimmed administrative costs. Ciara O’Brien has the details.

Kenmare Resources near-term need for cash plays into the hands of its Abu Dhabi bidder’s hands, writes Cantillon.

In Me & My Money, Radio Nova presenter Marty Miller tells Tony Clayton-Lea how during Covid, he built a camper van that is old but “as strong as an ox”.

If you’d like to read more about the issues that affect your finances try signing up to On the Money, the weekly newsletter from our personal finance team, which will be issued every Friday to Irish Times subscribers.

]]>Eric Lee<![CDATA[Pretax profit at healthcare technology company Lanas rises to almost €20m]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/pretax-profit-at-healthcare-technology-company-lanas-rises-to-almost-20m/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/pretax-profit-at-healthcare-technology-company-lanas-rises-to-almost-20m/Tue, 24 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Profit at Irish-headquartered healthcare technology company Lanas rose last year as revenue remained stable and the company trimmed administrative costs.

Pretax profit at the company rose to almost €20 million in 2025, from €11.3 million in 2024.

The accounts, which cover the period to the end of December 2025, showed the company recorded revenue of €104.2 million, up from €103.3 million in 2024. Cost of sales was largely stable at just under €20 million.

That brought gross profit for the year to €84.26 million, up from just under €83 million a year earlier.

Lanas cut its administration expenses from €53.2 million to €50 million last year, with finance costs also significantly lower at €9.3 million, compared with €14.8 million previously. Operating profit for the year was €34.2 million, up from €29.7 million. Its corporate tax charge was €4.2 million last year.

Cash and cash equivalents at the end of the financial year was almost €10.7 million.

The company employed 881 people at the end of last year, down from 941 in the previous year. The accounts showed the majority of employees were involved in administration, customer service and training, and development.

The reduction in headcount meant Lanas’s wage bill was just under €30 million, down from €33 million in 2024. It incurred pension costs of €1.5 million and social security costs of €2.2 million, bringing its total payroll costs to €33.7 million for the year.

Lanas, which specialises in electronic healthcare record technology, was launched in November 2025 after global private equity company TA Associates acquired Irish healthtech company Clanwilliam, founded by Howard Beggs as Helix Health, in a deal estimated to be worth $450 million ($414 million).

The company was boosted by the digitising of the healthcare system in the wake of the Covid-19 pandemic, and also expanded through a series of acquisitions in different global markets.

Lanas builds, acquires and grows products used across primary care, community care, pharmacy, specialist care and care platforms. The company has a committed mergers and acquisition funding packet of €100 million.

The company appointed its first chief corporate development officer earlier this year, to help develop its acquisition strategy and expand its healthcare technology offering across international markets. Rob Hutcheson has taken on the role, leading global corporate development strategy and working with founders, management teams and investors to identify potential complementary technologies.

]]><![CDATA[Almost €6m moved from company at centre of apartment project row, court told]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/almost-6m-moved-from-company-at-centre-of-apartment-project-row-court-told/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/almost-6m-moved-from-company-at-centre-of-apartment-project-row-court-told/Tue, 24 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Almost €6 million was moved from a company at the centre of a lawsuit between a building firm and a group of well-known property developers, the High Court heard on Monday.

Builder Midland Construction and Engineering is suing the directors of Baystreet Ltd, including John McKeon, Brian Kennedy and Liam McSharry, and its shareholders, for €12.8 million, in a dispute over an apartment project where the properties sold for almost €23 million.

Paul McGarry, Midland’s senior counsel, told the High Court at a hearing on Monday that allegations in the case involve the removal of almost €6 million from Baystreet.

Baystreet, which is now in liquidation, repaid €5.8 million that was owed to its directors and shareholders between December 2023 and September 2025, according to an affidavit filed by Midland director Thomas Stronge.

The High Court this month ordered the enforcement of a €9.86 million arbitration award to Midland against Baystreet, which was found to have wrongly terminated a contract with the building company.

Baystreet’s liquidator, Tom Murray of Friel Stafford, confirmed Midland as a creditor of the company, but the builder has yet to receive any payment on foot of the award.

Separately, Midland – which is based in Kells, Co Meath – is suing Baystreet’s directors and shareholders for almost €12.8 million, including the arbitration award, interest and enforcement costs.

Judge Eileen Roberts admitted the case to the High Court’s commercial division by agreement between the parties on Monday.

Baystreet’s directors and shareholders have until December 14th to file their response to Midland’s claim.

The liquidated company, owned by McKeon, Kennedy, McSharry and members of their families, hired Midland four years ago to build 44 apartments at Ashbrook, Howth Road, Clontarf in Dublin.

They agreed an initial €9.6 million for the work, but subsequently increased that to €10.8 million.

Delays that included problems with the site’s water connection sparked a dispute between the builder and Baystreet, which ended the contract in February 2024 with the project almost complete. The two sides brought the dispute to arbitration in March last year.

The 44 apartments subsequently sold for a total of almost €23 million, the last one in August 2025.

Creditors put Baystreet, established to develop the Clontarf property, into liquidation in September 2025, appointing Murray as liquidator. He is a notice party to the case.

In February, arbitrator David O’Leary decided that Baystreet had unlawfully and invalidly terminated the contract with Midland and awarded the construction firm €9.15 million in total with interest.

Earlier this month, High Court president, Judge David Barniville, granted judgment for €9.86 million, which included interest on the original €9.15 million that O’Leary ordered Baystreet to pay.

Midland is suing Baystreet’s directors and shareholders directly for the money the building company maintains is due to it.

Their senior counsel, Andrew Fitzpatrick, told the court they could seek security for costs, a legal means of ensuring that Midland can cover any costs should it lose the case. They intend to defend the case.

Baystreet’s directors are well-established figures in property development. Midland is a successful building and engineering contractor.

]]><![CDATA[Donald Trump’s rebranding of AI is doomed from the start]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/media/2026/11/24/donald-trumps-rebranding-of-ai-is-doomed-from-the-start/https://www.irishtimes.com/media/2026/11/24/donald-trumps-rebranding-of-ai-is-doomed-from-the-start/Tue, 24 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000On Friday November 13th, the United States faced its biggest aviation shutdown since 9/11. Every departure had been halted and some 4,000 aircraft were still in the skies when homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin briefed reporters outside the West Wing.

Despite the seriousness of the crisis, he found time for a vocabulary lesson. When a journalist asked whether artificial intelligence (AI) might be at fault, Mullin interrupted. “We call it SI [super intelligence] around here,” he said.

The actual culprit turned out to be overloaded routers. Super intelligence, as the Trump administration insists on calling it, had nothing to do with it. But the point had been made, even if Mullin let other reporters who said “AI” off the hook.

The term was chosen in characteristic fashion. US president Donald Trump offered Truth Social followers a choice between “super intelligence” and “superior intelligence”, and the former won comfortably.

At the UN General Assembly in September he complained that “artificial” made the technology sound fake. A week later, flanked by the bosses of the biggest tech companies, he ordered federal agencies to replace “AI” with “SI”. Elon Musk has since been caught correcting himself mid-flow.

There is an obvious problem. Among researchers, superintelligence already means hypothetical machines that outstrip humans across the board, which is exactly what the technology’s critics fear.

But this is an administration that cannot leave a name alone. Alaska’s Denali became Mount McKinley again on day one. The Department of Defense took on the secondary title of Department of War in September 2025. Lake Ontario was rechristened Lake America in August, midway through a trade war with Canada.

RTÉ must explain why its podcast strategy contradicts its own values

The Kennedy Center in Washington spent several months as the Donald J Trump and John F Kennedy Center until a federal judge ruled that only Congress could change its name.

In February 2025 the White House barred the Associated Press (AP) from the Oval Office and Air Force One because its stylebook continued to refer to the Gulf of Mexico.

The AP was hardly alone. The New York Times, the BBC and the Guardian never adopted Gulf of America either. But the venerable wire service is the default rule book for most American local newspapers, broadcasters and press offices. Change one AP entry and thousands of publications follow. In fact it is the nearest thing the English-speaking world has to the academies that police the language in France or Spain.

English is famously protean and mutable. Many see that as the reason for its global dominance (along with a spot of imperialism, of course). That has not stopped people trying to bend it for political ends.

Trump’s efforts may be unusually crude but they are far from unprecedented, and media organisations regularly have to decide whether to go along or hold the line.

Take the AP’s own decision in June 2020, weeks after the murder of George Floyd, to capitalise “Black”. The argument was that the word denoted a shared history and identity, particularly among Americans whose enslaved ancestors had been cut off from any national origin.

“White” stayed lower case, supposedly because it described no comparable culture and because white supremacists liked the capital. Many, including the National Association of Black Journalists, found that asymmetry hard to justify.

Still, the change swept American media, including Fox News and the Wall Street Journal. It travelled less well across the Atlantic, where it remains largely lower case, or inconsistent, in Irish and British media. And the Irish writer Emma Dabiri has argued against the capital letter altogether, on the grounds that it entrenches racial categories she regards as inventions of white supremacy.

Opinion polls are core to how media covers politics, but is that a good thing?

An even less successful innovation was “Latinx”, a gender-neutral alternative to Latino and Latina. It caught on in parts of academia and the media, but the AP only ever allowed it in quotes or for people who requested it, and barely one in 25 Hispanic Americans used it.

It became shorthand for woke excess, imposed by English-speaking language police on people who never asked for it.

Left and right do seem to approach these issues differently. Progressives have drawn on theories of language as an instrument of power and sought to reshape attitudes by reshaping vocabulary. The right’s approach, exemplified by the AI-to-SI switch, owes less to Michel Foucault than to Madison Avenue.

Two examples from half a century ago illustrate the point. In the early 1970s, opponents of abortion rebranded their movement as “pro-life”. It worked, up to a point, uniting supporters under a positive banner. But the term never shed its partisan charge, and most newsroom style guides, including those of the AP and The Irish Times, still avoid it.

Around the same time, Gloria Steinem launched Ms magazine. The honorific dated from 1901, but the activist Sheila Michaels revived it on New York radio in 1969. The New York Times held out until 1986. Ms is now the unremarkable default on forms and in correspondence, because it solved a practical problem people of every political stripe recognised.

Latinx may be in retreat, but de-gendering remains a live battle in languages where gender is built into nouns and adjectives. The French Senate voted in 2023 to outlaw gender-neutral “écriture inclusive” in official documents. Bavaria and Germany’s federal government have restricted gender asterisks. Sweden, by contrast, added the neutral pronoun “hen” to its official glossary in 2015, and about half the population now uses it.

For editors in the English-speaking world, the lesson is that the words that last are the useful ones. Fashionable theories and rebranding campaigns will always come second to how people actually choose to speak. Super intelligence seems doomed already, given that Markwayne Mullin himself couldn’t even keep it up for the whole press conference.

]]><![CDATA[Workhuman wants to grow its workforce intelligence platform despite 7% profit dip]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/workhuman-wants-to-grow-its-workforce-intelligence-platform-despite-7-profit-dip/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/workhuman-wants-to-grow-its-workforce-intelligence-platform-despite-7-profit-dip/Tue, 24 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Software company Workhuman saw operating profit fall 7 per cent last year, as revenue declined.

But the company said it planned to invest more than $60 million in research, development and innovation next year as the company seeks to expand its workforce intelligence platform.

Consolidated accounts for the company showed turnover last year was also lower, falling 6 per cent year on year to $1.13 billion. Profit before tax was $106.25 million, down from $116 million in 2024.

But Workhuman, which makes human resources software, said it generated net cash flow of $138 million last year, up 29 per cent from the $107 million it recorded a year earlier. Cash on hand was also higher at $617.3 million.

“In 2025, we maintained positive cash flow and a strong financial position, while staying focused on investing in the capabilities that will support our next phase of growth. Innovation remains central to that strategy, with Ireland at the heart of our R&D and innovation work,” the company said.

“We are combining what we know best, employee recognition, with industry-leading AI capabilities and 25 years of human workforce data to give organisations deeper insight into their people, their contribution and their potential. For us, that represents an exciting next step for Workhuman and for the category.”

Research and development costs last year were just over $65 million. The US-founded company has maintained investment in its business in recent years, with $59 million ploughed into the company in 2024, and a similar level of investment in 2026.

The company, which has a sizeable operation in Ireland, said the $60 million planned for 2027 would be used to develop its Human Intelligence AI suite, which includes its Future Leaders offering that predicts which employees will move into leadership roles over the following three to five years, and its AI assistant.

The company, which has dual headquarters in Dublin and Massachusetts, was founded as Globoforce in 1999. It rebranded to Workhuman in 2019 and now employs more than 500 people in Dublin, part of a global workforce of more than 1,000. That figure is down from around 600 Irish staff before the company implemented global cuts of about 10 per cent in 2023, when the wider tech sector suffered a retrenchment.

Operating employee reward and incentive schemes, Workhuman counts some of the world’s biggest companies among its clients, including PepsiCo, Coursera and Cisco.

]]><![CDATA[Energy supplier Yuno posts 23% rise in profits to €5.3m]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/energy-supplier-yuno-posts-23-rise-in-profits-to-53m/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/energy-supplier-yuno-posts-23-rise-in-profits-to-53m/Tue, 24 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Irish electricity prices remain vulnerable to Europe’s currently volatile natural gas market, according to Cathal Fay, chief executive of leading supplier Yuno Ltd.

Profits at the company behind Yuno Energy and PrepayPower climbed more than 23 per cent to €5.3 million, according to its latest accounts.

Fay confirmed that the company would freeze prices this winter “until at least March of next year”.

The company was among the leading suppliers that increased their prices this summer after the US-Iran war sent global energy prices soaring.

Continued volatility is driving natural gas prices higher in Europe, which feeds through to electricity prices, Fay noted.

Natural gas determines electricity prices as the fuel is used to generate around half the power consumed here. Storage levels are lower than normal and “a cold snap cold put pressure on supplies”, Fay cautioned.

Yuno, which supplies electricity and gas to homes and businesses, buys its energy in advance, so its prices do not directly reflect gas market volatility.

Fay explained that the practice allows the company give price certainty through the winter.

Yuno’s turnover rose 9 per cent last year to €457.7 million from almost €420 million in 2024, his company’s figures show.

Its three businesses, Yuno Energy, Yuno Energy Business and PrepayPower supply 380,000 customers in total.

Employee numbers rose to 539 from 487, according to a company statement. Yuno’s 2025 accounts predate this year’s price increases.

Fay said the group was pleased with the progress it has been making.

The primary reason for its growth was an increase in customer numbers, according to its directors’ report. Fay and his co-founders started the business as PrepayPower in 2010.

PrepayPower offers pay-as-you-go energy to customers while Yuno Energy’s clients are billed. Yuno Energy Business supplies electricity and gas to medium-sized organisations.

The group is branching into district heating, that is supplying homes with waste heat.

The Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment and the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland selected one of its projects for inclusion in a Government pilot scheme.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Kenmare’s need for cash plays into Abu Dhabi bidder’s hands]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/kenmares-need-for-cash-plays-into-abu-dhabi-bidders-hands/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/kenmares-need-for-cash-plays-into-abu-dhabi-bidders-hands/Tue, 24 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Kenmare Resources managing director Tom Hickey appeared sanguine in an interview with The Irish Times in September 2025 about the end of takeover talks earlier that year with his predecessor, Michael Carvill, and Abu Dhabi private equity firm Oryx Global Partners.

The titanium minerals miner, which owns the Moma mine in Mozambique, had rejected outright the consortium’s £473 million (€565 million), or £5.30-a-share, offer in March as undervaluing the group. It subsequently ended talks after the Carvill-led group indicated it might lower its bid, amid falling titanium mineral prices and protracted negotiations with the Mozambique government over a new royalties deal.

“One of the interesting things about the approach that we had earlier in the year is that it kind of shone a light on the fundamental value,” Hickey said at the time. “It reminded people that ... on certain metrics, we might be cheap ... and that this is a really high-quality asset.”

On Monday, Kenmare said it was willing to back a proposal priced 28 per cent below Carvill’s original offer.

Kenmare may own a high-quality asset, with Moma producing about 6 per cent of global titanium minerals and an estimated mine life of 100 years. But Hickey was forced late last year to take a $300 million impairment charge as the company lowered its long-term revenue assumptions amid pricing uncertainty.

The price of ilmenite, Kenmare’s main product, is now in its fourth year of decline. There is little sign of a recovery: Berenberg analysts recently cut their forecasts again and do not expect a rebound until 2028.

Kenmare finally secured a new royalties deal late last month, but four years of stop-start negotiations, including the threat of international arbitration, have damaged investor sentiment.

Meanwhile, after spending about $300 million on dividends and buy-backs over seven years and another $300 million since 2023 on a project to upgrade and relocate Moma’s main mining plant, Kenmare faces what it has called “liquidity constraints”. That has made a takeover proposal from another Abu Dhabi firm, International Resources Holding (IRH), at a 28 per cent discount to Carvill’s original bid, suddenly very attractive.

Kenmare’s Abu Dhabi suitor given four-week extension to make bid

Kenmare said it needs to raise $50 million in equity early next year to satisfy its bankers and secure amendments to its credit facility. It is in talks, in the meantime, to raise $25 million in interim funding. The other party? Its prospective buyer.

It’s hardly the strongest negotiating position from which to maximise shareholder value.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[UK-EU deal a good start to build upon, says new City of London mayor]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/uk-eu-deal-a-good-start-to-build-upon-says-new-city-of-london-mayor/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/uk-eu-deal-a-good-start-to-build-upon-says-new-city-of-london-mayor/Tue, 24 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000The City of London’s new lord mayor, Bronek Masojada, said in Dublin on Monday that the UK-EU deal, agreed on Friday, was good start for both sides to build upon in seeking a closer trading relationship.

The accord will remove barriers to trade in food and drink, link carbon emissions trading systems in the UK and EU, and allow up to 100,000 young UK citizens to move to the EU and work for up to three years, matched by a similar flow in the opposite direction.

Masojada, the South African-born former chief executive of insurer Hiscox, said he hopes in time that both sides will develop further co-operation in financial services.

“You’ve got to start somewhere, and you should start where you think you can make progress,” Masojada told The Irish Times in an interview. “And I’m very happy with where the progress has been made.”

Masojada said that the UK’s Youth Mobility Scheme has the potential to have the most long-term economic impact for both sides.

“It creates person-to-person relationships, which ultimately are the ones which will pay off over a five- or 10-year period,” he said. “To me, that’s probably the most meaningful one.”

The lord mayor took office on November 13th as head of the City of London Corporation, the governing body over the so-called Square Mile historic financial district. His visit to Dublin this week marks his first overseas visit in the role; meetings have been set up with senior officials from AIB, the Central Bank of Ireland, Irish Funds and the British Irish Chamber of Commerce to discuss cross-border investment, financial and professional services, fintech and innovation. It will also look at how London and Dublin’s complementary strengths can help businesses access capital and new opportunities.

Masojada declined to be drawn on whether UK prime minister Andy Burnham’s efforts to reset London’s relations with Brussels should ultimately go so far as to lead to a reversal of Brexit.

“There’s a debate to be had and I’m not a player in that debate. Views are mixed across the United Kingdom and we can’t prejudge,” he said. “But everyone would agree on the benefit of reducing barriers to doing business together.”

Ireland and UK in ‘a better space’ after UK-EU Brexit reset deal, Helen McEntee says

Burnham said in parliament on Monday that Brexit “has not worked” and that rejoining could be on the table in the next parliament. However, he said that rejoining the EU without first holding a public referendum would be “unthinkable” for the UK.

In financial services, Masojada said he sees clear initial opportunities for co-operation between the UK and EU in the areas of digital markets, including the tokenisation of investment units to make trading more efficient; and cybersecurity.

While London has seen tens of thousands of financial roles move to financial hubs in the EU, including Dublin, Frankfurt, Paris and Amsterdam as firms in the UK lost their ability to passport services across the EU, the City of London has seen employment numbers rise from about 540,000 to 678,000 in the past decade.

Masojada said that London’s continued standing one of the world’s main global financial centres should be seen – and used – by Europe as an asset.

“While they wouldn’t necessarily admit it in public, a lot of the European banks have increased their London headcount [since Brexit],” he said.

]]>Chris J. Ratcliffe<![CDATA[British firm PureGym having mixed fortunes as it seeks to open outlets in Dublin]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/pure-gyms-mixed-planning-fortunes-as-uk-operator-seeks-to-open-in-dublin/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/pure-gyms-mixed-planning-fortunes-as-uk-operator-seeks-to-open-in-dublin/Tue, 24 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000A local resident in Dublin 1 has raised concerns over the opening of a PureGym facility, one of two outlets the British parent company is seeking for its entry into the Irish market, on the grounds that it would attract antisocial behaviour in the area given its 24-hour operating model.

The private-equity-backed gym operator has, however, been granted permission by Dublin City Council to begin construction of a second outlet, also a 24-hour facility, in the College Square commercial development on Tara Street in Dublin 2, which, at 82m high, is billed as the tallest building in the State.

In a letter to the council’s planning office, a local resident said those living in the north inner city area “have suffered the expansion of late night/all night uses, with its added antisocial behaviour, nuisances, noise generation, security/safety threats that comes with 24-hour users”.

The resident asked the council “to modify or curtail the current proposal so that existing prime shopping or retail space hours of operation (7am to 6pm) would apply, effectively retaining the environment and impacts of the main shopping street”.

They urged the council “to consider existing residents in these efforts to control or limit the expansion of late-night uses ... to provide some structure and relief to existing residents and users”, the letter shows.

PureGym sought planning permission to occupy a ground floor and basement unit in the Parnell Centre shopping complex in Dublin 1, about 500 metres from O’Connell Street.

It would primarily occupy the basement level, PureGym’s planning application shows, with plans comprising a main gym floor, changing rooms, additional exercise and training areas and a free-weight zone.

A decision is yet to be made by the council on whether to grantpermission.

PureGym has, however, been granted permission to begin construction on its proposed gym in the College Square development on Tara Street.

The company first considered an entry into the Irish market more than 10 years ago and lodged planning applications for two sites in north Dublin; however, those plans never got off the ground.

It said at the time Ireland was “likely to be well suited to the PureGym customer proposition and operating model” of low-cost membership fees and stripped-back facilities. It is understood the company reconsidered expansion plans after the UK voted to leave the European Union in 2016.

Founded in 2008 in Leeds, PureGym operates more than 700 outlets worldwide, some two-thirds of which are located in Britain. It also operates in Denmark, the United States and Switzerland, with franchised outlets in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

Private equity funds Leonard Green & Partners and KKR are investors in the company.

Poland’s defence ministry has announced plans to establish a no-fly zone along the country’s eastern border with the aim of making it easier to shoot down Russian missiles and drones that violate Polish airspace.

Meanwhile, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski has again suggested that Poland should be allowed to shoot down Russian missiles that are over Ukraine but heading towards the Polish border. However, the defence ministry acknowledged today that NATO is so far opposed to the idea.

Wiceminister obrony Cezary Tomczyk zapowiedział wprowadzenie strefy zakazu lotów przy wschodniej granicy Polski.

Jak poinformował minister Tomczyk, rozporządzenie trafiło do rządowego zespołu, strefa ma obejmować od kilkunastu do 50 kilometrów przy granicy wschodniej Polski i ma… pic.twitter.com/3xF68uNNRU

— Dariusz Wiewiorka (@darekwiewiorka) November 25, 2026

Speaking on Wednesday at the opening of a new military satellite imaging centre, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk announced that his department “will request the government to establish a no-fly zone on the country’s eastern border, to ensure Poland’s security”.

Tomczyk acknowledged that, after three Russian missiles struck southeastearn Poland last Friday, NATO had offered support, including the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) to Poland.

“But at the same time, the Polish military must do everything possible to protect our interests here and now,” he added.

The defence ministry recently took one such step by allowing easier identification of objects that can be shot down, said Tomczyk. “The no-fly zone at the state border will be an additional factor supporting the operations of the Polish Air Force.”

 

At a subsequent press briefing, Tomczyk provided more details of the plan. The proposed no-fly zone would stretch for a distance of between “a dozen or a few dozen kilometres from the border”, he said.

“When a Polish fighter pilot knows that an aircraft is entering Polish airspace from Ukraine, is flying at a certain altitude and speed, is entering the no-fly zone and is detected on radar, this constitutes grounds for shooting down such an object…We will also urge NATO as a whole to establish such a rule on the eastern flank.”

The deputy minister said that a relevant regulation had already been submitted and “will be processed in the coming weeks”. He expressed hope that the measures could be in place by the end of December or in early January.

As well as last Friday’s missile strikes, on Monday this week a Russian drone entered Poland from Ukraine and spent a few minutes in Polish airspace. The Polish military had been authorised to fire upon it, but eventually did not do so after it turned back towards the border.

Poland is changing the procedures under which its military can fire upon foreign aircraft, citing the "growing threat from Russia".

Visual identification of targets will no longer be required, with other forms of data to be used instead https://t.co/foCWsBDazH

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 29, 2026

The government’s plans for a no-fly zone were, however, questioned by Mariusz Błaszczak, a former defence minister and now head of the parliamentary caucus of Law and Justice (PiS), the main opposition party.

Błaszczak noted that current regulations already allow the introduction of a temporary no-fly zone. He suggested that what the government had announced was simply a “cosmetic measure” and asked what “real operational capabilities” it would provide to the military.

Earlier on Wednesday, Bloomberg reported, based on unnamed sources, that Poland had, at a NATO meeting called on Monday to discuss last week’s Russian missile strikes in Poland, asked about the possibility of shooting down Russian missiles that are over Ukraine but heading towards NATO states.

Asked about the issue, Tomczyk said that he could not confirm Bloomberg’s reporting, but noted that discussion of shooting down Russian missiles over Ukraine had been going on for months.

“NATO is not in favour of this in any way,” said Tomczyk, quoted by broadcaster TVN. “If we want to make any decisions that concern the space over Ukraine, it must always be a decision of the entire NATO…Many months ago NATO decided that such a procedure was out of the question. And that’s where we stand now.”

NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System to Poland in response to three Russian missiles striking Polish territory last week.

Hours after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone https://t.co/gudQJsPlQ5

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 24, 2026

On Wednesday morning, before Bloomberg’s report had been published, Sikorski, the foreign minister, was asked during an interview with Polskie Radio about the idea of shooting down missiles over Ukraine before they reached Poland.

“A missile or drone approaching our airspace already poses a direct threat to us, so I believe that shooting [it] down over Ukraine at Ukraine’s request would fall within the definition of self-defence,” said Sikorski. However, he acknowledged that any such policy would need to be agreed by NATO.

As far back as 2024, Poland proposed the idea of shooting down Russian missiles over Ukrainian territory. But it was rejected by NATO, whose then-secretary general, Jens Stoltenberg, said that it would risk NATO “becoming part of the conflict”.

The mayor of Warsaw has refused permission for opposition protests outside the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which was taken over last month by a group of government-backed judges, to continue.

City hall, which is under the control of Poland’s main ruling party, the centrist Civic Coalition (KO), says that the demonstration threatens public safety. However, opposition figures have condemned the decision as “authoritarian” and one of the organisers of the protest has pledged to challenge it in court.

Bum.
Jest zakaz organizacji kolejnej manifestacji przed Trybunałem Konstytucyjnym.https://t.co/Ol8gQxC3A1 pic.twitter.com/bUqAkdojxe

— Tomasz Skory (@TomaszSkory) November 25, 2026

On 30 October, a group of eight judges chosen this year by the government’s parliamentary majority – but five of whom opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has refused to swear in – effectively took control of the TK.

They declared that the tribunal’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, was suspended. Meanwhile, riot police surrounded the court and held back protesters, including Święczkowski himself.

Since then, the demonstrators have maintained a constant presence outside the court, while Święczkowski has also periodically appeared. He and Nawrocki argue that the actions of the eight “usurper” judges are illegal and that Święczkowski remains chief justice.

 

Given the ongoing demonstration in front of the court, the judges currently controlling the TK have used a separate entrance that leads in from the next-door chancellery of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

On Monday this week, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, the judge who has declared herself acting head of the court, arranged a meeting with Warsaw’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, and the commander of Warsaw police, Krzysztof Ogroński, to discuss the protest.

She argued that, by preventing access to the tribunal, the demonstrators were “violating the constitutional and European standard of the right to a court”.

On Wednesday morning, Warsaw city hall announced that Trzaskowski, who is a deputy leader of Tusk’s centrist KO party, had rejected a request for permission to continue the public assembly outside the TK from the end of November until January.

‼️ Rafał Trzaskowski zakazał zgromadzenia pod Trybunałem Konstytucyjnym!

Protest trwa tam od września i dotyczy sporu o to, kto ma w TK zasiadać.

W poniedziałek osoba podająca się za „Zastępującą Prezesa TK” zaprosiła ratusz i Policję, by „przywrócić” wstęp do Trybunału. Dwa… pic.twitter.com/a0EzqVzRDn

— Magdalena Majkowska (@MagdaMajkowska) November 25, 2026

“While the freedom to organise and participate in peaceful assemblies constitutes a fundamental constitutional freedom, it is not unconditional,” wrote the municipal authorities.

They noted that the current gathering outside the TK has been ongoing since 17 September (as protesters anticipated an attempted takeover of the court) and that the organisers had given assurances that they would not obstruct the roadway.

In fact, tents, a television stage and other structures have blocked the road, wrote city hall. This “causes significant disruption for local residents” and “undoubtedly hinders emergency service vehicles, thereby threatening the life and health of residents”.

The authorities also noted that, while the protests were initially peaceful, there had later been a number of “dangerous incidents”, including attempts to block vehicles from entering the TK and scuffles with police, which included throwing objects at officers, physical confrontations, verbal abuse and spitting.

Such developments “have caused the gathering to lose its peaceful character”, wrote city hall. There are also “grounds to assume that the intention is, in effect, a long-term blockade of the entrance to the Constitutional Tribunal and the street itself”.

One of the organisers of the protest, Adam Borowski, told Polsat News that it is a “lie” that they are preventing the TK from functioning properly. It is the judges “illegally occupying” the tribunal who are responsible, he said.

Borowski announced that they would appeal against the city’s decision in court. They have 24 hours from the issuing of the decision in which to do so.

PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, meanwhile, declared that the decision to ban the protest was “authoritarianism in its purest form…trampling citizens’ constitutional rights”.

]]> Russia denies its missiles hit Poland and accuses Warsaw of “stoking anti-Russian sentiment” https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/25/russia-denies-its-missiles-hit-poland-and-accuses-warsaw-of-stoking-anti-russian-sentiment/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 10:37:33 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=107481

Russia has “categorically denied” that the three missiles which struck Poland last week were Russian and has accused Warsaw of seeking to “stoke anti-Russian sentiment” around the incident.

Its remarks came after Poland’s foreign ministry on Tuesday summoned Russia’s ambassador, Georgy Mikhno, to present him with a protest over the missiles. Today, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski said that expelling the ambassador is “one of the options” Poland could take, though it remains unlikely.

⚡️Komentarz Ambasady Rosji w Polsce

24 listopada 2026 r. JE Pan Gieorgij Michno, Ambasador Federacji Rosyjskiej w Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej, został zaproszony do MSZ kraju przyjmującego, gdzie przekazano mu protest w ramach rzekomego „powiązania” naszego kraju z incydentami… pic.twitter.com/GUJB0RWZgt

— Russian Embassy, PL (@rusemb_pl) November 24, 2026

On Friday morning last week, three objects struck at different locations in southeastern Poland, not far from the Ukrainian border, amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine. On Sunday, Poland confirmed that all three were Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles.

Subsequently, on Monday night this week, a Russian drone entered Polish airspace from Ukraine and spent a few minutes above Poland before turning back into Ukraine.

On Tuesday, Mikhno was summoned to the Polish foreign ministry, which said it had presented him with “a very strong diplomatic note” regarding the missile strikes.

 

Afterwards, Mikhno read a statement to the media saying that “Russia categorically rejects the accusations of involvement in the incidents”, which were being made based on “political judgements and unsubstantiated assumptions”.

He also condemned what he said was “openly Russophobic rhetoric around the incident”, which suggests “a desire to exploit the situation to further stoke anti-Russian sentiment”.

The ambassador claimed that “no convincing and verifiable evidence has been presented” to establish the origin of the missiles. He then refused to answer journalists’ questions before leaving.

Russia has installed an exhibition titled “Ten Centuries of Polish Russophobia” outside a cemetery for thousands of Poles murdered by the Soviets in the 1940 Katyn massacre.

It opened just before Poland marked its annual day of remembrances for victims https://t.co/HcfmeNrerB

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2026

Mikhno’s claims were immediately rejected by the Polish foreign ministry’s spokesman, Maciej Wewiór, who said that it was “beyond dispute” that the missiles were Russian and that Moscow “knows [this] perfectly well”.

On Sunday, Polish prosecutors said that the remains of the missiles leave no doubt they are Russian, and added that preliminary findings even indicate which specific factory they were manufactured in and when.

A number of Poland’s NATO allies, as well as the alliance’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, have also condemned Russia over the missile incident and expressed solidarity with Warsaw.

NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System to Poland in response to three Russian missiles striking Polish territory last week.

Hours after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone https://t.co/gudQJsPlQ5

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 24, 2026

On Wednesday morning, Sikorski was asked during an interview with Polskie Radio whether a “strong diplomatic note” was a strong enough response, given Russia’s repeated and continued hostile actions towards Poland.

When it was put to the foreign minister that Poland should expel the Russian ambassador, Sikorski said that “this is one option” and “of course, it can be done”. However, he added that “we won’t pursue it yet” and noted that any such action would be met with an equivalent response from Moscow.

In 2024 and 2025, Sikorski successively ordered Russia to close all of its consulates in Poland in response to Russian acts of sabotage. Moscow responded by shutting down all Polish consulates on its territory.

🗣️ "Czy jest sens rozmawiania z ambasadorem Rosji? To symboliczny gest pokazania dezaprobaty. Liczą się sankcje i naciski gospodarcze. (…) Nie ma decyzji, by zerwać stosunki dyplomatyczne, ale one wiszą na cienkim włosku"

Rzecznik rządu @adamSzlapka w rozmowie z @Piekarski_M… pic.twitter.com/JU9up9cm5N

— tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) November 25, 2026

On Monday morning, Polish government spokesman Adam Szłapka told broadcaster TVP that “relations [with Russia] are hanging by a thread”.

He added that, while presenting a protest note to the Russian ambassador had been “a symbolic gesture of disapproval”, most important are “the sanctions and the pressure on Russia”.

“I think [this pressure] is strong from the entire European Union…[but] we’ve had doubts from the United States regarding these sanctions in recent months,” said Szłapka. “Poland believes [the pressure] should be consistent and stronger…I hope the entire Western world will be very clear on this.”

]]> Poland and US sign defence technology cooperation agreement https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/24/poland-and-us-sign-defence-technology-cooperation-agreement/ Tue, 24 Nov 2026 20:15:01 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=107444
