Poland and the United States have signed an agreement on defence research, development, testing and evaluation, concluding 17 years of negotiations and opening the way for deeper technological cooperation.

The agreement establishes a framework for joint defence projects, as well as the exchange of technical data and expertise, giving Poland – which is already a major importer of US arms – a formal role in the development of American defence technologies for the first time.

Under Secretary Emil Michael (@USWREMichael) and Mr. Cezary Tomczyk, Poland’s Secretary of State at the Ministry of National Defence, signed the Agreement Between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of the Republic of Poland for Defense Research,… pic.twitter.com/7EAgK3nD2i

— Department of War CTO (@DoWCTO) November 23, 2026

The agreement was signed at the Pentagon by Poland’s deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk and US under secretary of war for research and engineering Emil Michael.

According to the Department of War, the deal will help “turn research and development into validated military capabilities to jointly support US and Polish warfighters”.

Tomczyk said the agreement would allow Polish universities, research institutes and companies to participate in joint research and development work on defence technology with US partners and would enable such technologies to be tailored more closely to the requirements of the Polish armed forces.

During a briefing in Washington, Tomczyk admitted that the agreement had been negotiated for what he described as a “probably record-breaking” 17 years, but he noted a “significant acceleration in relations” between the US and Poland over the last six months.

 

General Marcin Górka, who oversees innovation in the Polish armed forces and accompanied Tomczyk to the United States, likewise welcomed the agreement, which he said would “open the doors to American military laboratories for our scientists and engineers”.

Górka also said the agreement would enable Poland and the United States to jointly develop anti-drone systems and advanced drones, with testing taking place in both countries.

Poland is a major importer of US military hardware. Between 2021 and 2025, it was the biggest overall importer of arms in NATO, with around 44% of that equipment coming from the US, including F-35 fighter jets, Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence systems and HIMARS rocket launchers.

But Poland has recently sought to move from being a client of the US defence industry to more of a partner. Earlier this month, Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth signed a declaration on expanding bilateral defence-industrial cooperation.

Poland and the US have signed a statement of intent on strengthening defence industry cooperation.

Polish defence minister @KosiniakKamysz said his country would be "the US ambassador in the EU", including seeking EU funds for jointly produced equipment https://t.co/SKHrxTEKIW

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 11, 2026

Last month, Poland was chosen as the location for a planned Patriot missile maintenance and servicing facility, the first of its kind outside the United States. In May, an agreement was signed to establish a centre in Poland for servicing the engines of Abrams tanks.

This year, Polish state defence group PGZ was chosen as the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles, while US defence giant Northrop Grumman and Polish arms manufacturer Niewiadów-PGM announced plans to jointly produce artillery shells in Poland.

Poland is also seeking to host a new permanent US military base, with Tomczyk reiterating during his Washington visit that a decision is expected from the Trump administration in early December.

NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System to Poland in response to three Russian missiles striking Polish territory last week.

Hours after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone https://t.co/gudQJsPlQ5

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 24, 2026

The new agreement on defence technology was signed amid heightened tensions with Russia. On Friday, three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles struck separate locations in southeastern Poland, near the Ukrainian border.

Tomczyk said the Polish delegation had briefed Pentagon officials on the missile strikes, which he described as a “provocation” by Russia. The Polish minister was also asked about US President Donald Trump last week calling Russia’s Vladimir Putin his “friend”.

“One thing is certain: Vladimir Putin is not our friend; he is a threat to us,” replied Tomczyk. “This is the most important message that should come from Poland and resonate with the people of the United States.”

Subsequently, on Monday night, a Russian drone entered Polish airspace from Ukraine for a few minutes before turning back.

]]> Poland, Lithuania and Latvia violated rights of migrants sent back to Belarus, finds European court https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/24/poland-lithuania-and-latvia-violated-rights-of-migrants-sent-back-to-belarus-finds-european-court/ Tue, 24 Nov 2026 15:03:07 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=107447

Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Poland, Lithuania and Latvia violated the human rights of migrants from Afghanistan, Iraq and Cuba who entered their countries illegally from Belarus in 2021 and 2022, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has ruled.

However, the ECHR did also recognise that states have the right to prevent the entry of migrants who have been “instrumentalised” by Belarus in order to create a crisis on the European Union’s eastern borders.

That latter finding prompted Poland’s deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy to hail today’s rulings as a victory and endorsement of the government’s tough border policies. It was also described as a groundbreaking moment by a leading human rights organisation.

📽️ Watch a video explainer on the Grand Chamber cases concerning instrumentalisation of migration.

📽️ Regardez la vidéo explicative sur les affaires de Grande Chambre sur l'instrumentalisation de la migration. pic.twitter.com/ZhXqZ6lIur

— ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 24, 2026

In 2021, Belarus began encouraging, assisting and, in some cases, forcing tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to irregularly cross into the neighbouring EU states of Poland, Lithuania and Latvia.

Belarus engineered the migration crisis as part of the various “hybrid actions” undertaken alongside its ally Russia with the intention of destabilising countries they regard as hostile.

In response, Poland, Lithuania and Latvia took a variety of measures intended to prevent the entry of irregular migrants from Belarus. In many cases, they carried out so-called “pushbacks”, sending migrants who had crossed the border back into Belarus.

 

On Tuesday, the ECHR announced three sets of rulings on cases brought against Poland, Lithuania and Latvia in relation to actions they had taken against specific migrants who had entered from Belarus.

The European court noted that the migrants had “entered unlawfully” as part of Belarus’s “instrumentalisation of migration”, which it described as a “hostile action” that had  “the intention of destabilising the respondent states or the wider region”.

This “represented a deliberate threat to the state” and “was liable to put at risk its essential functions, including the maintenance of law and order and the safeguarding of its national security”.

Poland wants the European Union to deny the right to asylum for migrants who cross EU borders in organised, aggressive groups, just as Poland has itself done on its border with Belarus https://t.co/7Gbsvs6I1e

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026

The court found that states do have the right to control entry, and even fully close their borders, as well as to “remove a foreign national to the instrumentalising state”, without it automatically being a violation of the human rights convention.

However, the ECHR also deemed that, “before removing an individual in such circumstances, national authorities had an obligation to detect those individuals who would be particularly at risk of suffering or enduring ill-treatment”.

That included those who had personal vulnerabilities (such as old age, ill health or a disability) or who would face a threat to their life or serious risk of mistreatment by being returned to Belarus.

In the cases of Poland and Latvia, the ECHR found that they had breached the obligation to undertake such an assessment before returning certain migrants.

A court has found that Poland's border guard violated the law when sending two Afghan and Ethiopian men back to Belarus after they injured themselves crossing the anti-migrant border fence.

One of them had made clear his wish to claim asylum in Poland https://t.co/42yOuGEgns

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2024

For Poland, the case concerned an unnamed Afghan national who had been part of a group that had crossed back and forth over the Polish-Belarusian border multiple times, as often happened in the early stages of the crisis.

The ECHR noted that it had, at the time, issued an interim measure requiring that the Afghan man not be returned to Belarus.

However, the Polish authorities did not take this into account, and sent him back to Belarus on 20 October 2021, thereby demonstrating they had not complied with their obligation to properly assess his need for protection, found the ECHR.

The court also ruled that, in the case of that applicant as well as a fellow Afghan national, Poland had violated their rights by preventing lawyers from having access to them. It ordered Poland to pay the two men €20,000 (89,000 zloty) and €5,000 respectively as compensation.

Two Afghan asylum seekers who crossed from Belarus into Poland have been awarded compensation for their mistreatment by Polish border guards.

They were detained and driven back towards the border by officers, who did not accept their asylum applications https://t.co/M9bSHakS5j

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2025

In Latvia’s case, the ECHR ruled that the country had violated its obligations by sending Iraqi Kurdish children, some of whom were infants, back into Belarus, “disregarding the[ir] evident vulnerability”.

At the same time, the European court dismissed further complaints by adult migrants against Latvia and Lithuania, finding that they had not demonstrated any vulnerability or risk.

However, it did find that Lithuania had violated some Cuban migrants’ rights by failing to properly inform them of the reasons they were being held in a detention camp and thereby also of their right to legally challenge their detention.

Warsaw’s first astronomical observatory open to the public and run by a local municipal institution launched on Sunday.

Its organisers say the facility, with two telescopes allowing safe observation of the Sun and photography of the cosmos, is aimed at astronomy enthusiasts as well as children and young people, who will be able to watch the night sky and participate in recording data without needing their own equipment.

The new observatory, which is located on the roof of the Gocław Culture Terminal in the Praga-South of Poland’s capital, was created in response to growing public interest in astronomy, science and new technologies, says city hall.

“Under the three-metre-high dome, specialised equipment awaits, allowing for observation of the sky, including safe viewing of the Sun,” said mayor Rafał Trzaskowski, who visited the facility last week ahead of its official opening.

“Anyone who is interested can come here and learn about space through observation, photographing the sky and hands-on activities,” he added.

The observatory will be free to use but only accessible during organised events, owing to limited space and the expensive equipment it contains, reports newspaper Super Express.

“The dome houses very expensive equipment. For most of the year, it will function as a broadcasting station, and images from the telescopes will be projected onto screens in the main hall of the terminal,” Jacek Białek, head of Gocław Culture Terminal, told the newspaper.

“We will invite people inside the dome as part of programs, the dates of which will be published on the cultural centre’s website,” he added.

Participants in workshops and events will also be able to help collect and analyse data, with Białek noting that the centre will be working closely with scientists from the University of Warsaw

The new facility cost around 500,000 zloty (€111,000), most of which was covered from the district budget, with contributions from private donations as well as grants from the state-owned military optoelectronic equipment company PCO and the national lottery foundation.

 

The core of the new facility is a 14″ DO-GSO (Ritchey-Chrétien) telescope with a mirror diameter of approximately 35 cm and a focal length of approximately 2,850 mm, placed on an EQ8-RH equatorial mount with automatic sky tracking.

This setup, along with a QHY268M Pro monochrome camera, a filter wheel and an electronic focuser, will be used for astrophotography and targeted photometric measurements, producing images suited to Warsaw’s atmospheric conditions.

The observatory also boasts a specialist Sky-Watcher Heliostar 100 H-Alpha telescope, which is used for safe and detailed observation and astrophotography of the Sun, allowing viewers to see structures in the solar atmosphere invisible through an ordinary telescope.

The telescope allows solar prominences – large, bright features extending out from the Sun’s surface – to be observed and compared with images produced on other days. The telescope is protected by a three-metre dome that automatically opens and rotates.

The takeover follows years of rapid growth for InPost, which pioneered the use of parcel delivery lockers in Poland before spreading rapidly in major western European markets, including France, Spain and the UK.

The consortium acquired InPost at a price of €15.60 per share, valuing the company at approximately €7.8 billion.

Two Ukrainians have been charged in Poland with working on behalf of Russia to paint slogans praising the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a nationalist formation responsible for massacring Poles during World War Two, on three monuments in the Polish city of Poznań.

Polish prosecutors say that the operation was intended to fuel hostility between Poles and Ukrainians. The incidents in Poznań were part of a seemingly coordinated wave of similar graffiti on monuments in three other Polish cities.

In early November, the words “Slava UPA” (“Glory to the UPA”) were painted in red on three monuments in Poznań commemorating World War Two soldiers.

While the UPA is remembered by many in Ukraine for fighting for independence from Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is primarily associated with leading the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, were slaughtered as part of an ethnic cleansing operation.

The history of those massacres, and the continued veneration of the UPA by some in Ukraine, has regularly stirred tension between Poland and Ukraine, who are otherwise close allies.

 

On Thursday, the National Prosecutor’s Office confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that two Ukrainians, who can be named only as Nikita S. and Dmytro Y. under Polish privacy law, had been detained and charged in relation to the vandalism.

According to prosecutors, Nikita S., “acting on behalf of Russian intelligence and in order to obtain financial benefit of $500”, persuaded Dmytro Y. to “commit an act of sabotage by painting the slogans” with the aim of “publicly inciting hatred based on national differences between the Polish and Ukrainian peoples”.

The suspects were identified by police and the Internal Security Agency (ABW), who had analysed surveillance footage of the perpetrator, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. Both were detained in Poznań, according to PAP.

In the wake of the Poznań vandalism, Poland-based Belarusian news outlet MOST reported that, a few days before the graffiti appeared, an advert offering $500 for someone to paint pro-UPA slogans on monuments in the city had appeared on messaging service Telegram.

When an undercover journalist from the outlet contacted the person offering the job, they were told that similar work was available in other Polish cities.

Around the same time, almost identical graffiti praising the UPA appeared on further monuments in the cities of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Warsaw, including one dedicated to the heroes of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising.

Around a dozen monuments in Poland, including one dedicated to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, have been defaced with graffiti glorifying the WWII Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA).

Last week, local police in Gdańsk confirmed that they had detained a 17-year-old Ukrainian suspected of carrying out the graffiti there and in Gdynia. He has been charged with promoting fascist ideology, incitement to violence and hatred based on nationality, and desecration of monuments.

The Ukrainian embassy in Poland has condemned the acts of vandalism, calling them a “disgraceful provocation” and “a manifestation of the hybrid war that Russia is attempting to wage by any means in European states”.

Poland has been a primary target for Russia’s so-called hybrid actions in Europe, which have included acts of sabotage, espionage, disinformation and efforts to stir hostility towards Ukrainians.

Such operations are rarely carried out by Russian operatives themselves. Instead, Russia often recruits people already on the ground, often members of Poland’s large Ukrainian and Belarusian migrant communities, as well as Poles themselves in some cases.

In July this year, a Ukrainian teenager was indicted by Polish prosecutors on charges of painting dozens of pro-UPA slogans in public places, including on a monument to victims of the Volhynia massacres.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Wed, 25 Nov 2026 18:15:00 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.5 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Poundland collapsed after owner withheld funds, bosses say https://www.cityam.com/poundland-collapsed-after-owner-withheld-funds/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 18:05:48 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2483329

Poundland’s owners withheld the funds the retailer needed to stay afloat, its management has said, leaving the company with no option other than administration.  The now-collapsed retailer’s directors told its 12,000 staff that they were forced to trigger an administration after they “exhausted all options to have adequate funds released that would allow the business [...]]]>

Poundland’s owners withheld the funds the retailer needed to stay afloat, its management has said, leaving the company with no option other than administration. 

The now-collapsed retailer’s directors told its 12,000 staff that they were forced to trigger an administration after they “exhausted all options to have adequate funds released that would allow the business to trade solvently”.

Poundland’s collapse is one of the biggest high street failures in years. It has been described as “deeply concerning” by Andy Burnham and “devastating” by the UK’s retail workers’ union. 

Barry Williams and Shaun Wills, the retailer’s board of directors, told staff that this collapse was triggered after it was starved of cash by Gordon Brothers, the US investment firm which owned it.

In a memo seen by City AM they wrote: “It is with sincere sadness and intense regret that we have to tell you that we had no alternative but to take this decision, bringing to a close 36 years of history at Poundland and Dealz in Ireland as we know it.

“Following the removal of all borrowing facilities and access to our bank accounts by our lender and majority shareholder on Tuesday 27 October, the Board has explored – and sadly exhausted – all options to have adequate funds released that would allow the business to trade solvently.

“Furthermore, we have been informed today, despite our positive engagement with prospective bidders, there is no prospect of an acceptable solvent offer, and consequently there is no prospect of our owner and lender continuing to fund the business.”

Williams and Wills added that it became “impossible” for management to see how it could continue to operate Poundland as a solvent business without access to more funds.

They added: “We would like to take the opportunity to put on record our unreserved thanks and gratitude to all our colleagues, who have worked tirelessly in returning the business to positive sales and profit over the past 18 months.”

In collaboration with Alix Partners, who were appointed as the administrators to Poundland, the retailer’s management will be holding a number of in-person and virtual meetings with staff on Thursday, sources said.

During Gordon Brothers’s sale of Poundland it faced repeated accusations that it had been stopping the retailer from accessing vital funds needed to keep trading. Liam Byrne MP, chair of Parliament’s business select committee, has accused the firm of “starving” Poundland of access to funds.

After the retailer’s management filed their intention to appoint administrators in late October, Gordon Brothers agreed to release the funds the company needed to continue trading.

The investment firm decided that it would not provide the further funds Poundland’s management say they needed to continue trading for any longer under the notice to appoint administrators, it is understood.

“This was a decision between either putting in more money or finding a buyer. They were the only ways to move forward. They elected not to put in more money, and they couldn’t find a buyer,” one person with knowledge of the matter told City AM.

A spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said it “continued to approve funding for payments which were necessary for the trading of the business during the NOI period.”

After failing to find a viable bid to take over the entire company, Gordon Brothers and Poundland’s directors decided that administration was the only option remaining for the retailer.

The spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said: “This appointment follows an extensive three-month M&A process, which explored every avenue to secure a sale of the whole company. 

“Commercial negotiations with interested parties for both the whole of the company and with established retailers interested in acquiring substantial portions of the business will now continue, led by the Administrators, and conclude through the administration process.”

The spokesperson added that Poundland has faced “several years of instability”. Gordon Brothers propped the retailer up with £85m in new financing to “stabilise a business that was in free fall,” they added.

Businesses and households face the risk of another interest rate hike as Bank of England policymakers warned that energy costs would begin to pass through to the prices of other consumer goods and services.  Bank officials, who voted to hike interest rates to four per cent earlier this month, told MPs that there had so [...]]]>

Businesses and households face the risk of another interest rate hike as Bank of England policymakers warned that energy costs would begin to pass through to the prices of other consumer goods and services. 

Bank officials, who voted to hike interest rates to four per cent earlier this month, told MPs that there had so far been low levels of pass through from international energy prices to other goods and products across the economy. 

The dovish rate-setter Swati Dhingra, who described her latest vote to hike interest rates as “additional insurance”, said she was “surprised” by how businesses had not yet passed on higher input costs onto consumers. 

She said impacts from the Iran war on inflation had been “more muted” although she warned of the possibilities of price pressures building in the economy over the coming months. 

While Bank governor Andrew Bailey said the Bank’s forecast showing that inflation will rise to nearly five per cent in the middle of next year would “mechanically would be lower” if oil prices remained around $90 per barrel, it was “too unpredictable” to rely on current market pricing when voting on changes to monetary policy. 

Bailey said he was “repeatedly” told that business owners were “finding this a very hard environment to pass cost increases on into pricing”. The comment could suggest that inflation may not spike as high as it did in 2022. 

But he also said: “We’ve got quite a sharp pickup in energy price inflation, we’re concerned about heading off the indirect and second-round effects [where higher inflation pushes up wages, and vice-versa in a spiralling effect]. 

“Meanwhile we’re not seeing those effects as strongly as we thought, but the pipeline—which is the energy effects—now looks much stronger.

“That really started to weigh on me.”

Interest rates looms in December

Deputy governor Clare Lombardelli and Catherine Mann, who are both seen as likely to back further hikes in interest rates, respectively suggested that strong growth in the UK economy and the Bank’s own credibility in managing inflation were factors influencing their recent votes. 

Lombardelli added: “We know we’ve got these higher prices that have happened over months up until now, and that will filter through.”

She also admitted that while food price inflation had remained lower than expected. It could go up as high as five per cent in the middle of next year, according to Lombardelli.

The Bank’s next decision on interest rates is in December. Analysts are split on whether the Monetary Policy Committee will decide to hike rates to 4.25 per cent or leave them on hold. 

]]> 2483284Maurício Alencar Maurício Alencar Poundland owners hauled back to parliament over ‘devastating’ collapse https://www.cityam.com/poundland-owner-hauled-back-to-parliament-after-devastating-collapse/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 16:38:13 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2483227

Poundland’s owner has been ordered to appear in front of MPs after the retailer collapsed into administration on Wednesday, in what the Prime Minister described as ”deeply concerning” news for the retailer’s near 12,000 strong workforce. Mark Newton-Jones, the Europe chief of US investment firm Gordon Brothers, has been summoned for a second grilling from [...]]]>

Poundland’s owner has been ordered to appear in front of MPs after the retailer collapsed into administration on Wednesday, in what the Prime Minister described as ”deeply concerning” news for the retailer’s near 12,000 strong workforce.

Mark Newton-Jones, the Europe chief of US investment firm Gordon Brothers, has been summoned for a second grilling from Parliament’s business select committee to answer questions on how the discount retailer was allowed to fail.

The hearing would be held in public and could take place early in the new year, City AM understands. 

MPs have taken an active interest in Poundland’s troubles given the retailer’s importance to local high streets and employment of around 12,000 people across the country.  

In a statement after the company appointed administrators, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Poundland was “part of the fabric of high streets” and the government wanted “every effort made to secure a deal that protects jobs and keeps as many shops open as possible”.

“The news that it has gone into administration just weeks before Christmas will be deeply concerning for workers and their families,” he said, adding that the administration process “does give other potential buyers the opportunity to engage”.

“We will work hard with all the relevant parties to ensure the best possible outcome,” Burnham said.

The high street chain’s directors formally appointed administrators on Wednesday night after Gordon Brothers had failed to find anyone to buy Poundland as a going concern during a weeks-long sale process.

Liam Byrne MP, chair of the select committee, wrote to Newton-Jones: “We are committed to ensuring the best possible result for Poundland’s employees and suppliers and so I will provide a date for the hearing as soon as I judge any jeopardy for a successful outcome to the administration has passed.”

Minutes after the announcement, Reform UK’s Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick hit out at business secretary Jonathan Reynolds and Andy Burnham for letting the company collapse.

“Instead of trying to save 12,000 jobs, Burnham has been chuntering away on Tik Tok and dreaming up his 10-year plan,” Jenrick said. 

“He’s stood by as the ‘Greedy Brothers’ strip out a high street store and risk 12,000 jobs, which could have been saved by multiple buyers. It’s an outrage.”

No10: Poundland collapse ‘concerning’

The select committee has urged Newton-Jones to vow that neither “Gordon Brothers or any related party will not act as administrator, liquidator or in any other insolvency capacity in relation to Poundland”.

Hilco Capital, a private equity firm that had been in the running to buy Poundland last year before it was snapped up by Gordon Brothers, has been approached to liquidate the retailer’s stock, the Financial Times has reported.

Mark Newton-Jones appeared in front of the committee earlier this month, where he failed to promise that his company would prioritise protecting jobs over Gordon Brothers’s financial returns. 

Following the two-hour grilling, Byrne accused Gordon Brothers of “jeopardising thousands of jobs on the British high street”.

City AM reported that there were at least four bidders racing to snap up Poundland ahead of the impending administration. One parliamentary source described a preference for a proposal brought forward by Zachert Private Equity, which is a German firm run by a former Bloomberg journalist.

Bally Auluk, national officer of retail union Usdaw, described Poundland’s administration as “devastating news” for the retailer’s nearly 12,000 staff.

He said: “This decision has been made by the owners Gordon Brothers, despite failing to engage with Usdaw, which is a disgraceful way to treat our members. 

“We are now seeking urgent meetings with the administrators, where we will be looking for an open dialogue about how we can save as many stores and jobs as possible.”

A spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said the investment firm’s “thoughts are with Poundland colleagues. We recognise how difficult the continued uncertainty is for them. Efforts to preserve as many jobs and stores as possible will continue, led by the Administrators.

“This appointment follows an extensive three-month M&A process, which explored every avenue to secure a sale of the whole company.”

A government spokesperson said: “Poundland stores are a vital part of many high streets and communities. They are valued by families for their affordable goods and the local jobs they provide. 

“News of its administration is very concerning particularly for the almost 10,000 workers and their families. We stand ready to support affected staff and want to see as many jobs and stores saved as possible. 

“We understand there is still strong interest from bidders for the whole business and parts of the business. The administrators must now be given time and space to do their job.”

Poundland has collapsed into administration in one of the biggest failures on Britain’s high streets in years.  Its owner, Gordon Brothers, had been in talks with multiple potential buyers for weeks but failed to find a home for the discount retailer before a notice to appoint administrators came into effect. The decision to trigger Poundland’s [...]]]>

Poundland has collapsed into administration in one of the biggest failures on Britain’s high streets in years. 

Its owner, Gordon Brothers, had been in talks with multiple potential buyers for weeks but failed to find a home for the discount retailer before a notice to appoint administrators came into effect.

The decision to trigger Poundland’s administration was announced to staff at an all-store meeting this afternoon, multiple people with knowledge of the situation told City AM.

The US investment firm, which bought Poundland little more than a year ago, will now face intense scrutiny over whether it did enough to prevent the collapse, which puts the retailer’s 600 stores and near-12,000 employees at risk.

In a statement released after the company called in administrators, a spokesman for Gordon Brothers said efforts to “preserve as many jobs and stores as possible will continue” under the administrators’ control.

“This appointment follows an extensive three-month M&A process, which explored every avenue to secure a sale of the whole company,” a spokesman said. “Commercial negotiations with interested parties for both the whole of the company and with established retailers interested in acquiring substantial portions of the business will now continue, led by the administrators, and conclude through the administration process.”

Gordon Brothers had been holding talks with multiple bidders in recent days: Irish property firm MPG, little-known investor Xyra Group Holdings, German-based Zachert Private Equity and Middle Eastern wholesaler Quality Premier Foods.

Any one of these buyers could still buy Poundland out of administration, though they had initially been attempting to buy the company as a going concern. The parties involved would not have let the retailer fall into administration if it was not confident that a sale of the company could still be possible after this point, people close to the matter told City AM.

If none of the bidders in talks with Gordon Brothers are willing to buy Poundland out of administration, it will likely be broken up among a number of retail buyers. 

Tesco, B&M, Lidl, Iceland and The Range are among those who have expressed an interest in buying some Poundland stores out of administration. Administrators at Alix Partners will be in charge of running this break-up process. 

A spokesperson for Alix Partners said: “We appreciate this is a deeply concerning time for all involved – customers, suppliers and, in particular, Poundland colleagues.

“Our priority now is to work with all stakeholders, including representatives from government and USDAW, as we identify the best possible route forward. We would encourage anybody interested in acquiring the business in part or as a whole, as well as UK retail operators with open employment opportunities, to contact the administrators.” 

Poundland’s management made the court filing on Wednesday, after initially filing the notice to appoint administrators late last month and extending it two weeks later, in a bid to buy extra time to find a new home for the retailer.

Gordon Brothers had rejected multiple bids from MPG over its insistence that it be repaid for a £30m loan attached to Poundland, of which it holds £22.5m. PepCo, the retailer’s former owner, had offered to defer repayment of its £7.5m chunk of this loan.

Xyra has been working with former BHS boss Tony Brown on its bid, which would have seen the retailer expand its store count in the UK and roll out more exclusive ranges in a bid to fatten its margins.

Zachert and Quality Premier Foods emerged as potential buyers later on in the process and have been holding talks with Gordon Brothers in recent days.

Political firestorm

Preventing cyberattacks should be seen as fundamentally an economic as well as a technical problem, writes Paul Ormerod

Cybersecurity used to be something only nerds and geeks had heard about. Now, it seems hardly a day passes without some new attack being featured in the media.

In March, for example, a vulnerability in Companies House’s Web Filing service left the personal data of company directors across 5m registered UK businesses accessible to anyone with a login. Last month, online fashion retailer ASOS confirmed a breach exposing customer names and contact details. Companies this year have still been dealing with the aftermath of major attacks in 2025 such as the one on Jaguar Land Rover.

A government survey estimates that 69 per cent of large businesses experienced a breach or attack over the past year. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) suggests that malicious cyber activity costs businesses some £15bn a year.

Cybersecurity is an economics problem

The problem is often seen as being essentially a technical one. Technology, and increasingly AI, causes the issues, so technology and AI should be used as the main line of defence.

It is obvious that technology has to be used. But this simply sets up a classic evolutionary game, in which both attackers and defenders are constantly changing and developing their strategies. There is no guarantee that the good guy wins. Their generative AI-developed tool will quite frequently be better than yours.

A paper just published by top Stanford economist Susan Athey and colleagues in the leading Journal of Economic Perspectives offers a different perspective. They argue that cybersecurity is fundamentally an economic as well as a technical problem. Bringing the economics in provides an additional level of defence.

Modern economies rely heavily on a small number of digital platforms, software products and technology providers. When vulnerabilities emerge in these concentrated systems, failures can affect thousands of organisations simultaneously, creating systemic cyber risk analogous to systemic risk in finance.

Regulation isn’t a silver bullet against cyberattacks

Athey and colleagues are very sceptical of highly prescriptive conventional compliance-based regulation, the immediate tool for which many policymakers instinctively reach.

Regulators typically specify a long checklist of requirements. But technology and attack methods change faster than the regulatory process.

The authors explicitly worry that EU-style detailed regulation can consume resources negotiating rules and compliance procedures without knowing whether the requirements actually generate commensurate security benefits. Further, it can so easily degenerate into a tick-box exercise in which the main aim is to satisfy the regulator rather than solve the problem.

But neither are markets

But they are also not enamoured of a much more market-based approach. Several factors mean that firms will usually under-invest in cyber security.

For example, the firm itself rarely bears the full cost of incidents, which often fall on customers and other organisations rather than the provider. In the jargon of economics, this is a negative externality. The classic example is the factory which pollutes the neighbourhood.  

Remarkably, a problem is also created by the very opposite effect, namely positive externalities. My security investment can make you safer, so there is always an incentive for you to free ride on my cybersecurity spend.

They do not pretend to have a silver bullet. But Athey and colleagues, both of whom are cyber experts, make several interesting suggestions.

They do not dismiss regulation but argue that it should be pruned to focus on the rules which produce greatest benefit relative to cost. Government should increase substantially the amount of information it provides on matters such as which products work best.  

They advocate much greater sharing by companies, through sector-specific Information Sharing and Analysis Centres and disclosure to government regulators, with commercially sensitive information protected. And given that the market will underprovide, subsidies for cyber investment are needed.

The main point is a simple one. Technology alone will not defeat cybercrime. Incentives have a key role to play.

Paul Ormerod is an honorary professor at the Alliance Business School at the University of Manchester. You can follow him on Instagram @profpaulormerod

A judge threw out the UK government’s bid to disqualify the founder and former chairman of a collapsed property development firm over allegations he knowingly breached rules to secure £400,000 in Covid-era business loans.

The government’s business department filed a disqualification order against Gary Forrest, of the High Street Group, known for constructing Newcastle’s tallest building, Hadrian’s Tower, after the firm and its eight subsidiaries entered administration and were liquidated.

In May 2020, Forrest had applied for and secured the loans, valued at £50,000 each, under the government-backed Bounce Back Loan (BBL) scheme for businesses during the pandemic, which permitted only one loan per corporate group.

In a judgment handed down on Tuesday, deputy insolvency judge Stephen Baister ruled that while Forrest had breached the rules in securing the loans, the Insolvency Service failed to prove Forrest “knew, or ought to have known” he was breaking the rules, which the government had argued.

Judge Baister said that when concluding whether Forrest “had actual knowledge” of the terms of the loan scheme he was claimed to have breached, the judge had “little difficulty in concluding that he did not” have that knowledge.

The judge, referring to the Insolvency Service’s argument, said there “is no evidence that he was given or otherwise put on notice of the terms of the BBL scheme which, as I have already observed, are not in evidence.”

‘Cavalier’ approach to loan applications

The judge said Forrest “was cavalier (even reckless)” in his approach to the loan applications, but that it “was a mistake.”

“It amounted to incompetence but not to incompetence to the marked degree necessary to make him unfit to be a director and warrant making a disqualification order,” Baister said.

“Critically, the court held that Mr Forrest neither knew, nor ought to have known, that the companies who applied for the Bounce Back Loans were breaching the terms of the Bounce Back Loan Scheme,” Vivienne Burbidge, partner at Orwins, who represented Forrest in the proceedings, told City AM.

“He made a mistake, but his conduct was not such as to make him unfit to be a director and warrant making a disqualification order,” she said, adding that “very few disqualification cases are successfully defended.”

A spokesperson for the Insolvency Service said in a statement on the ruling: “We note the court’s judgment and have nothing further to add at this point.”

Over £200m of debt left behind

The High Street Group plunged into administration in 2021, but was wound up in August 2024 after administrators could not recover any funds for creditors.

According to Companies House filings from 2024, the firm left behind an estimated £212m in debts, including £123.5m owed to secured loan note investors and nearly £1m to HMRC for overdue PAYE payments.

Administrators reported in the filings that they had recovered no assets, leaving creditors facing total losses.

City AM revealed in April 2024 that the Insolvency Service has successfully disqualified over 800 directors for misusing the loan scheme.

Why is the Treasury ignoring Milburn’s most crucial policy?

How depressing that the ink was barely dry on Alan Milburn’s flagship plan to tackle youth unemployment before the Treasury let it be known that it had no intention of implementing one of its most important recommendations.

Milburn’s review, published last week, was the result of a great deal of time, thought and intellectual effort.

As someone who opposed Rachel Reeves’ £25bn hike in employers’ National Insurance even before it was introduced, I was pleased that Milburn accepted that a central part of solving the Neets crisis was making it “easier, cheaper and less risky” for companies to hire young Britons.

This is essential, because over the past five years, the annual statutory cost of employing a full-time minimum-wage young worker in the UK – including wages, employer NI and minimum three per cent auto-enrolment pension contributions – has risen by £8,365 to £10,420 per year, depending on age. That’s an increase of up to 65 per cent.

In this context, Milburn proposed a new “bargain between government and employers”. A central part of this, he said, should involve cutting employers’ NI for workers aged 21 to 24, by doubling the annual earnings threshold at which contributions are made from £5,000 to £10,000.

The cut should start in the retail and hospitality sectors, which provide over one-third of jobs for young people, and should be phased in over five years as fiscal conditions allow. In my view, this is too little, too slow, but would at least be a start on what we need to see in terms of taxes on jobs.

However, the Treasury insisted in “private briefings” that it would not be implementing Milburn’s “hugely expensive” and untargeted National Insurance proposal, arguing that it would not be cost effective.

Frankly, this is staggering and unacceptable – particularly from the department that has caused much of the damage to young people’s job prospects. What side is the Labour government on: that of young people, or, as the Anthropic flotation makes a few people very rich and the UK bends over backwards to accommodate the growth of an AI sector that is destroying traditional job opportunities, that of Wall Street and Silicon Valley?

This is a critical test for Andy Burnham. He must overrule his Chancellor and implement the Milburn recommendations in full, starting by cutting the cost of hiring young people.

A million young British people are not in work or education, so why is Burnham handing out opportunities to Europeans? Ask Rakib Ehsan

In the same week a report warned that Britain was on the verge of losing an entire generation to worklessness, the Labour government signed a new youth mobility deal with the EU.

Under the new scheme, the UK would offer 100,000 visas a year to EU citizens, with this being reciprocated. But if Andy Burnham was so serious about achieving what report author Alan Milburn has called ‘NEET Zero’ – the goal of having every single young Briton in some form of education, employment or training – would he have signed up to such a migration partnership with the EU?

First, it should be noted that this new UK-EU youth mobility scheme is different to freedom of movement – there is an annual cap, restrictions in terms of age, and a time limit of up to three years (initially two years with a one-year extension option) on the visas. However, the allocation of 100,000 visas a year comfortably exceeds the limit of 30,000 people wanted by Burnham’s predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer. Also, there are serious concerns over the timing of the Labour government signing this migration pact with the EU, considering that the UK has nearly 1m young NEETs. According to the most recent Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures, 981,000 people aged 16-24 years are not in education, employment, and training – 13 per cent of this age group, rising to 13.7 per cent for males. There is a crisis of youth inactivity in modern Britain.

By signing up to the youth mobility pact with the EU, the UK government is essentially inviting hundreds of thousands of young Europeans to come to Britain – increasing competition for jobs in sectors such as hospitality and retail, as well as entry-level roles. Poorer EU member-states with high levels of youth unemployment and existing diaspora networks in the UK – such as Romania – are likely to be prominent countries of origin among young European people who will benefit from this new visa scheme. Increasing the supply of foreign workers willing to take lower-paid and casual roles will reduce pressure on employers to raise pay and improve working conditions for domestic candidates.

Low wages and poor conditions

While the UK-EU youth mobility pact may please some bosses in Britain who are happy to keep wages low and offer substandard working conditions, it is not in the interests of the country of large – especially younger Britons in need of opportunities. Most young British people will not be remotely interested in relocating to the EU – they would much prefer opportunities in their own country. And if they do entertain the possibility of moving abroad, they are more likely to look at Anglosphere and Commonwealth nations such as Canada, Australia, and New Zealand, along with the United States.

The UK-EU youth mobility arrangement will be characterised by asymmetrical take-up. Based on historical trends and widespread English proficiency, it is highly likely that far more EU citizens will come to the UK than the other way around – contributing towards higher net migration.

As a result of his Euro-obsession, Burnham risks betraying the localist values of his beloved ‘Manchesterism’ as well as neglecting the strong cultural ties the UK has with the English-speaking democracies of the Anglosphere. While he may enjoy the limelight of Brussels, the PM should not take the traditional Brexit voters in his constituency of Makerfield for granted. Neither should he overlook the degree of goodwill and affection which exists towards Britain, outside of Europe.

Dr Rakib Ehsan is an academic specialising in immigration and integration.

Brits are set to receive their next set of tax codes online as HMRC looks to slash its swelling postage costs and end a system that involves mailing millions of letters to taxpayers.

Roughly 3.5m people will receive their annual tax code notices electronically from February 2027, as part of the tax authority’s plans to reduce spending on paper correspondence and postage and become a digital-first office.

The body’s annual print, postage and office supplies bill exceeded £70m in the 2025/26 financial year, according to its most recent accounts.

The change applies to people already using HMRC’s Personal Tax Account or app but yet to make the transition to online notices. Around 20m taxpayers currently use this service.

Customers who do not yet use the office’s online services will continue to receive their tax code notice through the post.

Encouraging digitalisation

The move comes as HMRC shifts more information online in its bid to encourage more customers to go paperless. It has committed to saving more than £50m a year in print and post costs from the 2028/29 financial year.

The body confirmed that of the 17.5m tax codes for the 2026/27 issued ahead of 6 April 2026, 34 per cent were digital, but 11.5m were posted at a cost of more than £8.2m.

James Murray, Financial Secretary to the Treasury and Paymaster General, said: “This will modernise the service it provides and will reduce the amount of taxpayers’ money being spent on printing and postage.

“Making annual tax code notices digital by default…is the first step to reduce print and postal costs.”

Monitoring changes

Industry figures noted that moving codes online is a “logical next step” for people using the app, but warned that a failure to properly inform some taxpayers of the change may lead to more issues.

“Convenience will count for little if taxpayers miss the message,” said Joseph Adunse, tax partner at Moore Kingston Smith.

“HMRC should monitor whether people are reading notices rather than simply ignoring the alerts. Those affected first are likely to be digitally savvy, but even they face a relentless stream of app notifications and emails. Important tax notices can easily disappear into digital noise.”

HMRC said it will monitor how the affected taxpayers respond to the new approach, including whether they ultimately view their code online, contact HMRC or request a paper copy in order to inform the wider digital rollout.

On this day, 25 November 2016, Cuban revolutionary Fidel Castro passed away aged 90 years old. Castro became, and remains, the murderous dictator it’s acceptable for mainstream politicians to admire, writes Eliot Wilson

Ten years ago today, Cubavisión, the state broadcaster of the Republic of Cuba, scrambled to broadcast an unexpected address by the President of the Council of State and First Secretary of the Communist Party of Cuba, 85-year old Raúl Castro.

“With deep pain, I appear to inform our people and our friends across America and the world that today, 25 November 2016, at 10:29 p.m., the Commander-in-Chief of the Cuban Revolution, Fidel Castro Ruz, passed away… In compliance with the expressed will of Comrade Fidel, his remains will be cremated in the early hours of Saturday 26; the funeral organising committee will provide our people with detailed information on the organisation of the posthumous tribute to the founder of the Cuban Revolution. ¡Hasta la victoria siempre!”

That last phrase, “Ever onward to victory!”, had been the sign-off of Che Guevara’s letter to Fidel Castro in 1965; the Argentinian revolutionary, iconic on a million posters and T-shirts, had resigned as Minister of Industries and was leaving to spread the gospel of Marxist-Leninist revolution in Africa and South America. Two and a half years later, Guevara was dead, clumsily executed by a half-drunk sergeant from the Bolivian Rangers. But Castro still had a long way to go.

The birth of Fidel Castro

Fidel Alejandro Castro Ruz was born a century ago, the son of a wealthy farmer and self-made businessman, originally from Galicia, and his mistress and housemaid, with whom he had six other children. Castro was educated at Jesuit-run schools on Santiago de Cuba, then in 1945 he enrolled at the University of Havana to read law. Inevitably, as the son of a hard-bitten entrepreneur, he was soon immersed in radical left-wing, anti-American and anti-imperialist student politics.

That Spain, the land of his father’s birth, had been the imperial power in Cuba for nearly 400 years did not faze him. Nor was he held back by any irony in joining the Party of the Cuban People – Orthodox, the slogan of which was Vergüenza contra dinero, “Shame against money”. For the young, revolution is always a cleansing fire.

Castro never lacked ambition. Before he was 21, he was volunteering for a military operation to unseat the President and Generalissimo of the Dominican Republic, Rafael Trujillo; in 1948 he went to Bogotá, to protest at the foundation of the Organization of American States, just weeks after the assassination of the Leader of the Colombian Liberal Party, Jorge Eliécer Gaitán.

Already well known as a left-wing activist, Castro still somehow managed to graduate as a doctor of law and start a legal practice, but his intense focus was politics, and the politics of revolution. When Major General Fulgencio Batista installed himself as President in 1954, practising what he called “disciplined democracy” and fuelled by deals with US sugar and fruit exporters and the Mob, Castro was given his purpose: to oust Batista and “free” the people of Cuba, even if he had to forge a dictatorship to do it.

First impressions on the world stage

A mood was shifting. If the United States had played a many-layered game during the Second World War partly to undermine the British Empire – and it had, successfully – the heady breezes of decolonisation, both physical and economic, were gusting through the Caribbean too. This was America’s back yard, the Monroe Doctrine had said so since 1823; but the people of Cuba, like those of the Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico, Panama, Colombia, Nicaragua or Guatemala, would not in perpetuity accept the substitution of the power of the dollar for the imperial occupation by Spain.

Having spent most of the 1950s waging the Cuban Revolution, Castro arrived in Havana on 9 January 1959 in triumph. Batista had fled the previous month and Castro had wrong-footed his rival against the régime, General Eulogio Cantillo. He had won hearts and minds: the liberal lawyer Manuel Urrutia Lleó was installed as a figurehead President, but it was Castro, initially as Representative of the Rebel Armed Forces of the Presidency, who was making the decisions. A month later, he became Prime Minister, a position he would hold for 17 years before transitioning to President of the Council of State, stepping down only in 2008, into his 80s.

At first it was hard to know what to make of Castro. His image was perfect: tall and imposing, in army fatigues, with a resplendent beard and long cigar, he had charisma to spare and was a gifted orator, though as his rule went on his speeches became endurance tests. In 1960, he harangued the UN General Assembly for four-and-a-half-hours, but his record was probably 1998, when he addressed the Cuban National Assembly for seven hours and 15 minutes.

Castro did not immediately style himself as a Communist, even if the United States still had a cohort who thought that anyone to the left of Adlai Stevenson was a suspected Red. After hosting Castro in Washington in April 1959, Vice President Richard Nixon told the press cautiously, “He is either incredibly naive about Communism or under Communist discipline – my guess is the former”. But 1962 changed everything, made everything startlingly clear.

The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 is often regarded as the closest the Cold War came to running hot. One clumsy move by either side could have brought the tension to a boil. Although Nikita Khrushchev agreed to withdraw the thermonuclear medium-range ballistic missiles from Cuba, which would have cut any warning the United States might have had from hours to minutes or effectively none at all, it showed that Cuba was a dagger at the throat of America and Castro was willing to brandish it. Relations between the two countries went into deep-freeze and have yet to thaw.

Castro’s death and legacy

By the time he died, it was almost impossible to comprehend how long Castro had spent on the world stage. He had been a thorn in the side of the Eisenhower administration; Harold Macmillan was Prime Minister; and the French Fourth Republic was still in its death throes. He was backed by Khrushchev and the Soviet Union. By 2016, there were carefully worded neutral formulations from Barack Obama and Theresa May, and warm tributes from President Francois Hollande and Vladimir Putin.

President-elect Donald Trump hid nothing: “Today, the world marks the passing of a brutal dictator who oppressed his own people for nearly six decades.” His reaction on Twitter had been more concise: “Fidel Castro is dead!”

Most baffling to many is how Castro became, and remains, the murderous dictator it’s acceptable for mainstream politicians to admire and praise. Certainly the United States had been clumsy, aggressive and paranoid in its approach to Cuba. But Castro was a brutal autocrat: 4,000 executions and extrajudicial killings may seem an underachievement in today’s world, but tens of thousands were held as political prisoners in a one-party state, and in the mid-1960s something like one in 400 of the population was incarcerated for political reasons.

And Cuba is a country beggared. Nine-tenths of Cubans live in extreme poverty, pharmaceuticals are frequently absent, rationing of food has been imposed several times, the population is ageing and falling. The Covid-19 pandemic slammed into Cuba violently, slashing the vital tourism sector. Yet Fidel Castro, a dictator for nearly 50 years, is an icon to many.

Sometimes nations have to choose between freedom and prosperity. Sometimes both can be achieved. It is the tragedy of the Cuban people that they have neither. ¡Viva Cuba libre! And soon.

In Nathan Fielder’s blockbuster documentary You Can See Everything, the payment of Elizabeth Holmes and her partner becomes a crucial plot plot. Is it fair to pay criminals to appear in documentaries? We hear the case for and against in today’s Debate

YES: Producers are profiting from Elizabeth Holmes’ story, so why shouldn’t she?

Documentaries about crime are big business. You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s film about Elizabeth Holmes, is drawing crowds and acclaim. Broadcasters, producers and streaming platforms all profit from stories like hers. Yet the one person we instinctively say should not be paid is the one whose life is on screen.

That instinct deserves scrutiny. When a production company films someone with a conviction, it is using their time, their memories and their labour. Asking them to give that for nothing is not a moral stance. It is extraction. People leaving prison already face closed doors in employment, housing and finance. Denying them fair payment for genuine work only deepens the exclusion that makes reoffending more likely.

There is also a rehabilitative case. Research on desistance, including my own, shows that people move away from crime when they can build a credible new account of who they are, and when others recognise that change. A responsible documentary can be part of that process. It gives people a platform to take responsibility in public, explain how harm happened and show who they are becoming. Paying them treats that contribution as legitimate, rather than as a spectacle others cash in on.

None of this means anything goes. Payment should be transparent and proportionate. Victims should be consulted. Where compensation or confiscation orders are outstanding, those must come first. Programmes that glamorise harm should not be made at all. But a blanket ban punishes the wrong people. It lets everyone else profit from crime stories while silencing those best placed to explain them. If we believe people can change, we should be willing to pay them to tell us how.

Dr Natasha Du Rose is a senior lecturer in criminology at London Metropolitan University

NO: Payment turns crime into a commodity and compounds the harm felt by victims

On paper, this appears to be a simple question. At its core, however, we are drifting into much murkier waters.

Documentary has travelled a long way since John Grierson described it as the “creative treatment of actuality”. We are now firmly in the age of “docu-tainment”. You Can See Everything puts this debate front and centre. One of the film’s key figures, Billy Evans, reportedly received payment for his participation, although it has since been reported that he donated the fee. Evans is not himself a criminal, but as the husband of convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, any discussion of who profits from these stories quickly becomes ethically complicated.

More interestingly, maybe we should ask if You Can See Everything is a documentary at all? It is a highly stylised, performative work in which Nathan Fielder is not simply documenting reality but actively shaping it. Fielder is an actor, and that blurring of performance and actuality makes the question of payment even harder to untangle.

My answer is still no. Criminals should not profit from appearing in successful documentaries. Payment further risks turning crime into a commodity and compounds the harm experienced by victims.

But focusing solely on whether offenders get paid may distract us from a bigger question. True crime is already a lucrative industry. Streamers, distributors and production companies routinely profit from criminal acts. If criminals should not benefit from these stories, perhaps we should ask what responsibility the industry has to direct some of those profits towards victims, support services and crime prevention.

Nina Jones is an academic at the University of Birmingham with a specialism in documentary filmmaking

THE VERDICT

It’s not often we need to start this section with a spoiler warning, but we couldn’t resist framing this week’s debate around You Can See Everything, a breakout documentary from Nathan Fielder about convicted fraudster and Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, which has sparked a number of questions about the ethics of crime-based entertainment.

The payment of Holmes and her partner Billy Evans for their participation becomes a key plot point in the film, with the audience forced to confront in-cinema that they may inadvertently be financing the couple (and potentially even their new business venture). That makes for uncomfortable viewing, and while Dr Du Rose is right that the alternative also raises unease – people, especially potentially vulnerable people, should be paid for their labour – overall we feel compelled to side with Ms Jones. Surely such payment will only fuel the worrying commodification of crime. Many documentarians consider it an editorial breach to pay subjects at all, let alone criminal ones.

The cap will cover the period of 1 January until 31 March, and reflects the cost of usage for the average household.

Ofgem looked at energy costs from August to the end of November 2026 to calculate January’s cap, during which time wholesale gas prices shot up as a result of the war in Iran.

Around 10 million households on fixed tariffs will not be affected by the cap increase. 

Households under pressure

But the price has been met with backlash from the industry, who have argued it “could not have come at a worse time”.

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. What Bolt actually is today looks very different from what Villig built in 2013. Ride-hailing still accounts for the large majority of its revenue, 82 percent in 2024, according to figures reported in public company profiles of Bolt, but the company has spent the years since methodically bolting on new verticals, largely by copying its own playbook of arriving in a category cheaper and faster than the incumbent. Bolt Food launched in Tallinn in August 2019 and now operates in more than 80 cities across 20 countries with over 30,000 partner restaurants. Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. That pattern, alumni from one successful company seeding the next, is common in tech clusters generally, but it is unusually visible in a country as small as Estonia, where the total pool of experienced software engineers was never large to begin with, and where a handful of Skype veterans and their networks touch a disproportionate share of what came after. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. Annus died in 2020, but the firm he helped start is still one of the more active early-stage investors operating out of Tallinn, another channel through which Skype’s original payout kept funding whatever came next.

The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. Playtech moved its primary listing to London years ago. Skype no longer trades as an independent business at all. What the figure does capture, reliably, is how much outsized technology output a small population has produced relative to its size, whatever has happened to any individual company since, and how much of that output traces back to a single, now-defunct voice-calling app and the state’s own earlier bet on wiring its classrooms. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.
