Shipping is a separate charge paid by the buyer at checkout, even though the seller receives a prepaid label. It is close to the inverse of how rivals like Poshmark and Depop have historically operated, charging the seller a cut instead. Vinted also sells optional promotion to sellers who want more visibility: a feature called Closet Spotlight puts five of a seller’s listings into other users’ feeds for a week for a flat fee, and a per-item “bump” pushes a single listing up in search results, priced dynamically by category and demand.

From a hobby site to a logistics network

Underneath the fee structure sits a harder problem: getting a stranger’s old jumper from a seller’s flat to a buyer’s front door, cheaply and reliably, across dozens of countries. That has turned Vinted into as much a logistics company as a marketplace. According to the company’s own 2025 financial results, its delivery partner network now gives users access to more than 500,000 pick-up and drop-off points across Europe, and the company runs its own parcel carrier, Vinted Go, directly in five markets: Belgium, France, the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain. In 2025 it also opened operations in Latvia, Estonia and Slovenia, seventeen years after that first Vilnius website, extending its reach into corners of Europe the original Kleiderkreisel-era patchwork of local sites never touched.

From a free site to a billion-dollar company

The money that built out Vinted’s logistics network came in stages, and the pace of it tracks how quickly investors decided the model was working. In November 2019, the company raised €128 million in a round led by Lightspeed Venture Partners, with Accel, Insight Partners, Sprints Capital and Burda Principal Investments also participating, pushing its valuation past $1 billion for the first time and making it, according to the reporting on the round, Lithuania’s first unicorn. Lightspeed partner Brad Twohig said at the time the firm looked for “outlier management teams building generational companies,” a fairly standard line for a venture press release, but one that in this case was describing two people who had started out solving a problem for their own friends.

Two years later, in 2021, a further round led by EQT Growth brought in $303 million and roughly quadrupled the valuation again, to $4.5 billion, with the same core group of earlier investors returning. That was the last outside funding round before the company turned its first profit in 2023, at which point continued growth could increasingly be funded from the business itself rather than from new investors.

What the 2025 numbers actually show

Vinted’s first profitable year, by its own account, was 2023, when it reported revenue of €596.3 million and a net profit of €17.8 million, a milestone The Next Web covered as the company’s first since founding. Two years later, the picture is bigger but less straightforwardly better. Vinted moved €10.8 billion in gross merchandise value in 2025, up 47 percent on the year before, and took €1.1 billion of that as revenue, up 38 percent, almost double the 2023 figure. But net profit, which had grown substantially in the years after 2023, fell 19 percent in 2025 to €62 million, and adjusted EBITDA slipped 5 percent to €151 million. CEO Thomas Plantenga framed the trade-off plainly in the release: the company is spending on expansion, including a push into Germany, category diversification beyond clothing, and the launch of a payments wallet called Vinted Pay, rather than banking the growth as profit this year.

That is a company reinvesting in expansion while remaining profitable, not a company in trouble. It is worth naming the distinction because the two can look similar on a spreadsheet, and a 19 percent drop in profit reads very differently once it’s clear the company was profitable at all only two years earlier, and is still profitable now, just less so by design.

A platform built on other people’s closets

What the €10.8 billion figure represents is how far secondhand clothing has moved from a hobby into ordinary consumer behaviour across Europe. The company has said it intends to bring the same model to the United States next, according to Dealroom’s coverage of the 2025 results. Whether Vinted’s European logistics playbook, built over seventeen years and hundreds of thousands of parcel points, transfers to a market with a completely different postal and returns infrastructure is the open question the 2025 numbers don’t answer.

Rapidly changing feed content may increase task switching and decision-making, which can make scrolling feel mentally tiring.]]>

An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

The part that stays behind

Switching also leaves something on the floor. Sophie Leroy, now a professor at the University of Washington Bothell, coined the term attention residue in a 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, after experiments in which people were pulled off one task and pushed onto another. Performance on the second task dropped, because a slice of their attention was still parked on the first, and the effect was sharpest when the first task had been left unfinished.

Scrolling has the shape of that setup. Post after post is dropped mid-thought and replaced by the next one, which looks a great deal like the unfinished condition Leroy identified as the costly one. Her participants were working through lab tasks, though. The parallel to a phone is drawn by analogy, and nobody has run the experiment there.

Forty-seven seconds

Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine, has been logging how long people stay on a single screen since 2004. Back then the average was about two and a half minutes. In an interview with the University of California, she put the recent figure at roughly 47 seconds, with a median of 40, meaning half of all observed stretches were shorter than that.

That number needs handling with care. It is assembled from separate studies across two decades, not one group of people followed the whole way, and what it measures is screen behaviour. People still read long books. They just do it somewhere other than a browser tab.

Why a book behaves differently

Does the medium itself change how much gets understood? Pablo Delgado of the University of Valencia and three co-authors pooled 54 studies covering more than 171,000 participants in a meta-analysis for Educational Research Review, and found a consistent, modest advantage for paper. The gap widened when reading was timed instead of self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative ones, and grew across the years studied, an unhelpful trend for anyone expecting digital natives to close it.

Pooling dozens of experiments makes that result sturdier than any single study, though the effect itself stays small.

Maryanne Wolf, who studies the reading brain at UCLA, argues in an op-ed for the Guardian that skimming squeezes out the slower processes that make reading useful: drawing inferences, making analogies, testing whether a claim is true, stepping into another person’s point of view. Move the eye fast enough and there is no room left for any of it.

Where the tiredness comes from

Fatigue needs its own explanation, and it comes from a separate strand of Mark’s research.

In a study presented at the 2008 CHI conference, Mark, working with Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, interrupted people mid-task and measured what happened. The interrupted group finished faster, with no drop in quality, which was the surprise. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

Compensation, in other words.

The brain appears to cover the cost of fragmentation by spending harder. Mark’s participants were working rather than scrolling, and the equivalent test has not been run on a feed, so the link is suggestive rather than established. Even so, the flatness and irritability at the end of a long scroll, the vague sense of having been mugged, match what those participants described.

Which puts the whole exercise in a different light. An hour on a feed involves several hundred small decisions made at speed, each one demanding a quick ruling on what the thing is and whether it matters. The content was the least of it. The deciding was the job.

Nobody sends an invoice for that. The tiredness is the receipt.

Across five studies of secondhand-market haggling, sellers were often more candid than buyers expected. Three minutes of small talk before the haggling narrowed the gap, and so did asking buyers to think about the seller's conscience first.]]>

A pair of speakers, two years old, is up for sale online. When no music is playing, they give off an annoying static noise, and the listing does not say so.

A buyer’s message ends with a pointed question: “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” In one of the experiments built around that exact question, 85 percent of sellers mentioned the noise, and fewer buyers than that expected their seller to mention a problem.

Shira Garber and three colleagues staged a string of these secondhand sales online across five main studies and a pilot, added a second pilot that surveyed people about what drives negotiators, and reported the results in an open-access paper in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin this July. Buyers, they found, often underestimated how honest sellers would be. Sellers also reported more concern with being honest, fair and kind, and less concern with the money, than buyers credited them with.

How often did sellers come clean?

In each of the five main studies, some participants played sellers of a secondhand device with a defect they had been told about: an iPod whose battery drained fast, an electric scooter with a faulty battery, the speakers with the static. The rest played buyers, who could earn bonuses for accurately predicting how honest sellers would be.

In the first four studies, a seller counted as honest only if a reply named the defect. Staying quiet counted as dishonest, and so did a dodge like a battery that “isn’t brand new.”

The first pilot set the pattern. Of 76 online workers playing sellers, 63.2 percent picked a truthful opening message over one describing the iPod as being in excellent condition. Of 85 observers given the same information, 43.5 percent predicted the truthful one.

In Study 1, the 176 sellers wrote their own replies to “What can you tell me about it?” and “Anything else?” Of those sellers, 51.7 percent disclosed the battery problem, while the 270 buyers guessed, on average, that 43.2 percent would. With the scooter and a direct question in Study 2, three quarters of sellers disclosed the fault.

The rate swung with the setup. One cause, a direct question, got its own test; other swings the researchers could not fully explain. Until the last study, the exchanges were also largely scripted, with sellers answering pre-written buyer messages rather than a live counterpart.

The way the question is asked

Study 3, with 483 participants, gave half the sellers the pointed “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” and half the open “What can you tell me about them?” Buyers here were not told about the static, which is closer to how a real listing works.

The direct question made sellers more likely to mention the noise. Buyers’ predictions did not move with it.

The gap between expected and actual honesty was statistically significant under the direct question and not under the open one, so even inside this paper it did not show up everywhere. Of several possible reasons Study 1 still found a gap with open questions, the authors single out one: sellers there had two chances to come clean, and concealing twice may weigh more on a seller’s conscience than concealing once.

A few minutes of small talk

Study 5 was the only one that paired people live. It matched 422 participants into 211 buyer-seller pairs on an online platform, and some pairs first spent three minutes chatting about something they had enjoyed recently or how they unwind after a busy day.

Across the study, buyers rated their seller’s likely honesty at 6.56 on a ten-point scale, while coders scored the sellers’ actual replies at 7.51. Among pairs who chatted first, that difference was no longer statistically significant. Sellers’ scores did not differ significantly between the two conditions. The chat raised buyers’ expectations of honesty instead.

Study 4 tried a different nudge on 358 participants. Some buyers were asked about the seller’s moral concerns before predicting, others afterward. Thinking about the seller’s conscience first raised buyers’ expectations, and the gap was nearly halved.

It did not close. The authors suggest one reason: 85 percent of sellers in that study disclosed, a rate higher than in the matching condition of Study 3 for reasons they say are not readily apparent.

Where the suspicion comes from

Study 2 measured three motives, adding the pull of money to the two that Study 1 had tracked. The 214 management undergraduates who took part rated, on a seven-point scale, how much the seller had been weighing being decent, feeling guilty, and getting the best price. Sellers put their concern with being a decent person at 4.99, and buyers guessed 3.78. Buyers put the seller’s interest in money at 6.03; sellers reported 5.06.

The sellers still cared about the money. They cared about it less, and about their own decency more, than the buyers pictured.

The paper’s explanation leans on moral typecasting, the idea that people tend to see others as either doers or feelers, rarely both. A seller holds the object and the information, so, the authors argue, a buyer casts them as a doer, and the competitive setting makes that doer look like someone chasing an advantage rather than guarding a clean conscience. In the abstract’s words: “While sellers tended to be honest because of moral identity concerns, buyers expected them to be driven primarily by self-interest.”

Two duller explanations get a hearing too, and the authors say their own mechanism is not the only one. Poor forecasting in general, they point out, gives no reason to expect guesses to run low rather than high. Plain caution, a buyer bracing for the worst to avoid a loss, gets mixed treatment: the Study 4 discussion offers it as a possible added force, while the general discussion says it cannot explain the results, because in the first pilot observers with nothing at stake still underestimated the sellers.

Their mediation analyses deserve a lighter touch than the abstract’s sentence suggests. Buyers and sellers answered parallel versions of the motive questions rather than the same ones, and the authors say the results should be “cautiously interpreted” for that reason. Sellers rated their motives after choosing whether to disclose, which leaves room for a flattering story told afterward, though the authors argue buyers’ parallel ratings may reduce that concern. And in Study 1, the measure of anticipated guilt and related feelings showed no significant difference between buyers and sellers.

Small stakes, narrow scope

The stakes stayed small. Most bonuses were paid by lottery, and a seller in Study 1 had a five percent chance of earning at most $7. The authors grant that low stakes may keep self-interest from fully switching on, while citing earlier work that finds self-interest at work even when stakes are small.

The honesty studied was one kind: telling a buyer about a defect the seller knew. Misrepresenting a bottom price or inventing urgency, both named by the authors, were outside the design. They describe the findings as “based primarily on Western participant samples,” and the sales were one-off exchanges between strangers, chosen to keep reputation largely out of play. Ongoing work relationships and repeat customers sit outside what was measured.

Suspicion is sometimes the sensible response, and the paper says so. A buyer facing a salesperson expected to use persuasion tactics, or shopping where one side knows far more than the other, as with used cars, has good reason for care. The paper does not argue for trusting everyone. It asks for work on when doubting a counterpart’s honesty hurts a negotiator and when it protects one.

Every finding in this piece comes from the published text and tables of one paper, read by an editorial desk that reports on research and does not train negotiators; the supplementary files the paper points to could not be opened. The studies compared predictions with replies across hundreds of people, which says something about buyers and sellers like the ones studied, taken as groups, and cannot tell anyone whether the particular seller in their inbox is being straight with them. For a purchase that matters, sensible safeguards include an independent inspection, a written description of the item’s condition, and the buyer protection some platforms offer.

This paper did not measure what the gap costs. The authors’ illustration is a used car that looks too good to be true, and a buyer who distrusts the seller, walks away, and settles for something worse. Examining what the honesty gap does to the outcomes of negotiations is what they call an important next step; they also call for testing the idea where far more money is at stake.

]]> Quote of the day: “Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself” https://siliconcanals.com/d-quote-of-the-day-sometimes-you-find-yourself-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-and-sometimes-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-you-find-yourself/ Thu, 17 Sep 2026 10:45:39 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109380

What happens when your plans collapse, your phone dies, and you're stranded at a gas station thousands of miles from home—and it's the best thing that could've happened.]]>

The last time I was properly lost, I was standing at a petrol station somewhere north of Chiang Rai with a dead phone, a warm bottle of water and a dog who clearly ran the place. My bus had left without me. I had four hours to wait, nothing to do and no way to tell anyone about it.

It was the calmest I had been in about eighteen months.

Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself.

Yes, it is the sort of line that ends up engraved on a bracelet and screwed to somebody’s kitchen wall. Both of which have happened, it turns out. I went looking for whoever wrote it and found nothing, only evidence that it has been circulating since at least 2014 with no author attached. Anonymous, then. It holds up better than most things sold at a craft market.

Nowhere is mostly an absence of audience

Here is what I think the line is really about. Nowhere has very little to do with distance. It is any situation where nobody knows your job title.

In a city you are surrounded by people who already have a version of you loaded. The neighbour who thinks you are the loud one. The old colleague who still introduces you by the thing you did in 2019. You end up performing that version without noticing, because it is easier than correcting everybody.

Take the audience away and something odd happens. For a day or two you feel faintly useless, because nobody needs anything from you. Then the noise drops. You start hearing your own opinions, which are less impressive and a good deal more honest than the ones you say out loud.

That is the whole mechanism. No mysticism required.

The year my diary went blank

I lost my business, restaurants, during the pandemic. The deal was agreed over a phone call while I sat on a plastic chair in a dining room with the lights off, and it was the least bad option available to me at the time.

For years my day had been decided for me by suppliers, staff rotas and the seven o’clock rush. Then it was not. I woke up on a Tuesday with an empty calendar and genuinely no idea what a Tuesday was for.

I would love to tell you this was peaceful. I reorganised the same cupboard twice. I developed strong opinions about a neighbour’s parking. I rang people I had not spoken to in five years and could hear them wondering what I wanted.

The useful part arrived about three months in, once I had run out of things to tidy. With no restaurant to point at, I had to work out what I would actually do with a day if nobody was paying me for it. The answer was writing, which was inconvenient, as it pays considerably worse than a burger.

You can get lost for the price of a bus ticket

You do not need to sell a business or fly to Patagonia. Nowhere comes in small doses and most of them are free.

Pick a district of your own city you have no reason to visit and spend three hours there on foot. Not a famous one. A dull one, with hardware shops and a wet market and nothing on sale to anyone carrying a suitcase. I do this in Bangkok about once a month and I have never regretted it, though I have frequently regretted the shoes.

Go somewhere your phone cannot help you. Not switched off, just outgunned: the lanes are not on the map and the only language on offer is one you do not speak.

Be a beginner at something in public. Take a class where you are visibly the worst person in the room. It is physically uncomfortable for about twenty minutes. After that it stops mattering, and what is left is quite close to fun.

And if you do travel, leave one day entirely unplanned. No booking, no list, no reservation you have to walk fast to reach. Most people schedule a trip so tightly that they never get further than a warmer version of their normal week.

What actually turns up

Let me manage expectations. You do not come back from a petrol station with a revelation.

What you come back with is a shorter list. Two or three things you thought you cared about turn out to belong to somebody else. One or two things you have never mentioned to anyone are suddenly all you think about when there is nothing else to think about. That is it. It looks like very little on paper. It does not feel that way at thirty-eight, when you are still doing a job you picked at twenty-two to impress someone who stopped watching years ago.

There is a trap in this, though. Some people use the middle of nowhere as somewhere to hide, and the giveaway is that they keep having to go back. If every trip is an escape from the same unaddressed thing at home, the scenery is doing the work of a conversation you have been avoiding. Distance is excellent for seeing a problem clearly. It has never once solved one for me.

The dog at the petrol station, for the record, took no interest in any of this. He sat under the ice cabinet, moved twice in four hours, and had evidently worked something out about Wednesdays that I am still catching up on.

Chronic offense-taking isn't performative outrage—it's a trauma response masquerading as oversensitivity.]]>

I used to think of a certain kind of person as a weather system. You know the type. You ask how the traffic was and somehow you have insulted their driving, their neighbourhood and their late mother. Everything lands as a slight. Everything requires a correction.

For years my take on this was simple and a bit smug. Attention seekers. People who enjoy the theatre of being wronged.

Then I started reading the actual psychology, and it turns out I had the story backwards. The people who seem offended by everything are rarely shopping for a fight. Most of them are running a security detail, and they have been running it since they were small.

When insults were the weather, everything looks like an insult

Here is the mechanism. If you grow up somewhere that regularly treats you as a target, your brain gets very good at spotting incoming fire. That is not a flaw. In the original environment it was survival. The problem is that the skill does not switch off when you move somewhere safer.

Psychologists call this hostile attribution bias, and it shows up early. Researchers followed around 1,300 children across nine countries and gave them scenarios where someone’s behaviour could be read as an accident or as deliberate. A shove in a corridor. A joke that could go either way. The children who consistently read hostile intent went on to show higher rates of persistent aggressive behaviour, even after accounting for how aggressive they had already been.

Two children see the same shove. One files it under accident, one files it under attack. Twenty years later, one of them is the adult who somehow takes offence at the weather report.

Being told you are too much is its own training

The other route in is quieter and I suspect more common.

Some people are not knocked around. They are simply corrected, constantly, about their own inner life. You are not upset. You are not tired. That did not hurt. Stop being dramatic. Clinicians call this an invalidating environment, a setting that consistently dismisses or punishes someone for expressing what they feel or need.

The theory behind that term was built to explain a specific clinical picture, so I would not go throwing it at your touchy colleague as a diagnosis. But the underlying logic travels. If your read on your own experience gets overruled a thousand times, you learn something ugly. You learn that your sense of things will not be taken seriously unless you make it loud.

And making it loud is exactly what the rest of us punish. We call it oversensitivity. We are reading the receipt and ignoring the purchase.

The tax the sensitive person pays

None of this is a free pass, and here is where it stops being sympathetic.

Researchers describe a disposition they call rejection sensitivity, meaning a tendency to anxiously expect rejection, spot it readily, and react hard when you think you have found it. People high in it tend to be less satisfied in their close relationships, and their partners report the same.

The trap is that the vigilance manufactures the thing it fears. You brace for the cold shoulder, so you go cold first. Your partner feels the chill and pulls back. Now you have evidence. Now the system that was built to protect your dignity has quietly started demolishing it.

I have watched this happen up close, over what I promise you was a genuinely neutral text message. There was no villain in that story. There was a very old alarm and a very ordinary Tuesday.

What actually helps when you are on the receiving end

Arguing about whether the offence was reasonable is a losing game. The alarm is not calibrated to this conversation. It was calibrated years ago, by somebody else.

Try naming the feeling without conceding the facts. Something like: I can see that landed badly, and I did not mean it that way. That costs you nothing on the question of intent, and it grants them something rare, which is agreement that their reaction was real. It does more work than an hour of you proving your innocence.

Be boringly consistent. Vigilance responds to evidence, not reassurance, and that takes months. You cannot talk someone out of a threat detector. You can only give it a long run of days where nothing bad happens.

And hold your line anyway. Understanding why someone snaps is not the same as accepting being snapped at. You can say plainly that you will not be shouted at and still mean everything above.

And if the thin skin is yours

Then start somewhere other than whether you were right. You often are. Slights are real, and some of the people telling you to calm down are exactly the ones worth watching.

The more useful question is what the alertness is costing you. Running security is expensive. It eats your Sundays. It makes you rehearse conversations that never happen and re-read messages for tone that was never there. My grandmother had a version of this. It made her formidable company. I think it also made her lonely.

So build a delay. When something lands wrong, wait a day before you respond. Graciousness has nothing to do with it. You are checking whether the feeling survives a night’s sleep. Usually it does not. The ones that do are worth taking seriously, and now you can take them seriously without the static.

]]>

The Go2 quadruped robot from Unitree, a prominent Chinese robot developer. | Source: Unitree

The FCC is right to treat connected robots as a security issue. Its recent action restricting foreign-produced advanced robotic devices reflects a real risk. These machines carry cameras and sensors, transmit data, take remote software updates, and make their own decisions inside factories, warehouses, stores, and airports.

But where a robot was assembled tells you little about who controls it once it’s deployed. A robot built entirely in the United States, with unsigned updates and open remote access, is a bigger risk than one built overseas with secure software. The real security boundary is the code, the data, and whoever can change them, not the chassis.

The FCC has already recognized this. Its definition of a covered device relies on software: firmware and AI or machine-learning model weights that control navigation, perception, data collection, and remote command and control. The agency has identified the layer that matters. The next step is to turn that critical layer into the standard.

Brain Corp builds autonomy software, so of course I think software deserves scrutiny. But that’s also why I know where the risk lives. Our technology runs more than 50,000 robots on six continents and has logged more than 25 million hours of autonomous operation. At that scale, the failures that matter are rarely in the hardware. They’re in how software gets updated, who can reach the machine, and what happens when it meets a situation nobody anticipated.

Regulate control, not just origin

Software provenance alone can’t mean where the code was written. Robots run on open-source libraries, globally trained models, and international engineering teams. What should matter is provenance of control, demonstrated rather than declared. Any robot deployed in a sensitive or public setting, wherever its parts came from, should be able to show:

  • Who can push code to it, and that every update is signed and verified before it runs.
  • That unauthorized code can’t execute.
  • Where its data goes, where it’s processed, and who can access it.
  • How remote access is granted, logged, and revoked.
  • How quickly a newly discovered vulnerability can be patched across the entire fleet.
  • An independent safety layer that the AI cannot override.
  • Independent audits and certifications that back up all of the above.
Submit your innovation now!

AI can be probabilistic. Physical safety can’t be.

The safety layer deserves emphasis, because AI is changing what robots can do faster than policy is changing how we judge them. When a chatbot gets something wrong, the result is a bad answer. When a robot gets something wrong, it could generate unsafe behavior in a crowded aisle or beside a worker.

AI models will make robots far more capable, but they shouldn’t be the final authority over physical behavior. Robots need deterministic constraints beneath the intelligence layer. If a model proposes an unsafe action, an independent mechanism must stop it, and sensor data should check the model’s reading of the world rather than defer to it.

The more sophisticated the models become, the more this separation matters, and the more it belongs in any serious security standard.

The next step

The industry doesn’t need to wait for regulators to adopt these standards. Developers can publish how their systems meet them today, and enterprise buyers can require them in procurement. But voluntary practice is no substitute for a clear rule.

The FCC has already recognized that a robot is defined by its software. The next step is to regulate it that way: not just where the parts were made, but who controls the code.

About the Author

David Pinn assumed the role of CEO at Brain Corp in 2022, where he has held various executive positions since joining in 2017, including chief strategy officer and chief financial officer. During his tenure, Pinn was instrumental in leading Brain Corp’s transformation from a robotics hardware company to a software as a service (SaaS) provider. He played a pivotal role in securing over $100 million in funding from prominent investors such as the SoftBank Vision Fund, Qualcomm Ventures, Hercules Capital, ClearBridge Investments, and Satwik Ventures.

Prior to joining Brain Corp, Pinn served as head of finance for Antenna79, a technology startup backed by L Catterton, the world’s largest consumer-focused private equity group, where he facilitated the raising of $94.9 million in private equity funding. Before his tenure at Antenna79, Pinn co-founded Snaptracs, Qualcomm’s consumer electronics subsidiary. Under his leadership, Snaptracs was successfully sold, leading to a merger with Whistle and a $117 million acquisition by Mars.

Pinn holds a Bachelor of Science degree in Electrical Engineering from the University of Texas at Austin and a Master’s in Business Administration from the University of California, Berkeley, Haas School of Business.

SoftBank has completed its acquisition of the Robotics and AI Institute (RAI) from Hyundai Motor Group, The Robot Report has learned. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. SoftBank responded to emailed questions from The Robot Report about the acquisition, but it declined to comment.

The Robot Report first reported the acquisition agreement in September 2026. The deal adds another prominent name to SoftBank’s growing portfolio of robotics companies.

Boston Dynamics founder Marc Raibert founded the RAI Institute in 2022 with more than $400 million in initial funding from Hyundai. Based in Cambridge, Mass., the institute focuses on solving fundamental challenges in robotics, including mobility, manipulation, perception, and intelligence.

RAI is also looking to expand its team. It currently has 24 open positions, including internships, across its offices in Cambridge and Zurich, Switzerland. The openings cover a range of technologies, including robot learning, manipulation, simulation, navigation, and hardware engineering.

SoftBank continues to build its robotics portfolio

The acquisition reunites SoftBank and Raibert. SoftBank acquired Boston Dynamics from Alphabet in 2017 before selling a controlling stake to Hyundai in 2021 in a deal that valued the robotics company at $1.1 billion.

Hyundai recently acquired SoftBank’s remaining 9.65% stake in Boston Dynamics, giving Hyundai Motor Group and its executive chairman full ownership of the robotics company. The deal marks the end of SoftBank’s nearly decade-long investment in Boston Dynamics.

SoftBank has since acquired or invested in a number of robotics companies, including 1X Technologies, Agile Robots, AutoStore, BALYO, Berkshire Grey, Brain Corp, Skild AI, and Symbotic.

It will be interesting to see how much collaboration takes place between the RAI and some of these companies. There are potential synergies, for example, between the research being done at the institute and the technologies being developed by Skild AI and Agile Robots.

It’s unclear whether SoftBank’s ownership will change the institute’s research priorities or whether it will continue to operate independently.

The deal also comes at a time when SoftBank’s planned $5.375 billion acquisition of ABB Robotics faces an uncertain future. Chinese regulators blocked the acquisition of ABB’s robotics business in China, putting the deal in jeopardy.

So much for robotics being in its post-Jensen Huang era. Just 11 days after his resignation amid allegations of personal misconduct and concerns about potential national security risks involving China, NVIDIA has reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO.

The company announced today that its board of directors unanimously voted to bring Huang back. Huang also returns to NVIDIA’s board, effective immediately.

NVIDIA said the board was satisfied with Huang’s candor and ability to lead the company. It also consulted with senior U.S. government officials before determining that his reinstatement poses no national security risk.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey Jones, NVIDIA’s board chair.

The decision marks a dramatic reversal for NVIDIA. During the company’s earnings call on Nov. 17, Jones explicitly ruled out bringing Huang back, saying the board had unanimously accepted his resignation and did not intend to reinstate him. Just six days later, the board unanimously voted to restore Huang to the position he had held since co-founding NVIDIA in 1993.

The reversal followed growing pressure from President Donald Trump, NVIDIA employees, investors and prominent technology executives. Trump publicly supported Huang’s potential return on Nov. 16, saying he would not object to his reinstatement. On Sunday, Nov. 22, Trump again urged NVIDIA’s board to bring Huang back.

Meanwhile, a “Stand With Jensen” petition attracted more than 200,000 signatures, including support from current and former NVIDIA employees, investors and technology leaders such as Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney.

NVIDIA also faced considerable financial uncertainty following Huang’s departure, with its market value falling sharply and questions emerging about who could replace an executive who had led the company for more than three decades.

It remains unclear precisely what persuaded the board to reverse course. NVIDIA did not identify which government officials were consulted or disclose what information they provided. The company also did not say whether the public campaign influenced its decision.

Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO following Huang’s resignation, will continue in her role as chief financial officer. Jones will remain board chair.

Robotics and physical AI companies have raised nearly $48 billion so far in 2026, but the rollout of fully autonomous machines in industrial settings isn’t a given. For robots to step beyond controlled environments onto the manufacturing floor, they need real-world data to learn from.

Most production facilities aren’t set up to provide it.

Consider the welding process. For a robot to improve its technique autonomously, it needs to understand how changes in welding angle, travel speed, workpiece position, and other key parameters affect the finished result. Experienced technicians develop this understanding through years of hands-on experience, but much of that knowledge isn’t captured in a form robotics partners can use to train autonomous systems.

Similar gaps exist in other manufacturing processes where technicians rely on experience to make adjustments that aren’t consistently documented.
Manufacturers looking to deploy physical AI need to close this data gap. Without information connecting process decisions to production outcomes, even sophisticated robotic systems may struggle to adapt to changing conditions.

These limitations could prevent manufacturers from achieving the efficiency and quality improvements they expect from physical AI.

Why industrial data remains a barrier to physical AI

Manufacturers already collect extensive operational data, but much of it was never structured for autonomous learning. Sometimes it is collected and never even reviewed at all!

Relevant contextual information often sits in separate systems. A machine may record operating parameters while a quality management system captures inspection results, making it difficult to connect process decisions with finished-part quality.

Manufacturing leaders are increasingly aware that these silos are an obstacle. According to the Manufacturing Leadership Council’s 2026 Smart Factories and Digital Production Survey, 37% of surveyed manufacturers cited a lack of data interoperability as a major roadblock to implementing their smart factory strategies, up from 22% in 2025.

However, improving interoperability alone won’t get robots the data they need to learn. Manufacturers also need to ensure that production records can be tied to measurable quality outcomes.

Submit your innovation now!

3 ways manufacturers can prepare for physical AI

Preparing a factory for physical AI requires more than collecting additional data or connecting disparate systems. Manufacturers need to understand what information their robotic systems will rely on, how that data reflects real production conditions and whether it can help systems make reliable adjustments over time.

Addressing these questions early, in collaboration with robotics partners, can help manufacturers identify gaps in their existing infrastructure and focus investments where they’ll have the greatest impact.

Here are three areas to prioritize before deployment.

1. Capture data that reflects real production conditions

Begin by identifying the production conditions your robotic systems need to recognize and respond to. Focus on capturing the complex interactions between the process parameters and quality outcomes to show how planned and unplanned changes in materials or equipment performance affect the finished product.

Consider metal additive manufacturing, where factors like powder (or wire) characteristics, processing temperatures, and environmental conditions can influence a component’s final properties and characteristic defect structure. Connecting these variables with inspection results gives your robotics partners a clearer picture of which conditions contribute to defects or variations in quality.

You can then use that information to train systems to recognize changing production conditions and develop more realistic simulations for testing their responses.

2. Connect data across the entire production process

The data you capture won’t have much value if it remains isolated within individual machines or production stages. The next step is to create a digital thread that connects production conditions with inspection results and finished-part quality.

I’ve seen this challenge firsthand in advanced manufacturing. AI-based image recognition is becoming table stakes for assessing quality within metal additive manufacturing printers, while downstream equipment such as heat-treatment furnaces may be far more difficult to integrate into the same system. Lior Susan of Eclipse rightly says: “If your physical asset isn’t generating real-time operational data, it’s a dead asset.”

The disconnect creates gaps in the production history of a component, making it harder to understand how subsequent processing affects its final properties.

To close those gaps, you need to connect equipment and quality management systems that weren’t designed to communicate. Start by identifying the data needed for a specific robotic application, then work with technology partners to establish consistent part identifiers and link process records to inspection results in a true digital thread.

By starting with a targeted application, you can build the data connections to support physical AI without having to overhaul your entire production infrastructure at once.

Submit your innovation now!

3. Build feedback loops around quality and repeatability

Finally, establish how autonomous systems will be evaluated and when human oversight is required. Work with your robotics partners to identify which process adjustments can be made automatically and how the system will determine whether those changes improved production outcomes.

In medical device manufacturing, for example, regulatory requirements often mandate validation of production processes to ensure consistent product quality. Changes to those processes may require additional testing and revalidation, limiting how freely AI systems can modify production parameters.

Before authorizing autonomous adjustments, work with your robotics partners to define acceptable operating limits and establish how the system will verify results.

Also develop clear criteria for when an unexpected outcome requires engineering review. A system that can modify operating parameters but can’t evaluate the resulting quality is not ready to make those decisions independently.

Preparing manufacturing data for industrial autonomy

As you evaluate data infrastructure investments, determine whether they will support your physical AI goals. Before adding more sensors or connecting another piece of equipment, have a plan for how the resulting information will help explain how a process adjustment affects product quality.

Where that connection is missing, you may get more value from linking existing process records to inspection results than from collecting additional machine data.

Industrial autonomy won’t depend on how much data manufacturers collect, but on whether their robotic systems are actually leveraging that data to make reliable decisions on the factory floor.

Jensen Huang keynote at CES 2025. | Credit: NVIDIA

Days before Christmas in 2023, Serve Robotics was on the verge of bankruptcy. A major investor pulled out of a committed funding round, leaving the developer of sidewalk delivery robots unable to make payroll and just days away from running out of cash.

With few options remaining, Serve Robotics co-founder and CEO Ali Kashani reached out to NVIDIA co-founder Jensen Huang. “We spoke at 6 a.m. the next day, and later that day I was having dinner with his executive team to find a way to bridge the company,” recalled Kashani. “Within days, they led a financing round that brought us back to life.”

Four months later, Serve Robotics was ringing the bell at Nasdaq to celebrate its public listing.

“I have heard similar stories from many other founders, as well as current and former NVIDIA employees, whose lives Jensen’s actions have changed,” Kashani said.

Over the past several years, few people outside the robotics industry have done more than Huang to elevate its profile.

Clad in his signature black leather jacket, Huang routinely dedicated portions of his marathon keynotes to robotics. He showcased humanoids on stage, introduced development tools, highlighted startups, championed open models and research, and made the case that robots would transform the world.

He also put NVIDIA’s money behind that vision.

Now, one of robotics’ most influential advocates is gone. NVIDIA’s board accepted Huang’s resignation on Nov. 12, and CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent successor.

A large stage for robotics

For an industry that spent decades fighting for mainstream recognition, Huang provided something few robotics executives could: one of the biggest stages in technology.

“Jensen was fantastic in painting the vision,” said Yaro Tenzer, co-founder and CEO of RightHand Robotics.

Tenzer said Huang helped expand investors’ imaginations about what robotics could become.

NVIDIA said during its third-quarter earnings call that its physical AI revenue nearly tripled year over year and is on track to exceed $25 billion in fiscal 2027. While that represents a sizable and rapidly growing business, it still accounts for only about 6% of NVIDIA’s projected annual revenue of more than $400 billion. And physical AI encompasses more than robotics.

The attention Huang afforded robotics was disproportionate to its short-term commercial contribution.

“NVIDIA introduced its Isaac robotics platform back in 2017, and Jensen kept robotics in his keynotes and in the company’s long-term story year after year,” said Deepak Jayaraj, vice president of hardware engineering and manufacturing at agricultural robotics developer Four Growers. “I think that steady attention made it easier for founders to make the case to investors.”

Unlike Tesla CEO Elon Musk, whose robotics advocacy is largely centered on his own company’s products, Huang promoted an ecosystem of developers, many of whom compete directly with one another.

NVIDIA stood to benefit financially regardless of which robotics companies succeeded. But that business model also positioned Huang to become an advocate for the broader industry.

Providing infrastructure

Perhaps NVIDIA’s lasting contribution to robotics will be the development infrastructure it built under Huang. Its portfolio spans much of the robotics development stack, from GPUs and CUDA for AI training to Omniverse and Isaac Sim for simulation, Isaac Lab for robot learning, GR00T and Cosmos foundation models, Isaac ROS software, and Jetson embedded computing.

Jan Zizka, co-founder and CEO of warehouse robotics developer Brightpick and co-founder of machine vision specialist Photoneo, experienced NVIDIA’s impact firsthand. Zizka said Photoneo participated in an early-access program for NVIDIA’s Jetson TX1 computing platform.

“He was almost pushing the market to make it happen,” Zizka said, pointing to Huang’s willingness to invest in emerging markets before demand fully materialized.

NVIDIA’s investments in open research and software helped lower barriers to entry for developers. Zizka noted that its efforts in embedded computing also encouraged competitors, including AMD and Qualcomm, to pursue robotics opportunities.

Under Huang, NVIDIA became one of robotics’ most prominent strategic investors, backing companies including Figure AI, NEURA Robotics, Skild AI, Wayve, Waabi, and Serve Robotics. Beyond capital, an investment from NVIDIA provided an endorsement that could help startups attract additional investors, employees, and customers.

“Jensen’s style will be hard to copy,” said Jayaraj. “I’d judge whomever it is by which robotics programs they keep funding.”

“NVIDIA has a business reason to stay in, since many robot companies train and simulate on its compute long before they ship at scale,” he added. “The keynote time and the early bets on young teams are the parts that could fade.”

Losing an advocate inside NVIDIA

Huang’s enthusiasm for robotics was perhaps just as valuable inside NVIDIA as it was outside the company. Its robotics teams had an advocate at the highest level of the organization. Having earned considerable credibility with investors through previous long-term bets, Huang enjoyed a latitude his successor might not.

NVIDIA’s next CEO will also inherit growing competition in its core data center business and potentially greater political and regulatory scrutiny following the Democrats’ strong performance in the midterm elections.

Robert Little, co-founder and former CEO of ATI Industrial Automation, is particularly concerned about how opposition to data center construction could affect NVIDIA’s ability to fund its longer-term investments.

“Robotics is being propped up from the money that’s being created in the data centers for NVIDIA that affords NVIDIA to have a team of people developing product for robotics,” Little said.

If growth in that business slows, NVIDIA’s willingness to fund robotics research, product development, and strategic investments could be tested.

“What’s the first thing you do when you start to see a negative financial situation? You cut anything that’s not making money,” Little said.

Conversely, those pressures could make diversifying NVIDIA’s business even more important.

One early indicator of NVIDIA’s strategic priorities could be its pending $12.9 billion acquisition of Hugging Face, whose LeRobot initiative has become an important resource for robotics developers. Whether NVIDIA follows through on the deal will be worth watching, although regulatory hurdles could also influence its outcome.

NVIDIA has not responded to multiple requests for comment from The Robot Report about its robotics strategy following Huang’s departure. If we hear back, we will update this story. Huang’s son, Spencer, remains at NVIDIA, where he has worked for the past four and a half years. He has served as director of product management for robotics for the past 9 months.

The robotics flywheel is already spinning

Despite his concerns about NVIDIA’s data center business, Little believes the robotics industry has enough momentum to withstand the departure of any individual.

“The flywheel has been created and it is spinning now,” Little said. “We’re too far in. The momentum has been created, and now it’ll just carry itself through.”

Google DeepMind, Physical Intelligence, Generalist, Skild AI and many others are developing their own approaches to robot intelligence. Semiconductor companies are looking to challenge NVIDIA in embedded computing. Little argued that a less aggressive NVIDIA could benefit competing technology providers. And if robotics researchers and engineers were to leave NVIDIA, their expertise would likely find its way to other companies.

Tenzer similarly believes the physical AI movement has established considerable momentum.

“The foundations are there,” Tenzer said. “I think that things are really accelerating, and you can clearly see it.”

Zizka is more cautious, particularly about the potential ripple effects of disrupting the relationships and trust Huang helped build across the technology ecosystem.

“The best possible case is that it will continue,” Zizka said. “But I think this is a negative.”

Putting humanoids to the test

The bigger test, according to Tenzer, might come 12 months from now. Many humanoid developers have raised substantial funding based on expectations that advances in AI will unlock multi-purpose humanoids for industrial use.

“I think for the next year, maybe it will be fine,” Tenzer said. “But then I think a lot of these companies will struggle with showing actual use cases and real business.”

As companies return to investors seeking additional capital, Tenzer expects some of the enthusiasm surrounding humanoids to dissipate if commercial progress falls short of expectations.

“Somebody needs to get on that stage and show some of the cool things that are happening and have this charisma and have the ability to do it,” Tenzer said. “I think this is where Jensen will be missed.”

As with the autonomous vehicle investment boom, even failed humanoid startups could leave behind advances in manipulation, actuation, sensing, and robot learning that benefit the broader industry.

“Funding is where I’d watch first, especially for humanoid companies whose business case depends on breakthroughs that are still years out,” said Jayaraj. “Jensen’s advocacy gave those bets a lot of credibility.”

“Founders should ask how much of their plan rests on informal support or tools that haven’t shipped yet, because that kind of support can walk out the door with one person.”

Huang helped give companies such as Serve Robotics a chance to prove what was possible. With robotics enjoying unprecedented attention and investment, the industry’s next challenge is turning that attention into sustainable businesses.

Supervised autonomous UAV inspection at an industrial facility. | Source: ZenaDrone

An autonomous drone can complete a carefully planned inspection route in a controlled environment and still struggle with the same route at an operating industrial facility. A steel structure may obstruct satellite signals, reflective equipment may distort depth measurements, and a wind gust may push the aircraft outside its planned trajectory. Each disturbance can be manageable in isolation. The difficulty emerges when several occur simultaneously. 

This exposes a fundamental challenge in industrial drone autonomy: performance depends on interactions between subsystems whose assumptions are rarely independent. 

A navigation algorithm may estimate position accurately under favorable sensing conditions. An obstacle detector may identify nearby structures during controlled testing. A flight controller may maintain stable tracking under a nominal payload. None of these results independently establishes that the integrated system can safely complete an inspection near energized infrastructure, confined structures, or operating machinery. 

Reliable deployment requires engineers to understand how uncertainty propagates through localization, perception, planning, control, and inspection-data acquisition. It also requires evidence that the system can recognize when its estimates are no longer trustworthy. 

Why industrial environments challenge autonomous navigation 

Industrial facilities introduce environmental conditions that are difficult to reproduce in laboratory demonstrations. 

Metallic surfaces, repetitive structural patterns, narrow access corridors, moving equipment, airborne particulates, and changing illumination can affect multiple sensors simultaneously. These conditions create both geometric constraints and uncertainty in the information available to the autonomy system. 

Consider a hypothetical UAV inspecting pipework beside a steel-framed processing facility. 

As the aircraft approaches the structure, GNSS measurements become less reliable. Repetitive pipes complicate visual feature matching, while reflective surfaces produce inconsistent depth observations. Meanwhile, the flight controller must reject aerodynamic disturbances caused by nearby structures. 

The resulting problem is not simply inaccurate positioning. The autonomy stack must decide whether its remaining localization confidence supports continued flight, whether detected free space is sufficiently reliable, and whether the planned maneuver remains dynamically feasible. 

These decisions are coupled. A localization error can corrupt obstacle coordinates, while a delayed perception update can cause the planner to act on geometry that no longer represents the aircraft’s surroundings. 

The practical engineering objective is therefore not uninterrupted autonomous operation under every condition. It is predictable behavior within a defined operational envelope, including when that envelope is exceeded. 

GNSS limitations and the localization problem 

Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) positioning provides an important absolute reference for outdoor autonomous UAV navigation. However, industrial structures introduce several failure mechanisms. 

Buildings, tanks, and overhead equipment can block direct satellite signals. Reflections from metallic surfaces create multipath interference, causing a receiver to process signals that have traveled indirect paths. 

Real-time kinematic (RTK) positioning can improve accuracy by using carrier-phase measurements and correction data. However, RTK does not eliminate obstruction, multipath, cycle slips, or poor satellite geometry. A fixed ambiguity solution should not be treated as an unconditional guarantee of accurate positioning. 

Combining absolute and relative localization

An inertial measurement unit (IMU) estimates angular velocity and specific force. Integrated inertial measurements support high-frequency motion propagation, but bias and noise cause errors to accumulate over time. 

Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) combines camera observations with inertial measurements to estimate relative motion. Published work such as VINS-Mono demonstrates nonlinear optimization approaches that integrate visual and inertial constraints for state estimation. 

Lidar-based odometry provides another approach, using geometric correspondence between successive scans. LIO-SAM, for example, combines lidar and inertial measurements in a factor-graph framework with mapping and loop-closure capabilities. 

These approaches have different weaknesses. Visual methods depend on illumination, image quality, and observable features. Lidar methods can struggle with insufficient geometric constraints, adverse returns, or sensor-specific limitations. 

Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) additionally maintains a representation of the environment while estimating the robot’s pose. Loop closure can correct accumulated trajectory drift when a previously visited location is recognized, although incorrect associations can introduce significant map errors. 

For industrial UAVs, engineers must also distinguish local consistency from global accuracy. A drone may maintain a stable relative trajectory while its estimated position gradually diverges from the facility’s surveyed coordinate system. 

This distinction becomes critical when an inspection requires repeatable measurements at known asset locations. 

Obstacle avoidance is more than detecting objects 

Obstacle avoidance is often described as a perception problem. In operational UAV systems, it is an end-to-end timing and control problem. 

A typical pipeline must acquire sensor measurements, estimate obstacle geometry, update the local environment representation, generate a collision-free trajectory, and issue commands that the aircraft can physically execute. 

Each stage introduces latency and uncertainty. 

Sensor limitations affect the available flight envelope 

Lidar provides active range measurements and can support geometric mapping under varying visible-light conditions. However, transparent materials, highly reflective surfaces, thin wires, and unfavorable incidence angles can produce missing or misleading returns. 

Stereo vision estimates depth from image correspondence. Its performance depends on camera geometry, texture, illumination, and disparity estimation. Depth uncertainty generally increases with distance for a fixed stereo baseline and disparity uncertainty. 

Active depth cameras introduce their own range, illumination, interference, and surface-response constraints. 

No single sensing modality provides reliable coverage of every industrial obstacle. A practical design must account for sensor field of view, blind regions, minimum detection range, and the possibility that a hazard remains unobserved. 

Planning latency becomes physical distance 

For a simplified one-dimensional braking model, the distance required to respond to an obstacle can be approximated as: 

d_required ≈ vT + v²/(2a) 

Here, v is the aircraft’s speed toward the obstacle, T is the combined detection-to-control delay, and a is the achievable deceleration magnitude. 

This model assumes constant speed during the delay and constant deceleration afterward. It excludes additional clearance margins, uncertainty, wind, and complex multi-axis flight dynamics. 

Nevertheless, it illustrates why latency matters. Doubling flight speed doubles the distance traveled during processing delay and quadruples the idealized braking-distance term. 

A collision-avoidance system must therefore be evaluated against the aircraft’s actual maneuvering capability, not simply its obstacle detection range. 

Dynamic obstacles add another complication. A path considered clear at the beginning of a planning cycle may no longer be safe when the corresponding control command is executed. 

Sensor fusion and state estimation under real-world conditions 

Sensor fusion improves navigation by combining measurements with complementary characteristics. It also introduces dependencies that must be explicitly managed. 

An extended Kalman filter (EKF), commonly used for state estimation, propagates the system state through a motion model and corrects that prediction using sensor observations. 

The measurement update depends on the estimated uncertainty of both the prediction and the observations. If those uncertainty models are inaccurate, the filter may become overconfident. 

For example, GNSS measurements affected by multipath may exhibit correlated errors that are poorly represented by a simple independent-noise assumption. Accepting such measurements with excessive confidence can pull the state estimate away from the true trajectory. 

Innovation residuals and normalized innovation squared tests can help identify inconsistent measurements. However, statistical gating depends on appropriate noise models and does not guarantee detection of every failure. 

Calibration and synchronization are part of navigation 

A camera and IMU must have accurately characterized spatial transformations and timing relationships. 

Even a small temporal offset can create systematic visual-inertial estimation errors during rapid rotation. Incorrect extrinsic calibration can similarly produce inconsistent motion estimates. 

The Kalibr calibration framework provides established methods for estimating camera-IMU spatial and temporal relationships. 

Engineers should also monitor estimator consistency, covariance behavior, measurement rejection rates, and the duration for which the system can operate without reliable absolute position updates. 

A crucial distinction is that estimator covariance represents uncertainty under the assumed model. It is not necessarily a complete measure of actual error when the model itself is wrong. 

Environmental disturbances and flight control reliability 

Autonomous navigation cannot be separated from the aircraft’s flight dynamics. 

Wind gusts introduce external forces and moments that disturb trajectory tracking. Near buildings, airflow can become spatially variable, producing disturbances that differ from those encountered in unobstructed flight. For additional operational context, an overview of drone wind resistance levels provides a practical explanation of wind ratings and operating constraints; those ratings still require interpretation against aircraft configuration and site conditions. 

Payload changes affect mass, center of gravity, inertia, and power requirements. Vibration can degrade IMU measurements and camera image quality, particularly when mechanical isolation and filtering are insufficient. 

Actuator saturation creates another important limitation. A controller may calculate a corrective command that the motors cannot deliver because of thrust limits, battery voltage, or competing attitude-control demands. 

Control-loop stability must therefore be evaluated across expected payload configurations and operating conditions. 

Embedded computing introduces competing constraints 

Autonomous UAVs often execute localization, perception, mapping, planning, communications, and mission management on limited onboard computing resources. 

Higher-resolution sensing may improve geometric detail but increase processing load, memory use, power consumption, and latency. 

A computationally intensive SLAM update can also compete with perception or planning workloads. 

Engineers need to characterize worst-case execution times, deadline misses, scheduling behavior, and degraded-operation strategies rather than relying solely on average processor utilization. 

A navigation system that produces accurate estimates too late for the controller to use them is not operationally reliable. 

Why autonomous inspection data can still be unreliable 

Successfully navigating an inspection route does not guarantee that the resulting measurements are suitable for engineering decisions. 

Navigation accuracy and inspection-data accuracy are related but distinct. 

A UAV may maintain a stable position while capturing blurred imagery, poorly calibrated thermal measurements, or insufficiently overlapping photographs. 

For photogrammetric inspection, reconstruction quality depends on camera calibration, image geometry, surface texture, exposure, and the distribution of viewing angles. High image overlap alone cannot compensate for weak geometry or systematic calibration errors. 

Georeferencing adds further dependencies, including coordinate transformations, surveyed control, camera-to-body alignment, and synchronization between position estimates and image capture. 

Thermal imaging introduces different limitations. Apparent temperature depends on emissivity, reflected radiation, viewing geometry, atmospheric conditions, and instrument calibration. A thermal anomaly should not automatically be interpreted as a confirmed equipment defect. 

Lidar inspection similarly depends on scan geometry, range noise, incidence angle, point density, and motion compensation. 

For repeat inspections, engineers should evaluate whether the same physical feature can be measured consistently across missions. 

That requires separating repeatability from absolute accuracy and recording sufficient metadata to identify changes in sensing conditions. An inspection workflow should therefore validate both the flight trajectory and the quality of the collected engineering evidence. 

Human oversight, failure recovery, and operational safety 

Autonomous operation does not remove the need for supervisory control. 

A robust system should define the conditions under which it can continue, pause, return, land, or transfer authority to a human operator. 

These decisions require explicit fault-handling logic. 

Loss of GNSS alone may not justify terminating a mission if alternative localization remains sufficiently reliable. However, simultaneous localization degradation and restricted maneuvering space may make continued autonomous flight unacceptable. 

Return-to-home behavior also has limitations. It depends on available localization, a suitable return path, obstacle clearance, and sufficient energy. 

In a GNSS-denied or structurally confined environment, returning along a predefined route may be less appropriate than executing a separately validated contingency maneuver. 

Lost-link procedures should distinguish temporary communication interruption from broader navigation or control failures. 

Human intervention remains meaningful only when operators have adequate situational awareness, clear authority, and enough time to respond. 

For U.S. operations, engineering procedures must also align with applicable FAA requirements and authorizations. Autonomous mission execution does not independently remove regulatory responsibilities. 

The relevant safety question is not whether a UAV can fly without continuous manual input. It is whether the combined autonomous and supervisory system behaves acceptably when assumptions fail. 

How engineers should validate autonomous drone deployments 

Industrial deployment readiness cannot be established through a single successful demonstration. 

Testing should combine simulation, hardware-in-the-loop evaluation, controlled flight trials, and progressively representative operating environments. 

Simulation allows engineers to reproduce faults and explore scenarios that may be unsafe to introduce during early flight testing. However, simulated sensor models, aerodynamic disturbances, and environmental geometry cannot capture every physical effect. 

Field validation is needed to establish whether the assumptions used in simulation remain credible. 

Define measurable acceptance criteria 

A practical validation program should include metrics that connect algorithm behavior to operational outcomes. 

Engineering metric  What should be measured 
Localization error  Position and orientation error against an independent reference, including drift during degraded sensing 
Obstacle avoidance  Detection probability, missed hazards, clearance margins, and behavior across obstacle classes 
System latency  End-to-end sensing-to-action delay, including tail latency and deadline misses 
Mission completion  Successful completion under explicitly defined environmental and operational conditions 
Operator intervention  Frequency, cause, timing, and outcome of human intervention 
Failure recovery  Fault detection delay, transition behavior, and success of validated contingency procedures 
Inspection quality  Measurement accuracy, repeatability, image usability, and coverage of required assets 

These metrics require careful definitions. 

Localization error should be evaluated against an independent reference where feasible, rather than against the estimator’s own reported trajectory. Root-mean-square error alone may conceal short-duration excursions that are critical near obstacles. 

Obstacle detection performance should distinguish false positives from missed detections and account for obstacle size, material, distance, and approach geometry. 

Mission completion rates should report the tested scenario distribution and failure definitions. A high completion rate in benign conditions provides limited evidence about operation near industrial structures. 

Intervention frequency is useful only when the criteria for intervention and the level of autonomy are consistent. 

Test interactions between failures 

Individual fault tests are necessary but insufficient. 

A more revealing scenario might combine intermittent GNSS, reduced visual texture, increased processing latency, and moderate wind disturbances. 

The purpose is not to demonstrate that the UAV can tolerate every conceivable combination. It is to identify the boundaries within which the system remains controllable and capable of making trustworthy decisions. 

Engineers should document these boundaries as operational constraints, including conditions that trigger mission suspension or recovery. 

Reliable autonomy is a system-level property 

Industrial drone deployments expose the limitations of evaluating autonomy through isolated subsystem performance. 

Accurate localization does not guarantee safe obstacle avoidance. Successful obstacle avoidance does not guarantee stable flight control. Stable flight does not guarantee useful inspection measurements. And successful mission execution does not demonstrate that the system will respond appropriately to degraded sensing or unexpected faults. 

Reliable autonomy emerges when sensing, estimation, planning, control, data acquisition, and human supervision are designed and validated together. 

For robotics engineers, the central challenge is not merely improving individual algorithms. It is establishing measurable operating boundaries, understanding how errors propagate between subsystems, and ensuring that the aircraft can recognize and respond when its assumptions no longer hold. 

That is the difference between demonstrating autonomous flight and engineering an autonomous system suitable for industrial operations.
