]]> Could Ukraine fly America’s retired F-15 Eagles? A former US general makes the case https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/us-retired-f15-eagles-ukraine-transfer/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 13:35:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57886 Why it arguably makes sense for Washington to transfer dozens of retired F-15 Eagles to Ukraine and why it is highly unlikely to.

The post Could Ukraine fly America’s retired F-15 Eagles? A former US general makes the case appeared first on AGN.

]]> Retired United States Air Force Lieutenant General David A. Deptula has written an opinion piece for Forbes arguing that the US should consider transferring 50-60 retired F-15C/Ds to Ukraine.

Deptula is now the dean of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies think tank. He is also a senior scholar at the U.S. Air Force Academy’s Institute for Future Conflict. The retired general recently returned from Ukraine, where he worked with the Ukrainian Air Force to improve its air operations.

The US has hundreds of mothballed retired F-15C/Ds

Deptula argues that Ukraine is in sore need of more fighter jets and that the US’s recently retired F-15C/Ds stored at the Davis-Monthan boneyard could be a solution. These have been replaced by F-35As and F-15EXs in US Air Force service.

He writes, “The United States should assess whether it can refurbish, equip, and transfer roughly 50–60 F-15C/D Eagles to Ukraine.”

The US has over 240 F-15C/Ds in storage at the Arizona boneyard, with more expected to join in the next few years. Some of these would require little work to be ready to be transferred.

Ukraine needs more aircraft in the air at any one point in time than it can manage with its existing fleet; fighter jets are indispensable for fighting off Russian air attacks.

Ukraine’s F-16s, Mirage 2000s, and legacy Soviet era fighters pay for these missions in heavy maintenance. He argues that with its fighters tied up in air defence, Ukraine lacks units to carry out offensive missions against Russia.

A case for sending F-15C/Ds to Ukraine

The F-15 Eagle is a much larger aircraft than the light/medium weight F-16 and can carry more rounds (940 vs 511 rounds) and many more rockets for short-range air defence. If older F-15s could take over air defence, then Ukraine’s F-16s could receive multirole missions for which they are better suited.

Some of the retired F-15C/Ds have received the APG-63(V)3 active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar, giving pilots markedly better detection range, tracking, and reliability than the radars on the F-16s or any of Ukraine’s other fighters.

He says the strongest argument is speed, as it takes time to produce and deliver new F-16s, Gripens, and Rafales. It also takes over a year to train pilots and maintenance crews.

Deptula notes, “Introducing another fighter type will pose some challenges for Ukraine: pilot training, maintenance, spare parts, ground equipment, infrastructure, and weapons supply must be resolved before aircraft are transferred.”

Washington unlikely to transfer F-15C/Ds to Ukraine

Even under the Biden administration, Washington refused to transfer retired F-16 Fighting Falcons to Ukraine, even though it has hundreds sitting mothballed in its boneyard.

This is not to say Washington didn’t aid Ukraine with F-16s. It did and does. Washington provided critical training and other facilitation roles, but it insisted the airframes had to come from European stocks.

In the last few weeks of 2026, Ukraine is expected to receive ten ex-Belgium F-16s, two ex-French Mirage 2000-5F, and possibly two or so ex-Polish MiG-29s depending on that particular set of colourful negotiations. The first of 16 ex-Swedish Gripen C/Ds are to arrive in January 2027.

🇺🇦 Ukraine will begin receiving Swedish Gripen aircraft in January 2027, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on November 23 📸: Wikipedia 🔗https://t.co/QjBBLbvX8m https://t.co/5fT4TrDcLW

— The New Voice of Ukraine (@NewVoiceUkraine) November 24, 2026

There is some wisdom to the maxim “never say never”, but under the current Trump administration, it seems highly unlikely it would seriously consider transferring old Eagles to Ukraine.

The latest opinion piece is no revelation that Uncle Sam has deep stores of active and mothballed fighter jets that Europe collectively lacks. The latest piece is an opinion of what Washington could do if it chose to, not a realistic assessment of what it will likely choose to do.

Instead, Ukraine is looking long-term to Europeans for its fighter needs. Its ageing, worn-out, and attrited fleet of Soviet Su-25s, Su-24s, MiG-29s, and Su-27s is likely to retire at the earliest convenience post-war.

These will be replaced by a fleet of up to 250 fighters (subject to political, financial, and industrial constraints). The fleet is to be made up primarily of Saab Gripens (mostly new Es), Rafales, and older ex-European F-16s.

]]> EASA adds eight Airbus A380s to accelerated wing crack checks https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/easa-airbus-a380-wing-crack-inspections-eight-more/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 12:58:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57901 EASA has added eight Airbus A380s to the group requiring accelerated inspections for cracks in the wing mid spars, with an inspection deadline of 31 January 2027.

The post EASA adds eight Airbus A380s to accelerated wing crack checks appeared first on AGN.

]]> Eight more Airbus A380s will require wing crack inspections before 31 January 2027. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) added the aircraft to an earlier list of superjumbos that need checks after Airbus found a potential problem with the wing mid-spars, structural members that help carry the wing’s loads. EASA says cracking in this part of the wing could weaken the structure if it goes undetected and uncorrected.

The new airworthiness directive took effect on 18 November. It replaces the emergency order EASA issued in June, when a check on one A380 turned up what the agency called “an unexpected level of findings”.

Further analysis brought the list from 16 aircraft to 24. Emirates operates 22 of the affected aircraft. Etihad Airways and Qantas operate one each, according to Aviation Week’s fleet data.

What the inspections are looking for

EASA’s December 2025 directive identified areas to check on both wings, including parts of the mid rear spar and the inner and outer mid front spars. A review of those inspection results led to the emergency order in June.

Aviation Week reported that hydrogen embrittlement had accelerated cracking in some wing spars on A380s that spent extended periods in storage. The process makes metal less able to deform under stress, so cracks can develop more readily.

When the 24 Airbus A380s need to be checked

The eight aircraft added in November have a January deadline. For the 16 already on the list, the original deadlines still apply. As AGN reported in June, five needed an inspection before their first flight after 24 June, with a limited allowance to fly without passengers to a maintenance site. The other 11 were permitted up to 25 take-offs and landings from that date.

Qantas told AGN in June that its affected A380, VH-OQI, was already in Dresden, Germany, for heavy maintenance. The airline said at the time that the emergency order would not affect its flight schedule.

Operators can count inspections they already carried out under the relevant Airbus instructions. The eight newly listed aircraft are subject to Airbus’s inspection instructions dated 6 November.

Aircraft coming out of storage need a check before flying

The November directive also changes what airlines must do when they bring an A380 back from long-term storage. An A380-841, A380-842 or A380-861 that has spent more than 12 months in storage needs a wing mid-spar inspection before it returns to service. The rule applies after each qualifying storage period.

Once an aircraft returns to service following a check under the directive, the operator has up to 36 months to inspect it again. The next check must also take place within 42 months of the start of the previous inspection. Whichever deadline comes first applies.

If inspectors find a problem, the airline must contact Airbus before the next flight and follow the manufacturer’s repair timetable. Airbus also asks for the results of checks that find nothing. Operators have 30 days to report, counted from the inspection date.

EASA says the November directive is an interim measure and further requirements may follow. The agency issued the directive ahead of consultation and asked for comments before 9 December.

The purchase would make Malaysia Airlines the country’s first Dreamliner operator. The group expects deliveries from 2032 to 2035.

Boeing has a composites operation in Malaysia which supplies parts and subassemblies for its commercial aircraft programmes, including the 787. The plant is Boeing’s first wholly owned manufacturing facility in Southeast Asia.

The latest order brings the total number of KC-46As contracted by the US Air Force and international customers to 203.

The contract also comes at an important time for Boeing’s 767 programme. Commercial production of the widebody is scheduled to end in 2027, but military orders for the KC-46A, which is derived from the 767, will keep the production line running for years to come.

“We’re grateful for the trust the U.S. Air Force continues to place in our team,” said Jake Kwasnik, Boeing’s KC-46 programme vice president.

“The KC-46 plays an important role in enabling military operations around the world, and we look forward to building on that partnership while staying focused on delivering on our commitments to support the warfighter.”

Boeing has so far delivered 116 KC-46As to the US Air Force, six to the Japan Air Self-Defense Force and two to the Israeli Air Force.

The airframer said the US Air Force’s KC-46A fleet had accumulated more than 180,000 flight hours since the first aircraft was delivered in 2019.

US Air Force urged to reconsider KC-46 purchases

As reported previously by Aerospace Global News, a study by the Washington-based Hudson Institute questioned whether continued investment in the KC-46A would adequately meet the US military’s future aerial refuelling requirements.

The report, Resilient Reach: Redesigning Aerial Refueling for Contested Global Operations, was written by researchers Timothy A. Walton and Shane Dennin.

While acknowledging the Pegasus’s performance in current operations, the researchers argued that its range, fuel delivery capacity and survivability could limit its effectiveness in future conflicts, particularly across the Indo-Pacific.

“The medium-range KC-46A has performed well in contemporary operations and would play an important role in any conflict,” the researchers said.

However, their modelling suggested that a medium-sized blended-wing-body (BWB) tanker could refuel more than twice as many groups of combat aircraft as the KC-46A or support them at more than twice the distance.

Unlike conventional aircraft, a blended-wing design merges the fuselage and wings into a continuous lifting surface, reducing aerodynamic drag and potentially improving fuel efficiency. The further a tanker travels to reach other aircraft, the more fuel it consumes itself, leaving less available to transfer.

The study estimated that acquiring and operating 250 blended-wing-body tankers could save $15.5 billion over 30 years compared with an equivalent fleet of KC-46As. Those figures are based on computer modelling rather than the demonstrated performance of an operational tanker.

The US Air Force is already exploring the technology. In 2023, it awarded California-based JetZero a contract to develop a full-scale blended-wing-body demonstrator in partnership with Northrop Grumman.

The demonstrator is scheduled to fly by the end of 2027, although an operational tanker based on such a configuration remains some way off.

KC-46 Pegasus: A programme beset by challenges

The latest order adds to a tanker programme that has experienced procurement controversies, development delays, technical difficulties and substantial financial losses for Boeing.

The US Air Force selected Boeing’s 767-based tanker in 2011 following a lengthy competition involving a rival proposal based on the Airbus A330 Multi Role Tanker Transport (MRTT).

The original programme envisaged the acquisition of 179 aircraft to begin replacing the ageing KC-135 Stratotanker fleet, which entered service in 1957.

Adapting an established commercial aircraft was expected to reduce development risks. However, integrating the military systems proved more complicated than anticipated.

Among the most persistent problems has been the KC-46A’s Remote Vision System (RVS), which allows boom operators to conduct aerial refuelling using cameras and digital displays rather than looking directly through a window at the receiving aircraft.

Problems with image quality under certain lighting conditions prompted Boeing to undertake a redesign of the system. The aircraft has also experienced difficulties involving its refuelling boom.

The programme’s fixed-price development contract has left Boeing absorbing billions of dollars in additional costs.

Despite these setbacks, the US Air Force has progressively expanded its use of the Pegasus in training, overseas deployments and operational missions.

Military orders extend the life of the Boeing 767

The additional tanker order is also significant for the future of Boeing’s 767 manufacturing operations at Everett, Washington.

As previously reported by AGN, Boeing is expected to conclude production of the commercial 767-300F freighter in 2027 ahead of the introduction of tighter international aircraft emissions requirements.

The 767 first flew in 1981 and became a widely used twin-engine widebody on domestic and international passenger routes.

Boeing delivered its final passenger 767-300ER in 2014 as airlines increasingly turned to newer aircraft, including the 787 Dreamliner.

Demand from cargo operators subsequently helped sustain production, with FedEx and UPS among the principal customers for the factory-built 767 freighter.

However, Boeing has not developed a freighter version of the 787, leaving it without a direct replacement for the 767-300F in the same market segment.

Military production will continue beyond the commercial manufacturing deadline.

The KC-46A is derived from the 767-200ER, incorporating elements of the 767 freighter’s design, reinforced structures, military communications equipment and cockpit technology developed for the 787 Dreamliner.

The tanker can carry approximately 212,000lb (96,160kg) of fuel and is powered by two Pratt & Whitney PW4062 engines.

It can refuel aircraft using both flying-boom and probe-and-drogue systems, allowing it to support a wide range of US and allied military aircraft.

The Pegasus can also be configured to carry passengers, cargo and patients requiring aeromedical evacuation.

Growing operational role for the KC-46A

Boeing highlighted recent KC-46A missions supporting humanitarian assistance, including the transportation of relief supplies under the US government’s Denton Humanitarian Assistance Program.

The aircraft has also participated in bilateral training involving the US and Japanese air forces, while long-distance deployments from Travis Air Force Base in California to Japan have supported operations across the Pacific.

The US Air Force, meanwhile, faces the challenge of replacing hundreds of ageing KC-135s while determining what kind of tanker it will require in the coming decades.

 .et_pb_column { position: relative; } </style> <style id="sie-custom-header-inline">/* ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
 SIE Custom Header — v1.1.2
 Zero-CLS, no JavaScript layout shifts.
 No panoramic image — lean 64px nav bar only.
 backdrop-filter is intentionally NOT used on .sie-hdr__bar.
 Any element with backdrop-filter becomes a CSS containing block for
 position:fixed descendants, which would trap the user-ui mobile bottom bar
 (position:fixed; bottom:0) inside the header instead of the viewport.
 ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */
/* ── Root variables ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
:root {
 --sie-hdr-brand:       #0056b3;        /* SIE brand blue                      */
 --sie-hdr-brand-light: #1a6fc4;
 --sie-hdr-bar-h:       64px;           /* nav bar height — fixed, prevents CLS */
 /* 2026-11-08: bar moved from bright brand blue (#0056b3) to the navy the
 homepage redesign uses (#12233D), so header, hero and institutions band
 share one anchor colour. To revert, put #0056b3 / 0.15 back. */
 --sie-hdr-bar-bg:      #12233D;        /* solid — no backdrop-filter needed   */
 --sie-hdr-bar-border:  rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.08);
}
/* ── Wrapper ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr {
 width: 100%;
 display: block;
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 /* Own stacking context so dropdowns render above Divi page content */
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1000;
}
/* ── Navigation bar ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__bar {
 height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter here — it would trap position:fixed children
 (user-ui mobile bottom bar) inside this element instead of viewport */
 border-bottom: 1px solid var(--sie-hdr-bar-border);
}
.sie-hdr__inner {
 max-width: 1280px;
 height: 100%;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 32px;
}
/* ── Logo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__logo {
 flex-shrink: 0;
 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-img {
 height: 54px;
 width: auto;
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-text {
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 17px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #fff;
 letter-spacing: -0.01em;
 white-space: nowrap;
}
/* ── Desktop navigation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__nav {
 flex: 1;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list {
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list li {
 position: relative;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 8px 14px;
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 text-decoration: none;
 border-radius: 8px;
 transition: background 0.15s ease, color 0.15s ease;
 white-space: nowrap;
 min-height: 48px; /* WCAG touch target */
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a:hover,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle:hover,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 color: #fff;
}
/* ── Resources dropdown ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: none;
 position: absolute;
 top: calc(100% + 6px);
 left: 0;
 min-width: 240px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 12px;
 box-shadow: 0 12px 40px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18);
 padding: 8px 0;
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 z-index: 9999;
}
/* CSS-only hover on desktop */
@media (hover: hover) {
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown,
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:focus-within > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
 }
}
/* JS-toggled state (mobile / keyboard) */
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown li {
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 display: block;
 padding: 10px 18px;
 font-size: 13.5px;
 color: #003B73;
 font-weight: 500;
 border-radius: 0;
 min-height: unset;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: #f0f7ff;
 color: #0b5394;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transition: transform 0.2s ease;
}
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transform: rotate(180deg);
}
/* ── Mobile hamburger ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: none;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: center;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 5px;
 width: 44px;
 height: 44px;
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 0;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger span {
 display: block;
 width: 22px;
 height: 2px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 2px;
 transition: transform 0.25s ease, opacity 0.25s ease;
}
/* Animate to ✕ when open */
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(1) {
 transform: translateY(7px) rotate(45deg);
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(2) {
 opacity: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(3) {
 transform: translateY(-7px) rotate(-45deg);
}
/* ── User-UI icon bar integration ────────────────────────────────────────────
 user-ui.php's desktop bar uses position:absolute; top:20px; right:30px — that
 was designed for Divi's header context. Inside our flex .sie-hdr__inner we
 need it as a normal flex child instead.
 Fixed-position children (auth drawer, mobile bar, destinations panel) are
 unaffected — position:fixed is always viewport-relative provided no ancestor
 has backdrop-filter, transform, or perspective (we intentionally avoid all
 three on .sie-hdr__bar).
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
/* Align our mobile breakpoint (860px) with user-ui's desktop/mobile split */
@media (min-width: 861px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: flex !important;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: none !important;
 }
}
/* Leonardo icon in the nav bar.
 user-ui's default .se-ai-icon is 86×86 px (fine for the mobile bottom bar),
 but that overflows our 64px-tall nav bar. Override to a crisp 36px square —
 the webp source is already high-res so it stays sharp at 2× on retina. */
.sie-hdr .se-ai-icon {
 width:  36px !important;
 height: 36px !important;
 border-radius: 50%;
 object-fit: cover;
}
/* Icon colours inside the header.
 user-ui defaults: map icon is #2f6fed (dark blue) and heart is #F44336 (red).
 The map icon is nearly invisible on our #0056b3 bar — lift all icons to white.
 The heart keeps its red via the !important below so favourited items still pop. */
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.85) !important;
}
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon:hover {
 color: #fff !important;
}
/* Fav heart — keep the red so it reads as "save" */
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link {
 color: #ff6b6b !important;   /* slightly lighter red, readable on blue */
}
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link:hover {
 color: #ff4444 !important;
}
/* ── Responsive ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 :root {
 --sie-hdr-bar-h: 56px;
 }
 .sie-hdr {
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 }
 .sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: flex;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav {
 /* Hidden off-screen when closed — no layout shift */
 position: absolute;
 top: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);           /* flush below the nav bar */
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter — same reason as .sie-hdr__bar */
 padding: 12px 0 20px;
 clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0);       /* collapses upward — no CLS */
 transition: clip-path 0.3s ease;
 z-index: 9998;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav.is-open {
 clip-path: inset(0);
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list {
 flex-direction: column;
 align-items: flex-start;
 gap: 0;
 padding: 0 16px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list a,
 .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 width: 100%;
 font-size: 15px;
 padding: 12px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 position: static;
 box-shadow: none;
 border-radius: 0;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.06);
 padding: 4px 0 4px 16px;
 margin: 4px 0;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.8);
 font-size: 14px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.08);
 color: #fff;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 480px) {
 .sie-hdr__inner {
 padding: 0 16px;
 gap: 16px;
 }
}
/* Hover-gap fix: invisible bridge spanning the 6px gap between the nav item
 and the dropdown panel, so the cursor never "leaves" while crossing. */
.sie-hdr__dropdown::before {
 content: "";
 position: absolute;
 top: -10px;
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 height: 10px;
}
/* Anti-FOUC guard for body-rendered overlays: their own CSS arrives 20KB+
 later in the HTML stream, so on slow connections they paint fully visible
 (the destinations grid "opens" during load). Force the CLOSED state from
 first paint — each component's .open/.is-open rules override these. */
.sie-dest-panel,
#sie-auth-drawer,
#sie-lead-form-drawer,
.sie-finder-overlay {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
} </style> <style id="sie-etmodules-font-display">@font-face{font-family:"ETmodules";src:url("https://www.studyineurope.eu/core/views/86f0928314/css/base/modules.woff") format("woff");font-style:normal;font-weight:normal;font-display:swap;}</style><meta name='robots' content='index, follow, max-image-preview:large, max-snippet:-1, max-video-preview:-1' /> <style id="sie-hide-divi-header"> /* Hide Divi's header (Theme Builder + classic) */

 /* Leonardo's panel: the button and its verified line read as one block,

 .lh-heroalt-panel{border:1px solid #C3C9CE;border-radius:6px;background:#fff;overflow:hidden}
 .lh-heroalt-panel:hover{border-color:#E0742B}
 .lh-heroalt-card--leo{border:0;border-radius:0;background:none;padding:15px 16px 13px}
 .lh-heroalt-card--leo:hover,.lh-heroalt-card--leo:focus-visible{background:#FFFDFB;border:0}
 .lh-heroalt-kicker{display:flex;align-items:center;gap:7px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;letter-spacing:1.2px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#12233D;font-weight:500}
 .lh-heroalt-kicker svg{color:#E0742B;flex:0 0 auto}
 .lh-heroalt-card--leo .lh-heroalt-hint{margin-top:7px;font-size:13.5px;color:#3C4F66}
 .lh-heroalt-verified{display:flex;gap:8px;align-items:flex-start;margin:0;padding:11px 16px 13px;border-top:1px solid #EDEAE3;background:#FBF8F2;font-size:12.5px;line-height:1.5;color:#4A525C}
 .lh-heroalt-verified svg{color:#1C7A4A;flex:0 0 auto;margin-top:2px}
 /* ── Make the search the priority, not an afterthought ────────────────
 Measured before this change at 1440x900: hero 1028px tall, search bar
 top at y=694. Tightened the vertical rhythm and moved the trust row
 below, which lifts the bar roughly 230px — comfortably in view. */
 .lh-hero.lh-hero{padding:clamp(28px,4vw,56px) 0 clamp(32px,4.5vw,64px)}
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-center{gap:clamp(16px,2vw,26px)}
 /* ⚠️ THE CAUSE OF THE BIG EMPTY GAP, and it was mine. The stylesheet sets
 .lh-hero-text{flex:1 1 380px} and .lh-portals{flex:1 1 420px}. Those were
 written for the original ROW layout, where flex-basis is a WIDTH. Turning
 the container into a column silently turned both into fixed HEIGHTS: the
 text box stayed 380px tall although its content ended after 187px, and
 the search row stayed 420px tall although the cards are 195px. That is
 ~420px of enforced emptiness. Resetting the basis is the whole fix —
 never set flex-direction on an inherited flex container without checking
 what flex-basis meant before. */
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-text{flex:0 0 auto}
 .lh-hero .lh-portals--search{flex:0 0 auto}
 .lh-hero .lh-badge{margin-bottom:10px}
 .lh-hero .lh-title{margin:0 0 12px}
 .lh-hero .lh-subtitle{margin:0;max-width:52ch}
 .lh-hero .lh-trust-row{position:relative;z-index:1;margin:clamp(14px,1.8vw,22px) 0 0;gap:10px 24px}
 /* The bar itself carries the emphasis: taller, larger type, and a navy
 action instead of the yellow one — yellow reads promotional, and on warm
 paper it was the loudest thing in the hero. Scoped to .lh-herosearch so
 the same widget elsewhere keeps the brand button. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-bar{min-height:64px;padding:4px 6px 4px 14px}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-input{font-size:17px}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-btn{background:#12233D;border-color:#12233D;color:#fff;font-weight:600}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-btn:hover{background:#1E3354;border-color:#1E3354}
 /* ── Results as a responsive grid, not a single strip ──────────────────
 .sie-res-list holds the program cards as direct children (verified live:
 18 cards, one parent, no headers in between), so one grid rule is enough.
 ⚠️ SCOPED TO THE HOMEPAGE ON PURPOSE. .sie-res-list is the shared
 SieFlowView markup — Leonardo renders into it too, with its own
 per-card animation offsets. Re-layouting it globally would change his
 results as a side effect of a homepage fix. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(320px,1fr));gap:16px;align-items:start}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list > .program-card{width:auto;max-width:none;margin:0}
 /* The flow view (AI matching on) groups results into one .sie-flow__branch
 per country. Each branch carries max-width:560px inside a 798px rail, so
 two never fit and they stack — the "single strip". Releasing the cap and
 tiling the branches gives two country panels per row at this width, and
 more on a wider screen, without touching the cards inside.
 ⚠️ Scoped to .lh-herosearch: Leonardo renders the same flow markup. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branches{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(360px,1fr));gap:18px;align-items:start}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branch{max-width:none;width:100%}
 /* ── The figures strip ────────────────────────────────────────────────
 Serif numerals, monospaced labels, hairline rules, no card, no shadow,
 no colour fill behind each figure. The register of a register. */
 .lh-stats.lh-stats--figures{background:#F4F2ED;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-bottom:1px solid #E4E0D8;padding:0}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stats-grid{max-width:1200px;margin:0 auto;padding:0 clamp(16px,4vw,48px);display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(4,minmax(0,1fr));gap:0}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat{padding:clamp(20px,2.4vw,32px) clamp(14px,2vw,28px) clamp(20px,2.4vw,32px) 0;border-right:1px solid #E4E0D8;text-align:left;background:none;border-radius:0;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat:last-child{border-right:0}
 /* Every cell except the first gets inner space on its left, so each rule
 sits with equal air on both sides instead of crowding the next figure.
 The first keeps padding-left:0 so its numeral lines up with the margin
 the hero headline uses. */
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat + .lh-stat{padding-left:clamp(18px,2.4vw,34px)}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat-num{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-size:clamp(27px,2.9vw,40px);font-weight:600;letter-spacing:-.5px;line-height:1.05;color:#12233D;background:none;-webkit-text-fill-color:currentColor}
 /* #6B7A8D measured 3.92:1 against the warm band — under the 4.5:1 that
 11.5px text needs. The cool grey was fine on the old cold background and
 quietly failed when the palette warmed up; #4F5967 measures 6.2:1.
 Worth remembering when warming any other background. */
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat-label{margin-top:8px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;letter-spacing:1.3px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#4F5967}
 @media(max-width:700px){
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stats-grid{grid-template-columns:repeat(2,minmax(0,1fr))}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat:nth-child(2){border-right:0}
 }
 /* Monogram instead of a repeated building glyph. Hairline tile, serif
 letters — it reads as a placeholder somebody chose, not as missing data. */
 .lh-uni-logo-placeholder{display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;background:#F4F2ED;border:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-radius:5px;color:#8A8578}
 .lh-uni-monogram{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-size:22px;font-weight:600;letter-spacing:1px;color:#12233D}
 /* ── For institutions ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
 The one full navy band on the page. It is dark on purpose: it marks a
 change of audience, so a student scrolling past knows at a glance that
 this part is not addressed to them. */
 .lh-inst{background:#12233D;color:#fff}
 .lh-inst-wrap *,.lh-inst-wrap *::before,.lh-inst-wrap *::after{box-sizing:border-box}
 .lh-inst-inner{max-width:1200px;margin:0 auto;padding:clamp(48px,6vw,88px) clamp(16px,4vw,48px);display:grid;grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1.35fr) minmax(0,1fr);gap:clamp(28px,4vw,64px);align-items:start}
 .lh-inst-badge{margin:0 0 16px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;letter-spacing:1.8px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#D7A83F}
 .lh-inst-h{margin:0 0 16px;font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-size:clamp(26px,3.1vw,40px);line-height:1.16;font-weight:600;letter-spacing:-.5px;color:#fff;max-width:20ch}
 .lh-inst-body{margin:0 0 26px;font-size:clamp(15.5px,1.4vw,17px);line-height:1.65;color:#C6D2E0;max-width:54ch}
 .lh-inst-actions{margin:0;display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:12px}
 .lh-inst-btn{display:inline-block;text-decoration:none;background:#fff;color:#12233D;font-size:15.5px;font-weight:600;padding:14px 26px;border:1px solid #fff;border-radius:4px;min-height:44px}
 .lh-inst-btn:hover{background:#F4F2ED;color:#12233D}
 .lh-inst-btn--ghost{background:none;color:#fff;border-color:#44597A;font-weight:500}
 .lh-inst-btn--ghost:hover{background:none;color:#fff;border-color:#D7A83F}
 .lh-inst-terms{margin:0;padding:0;list-style:none}
 .lh-inst-terms li{border-top:1px solid #28405F;padding:20px 0}
 .lh-inst-terms li:first-child{border-top:0;padding-top:0}
 .lh-inst-k{margin:0 0 6px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:19px;color:#D7A83F}
 .lh-inst-v{margin:0;font-size:15px;line-height:1.6;color:#C6D2E0}
 @media(max-width:860px){
 .lh-inst-inner{grid-template-columns:1fr}
 }
 @media(max-width:900px){
 .lh-hero .lh-portals--search{grid-template-columns:1fr}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list{grid-template-columns:1fr}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branches{grid-template-columns:1fr}
 .lh-heroalt{flex-direction:row;flex-wrap:wrap}
 .lh-heroalt-card{flex:1 1 220px}
 .lh-hero-scrim{background:linear-gradient(180deg,rgba(250,248,244,.97) 0%,rgba(250,248,244,.93) 62%,rgba(250,248,244,.72) 100%)}
 }
 /* ── Institutional pass, part 2 (2026-11-08, evening) ──────────────────
 Brings the sections below the hero onto the palette and type the hero
 already uses, so the page reads as one document instead of two designs
 stacked on top of each other. Everything here is homepage-only (it lives
 in this template) and is pure CSS: delete this block to revert. */
 /* The page itself: the site-wide body is cold pale blue (#E8F1FA), which
 showed through every transparent section (the institutions carousel and
 the study fields block) as a blue band between warm ones. */
 body.page-id-150{background:#FAF8F4}
 /* ⚠️ THE HEADLINE NEVER WAS SERIF. leonardo-homepage-css.min.css carries
 `.lh-wrap .lh-title{font-family:system-ui !important; font-size:44px
 !important; font-weight:800 !important; color:#003b73 !important}`, so
 the Source Serif rule earlier in this block lost on every device. Only
 !important with equal-or-higher specificity can beat it. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-title,.lh-wrap .lh-hero h2.lh-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif !important;font-weight:600 !important;font-size:clamp(34px,4.4vw,58px) !important;line-height:1.08 !important;letter-spacing:-.6px !important;color:#12233D !important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#12233D !important}
 /* The accent word: italic navy reads editorial; bright orange read promo. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-gradient-text{color:#12233D;-webkit-text-fill-color:#12233D;font-style:italic;font-weight:600}
 /* One label above the headline is enough. The H1 eyebrow ("STUDY IN
 EUROPE") already does that job; the extra pill only added noise. */
 .lh-hero .lh-badge{display:none}
 /* Phones: the hero had no side gutter, so the eyebrow sat flush against
 the screen edge while the centred text did not. Left-aligned, with the
 same 20px gutter as the rest of the page, it matches the desktop. */
 @media(max-width:900px){
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-center{padding-left:20px;padding-right:20px;box-sizing:border-box;text-align:left}
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-text,.lh-hero .lh-subtitle{text-align:left}
 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-title{text-align:left}
 .lh-hero .lh-trust-row{justify-content:flex-start}
 }
 /* ── Section headers: same voice as the institutions band ─────────────
 Serif headings and a small monospaced label instead of the rounded blue
 pills, which were the last "app" element on the page. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-section-header h2{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif !important;font-weight:600 !important;font-size:clamp(28px,3vw,40px) !important;letter-spacing:-.4px;line-height:1.15;color:#12233D !important}
 .lh-wrap .lh-section-badge{display:inline-block;margin-bottom:14px;padding:0;background:none;border-radius:0;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;font-weight:500;letter-spacing:1.8px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#8C5A23}
 .lh-wrap .lh-section-sub{color:#4A525C}
 /* Section rhythm: paper / white / paper, so each block has an edge. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-how{background:#FAF8F4}
 .lh-wrap .lh-unis{background:#fff;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8}
 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--origins{background:#fff;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8}
 /* How it works: the three steps were top-aligned, so the middle card
 (longer text) hung lower than its neighbours. Stretch evens them. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-steps{align-items:stretch}
 .lh-wrap .lh-step{background:#fff;border:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-radius:6px;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-wrap .lh-step-num{background:#12233D;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-weight:500}
 .lh-wrap .lh-step-icon{background:#F4F2ED;color:#12233D;border-radius:6px}
 .lh-wrap .lh-step-arrow{color:#B7B1A5}
 /* Cards: tighter corners and hairlines everywhere. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-card{border-radius:6px;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--origins a[class*="card"],.lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--origins [class*="card"]{border-radius:6px;border-color:#E4E0D8;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--countries a[class*="card"],.lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--countries [class*="card"]{border-radius:6px}
 /* ── Study fields block (rendered by [sie_study_fields] after .lh-wrap) ─
 Six bright category colours, gradient pills and a gradient CTA made it
 the loudest part of the page. Same content, one navy, warm neutrals.
 The branch colours arrive as INLINE custom properties and inline
 backgrounds, so these overrides need !important to apply. Scoped to the
 homepage: the study-field pages keep their colour coding. */
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-weight:600;font-size:clamp(28px,3vw,40px);letter-spacing:-.4px;color:#12233D}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-subtitle{color:#4A525C}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__source-pill{background:#12233D !important;background-image:none !important;box-shadow:none !important;border-radius:4px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__junction-dot{background:#12233D}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch{--branch-color:#12233D !important;--branch-bg:#F4F2ED !important;border:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-radius:6px;box-shadow:none}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch-accent{display:none}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch-icon{background:#12233D !important;border-radius:5px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch-count{background:#F4F2ED !important;color:#12233D !important}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__field-card{background:#FAF8F4;border:1px solid #EDEAE3;border-radius:5px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__field-card:hover{border-color:#12233D}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__field-icon{background:#F4F2ED !important;color:#12233D !important;border-radius:5px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__leo-link{color:#0B5FA5 !important}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-leonardo{background:#12233D !important;background-image:none !important;border-radius:6px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-leo-btn{background:#fff !important;color:#12233D !important;border-color:#fff !important;border-radius:4px}
 /* Alignment: the search widget carries its own 24px side padding, so the
 bar sat indented from the headline above it; and the trust row was
 centred under a left-aligned column. Both now share the text's edge.
 Only the LEFT padding goes: removing the right one too pushed the
 "AI-enhanced matching" toggle across the seam into the navy side. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-wrap{padding-left:0 !important}
 .lh-hero .lh-trust-row{justify-content:flex-start}
 /* Institution cards: the stylesheet tints each card top a different pastel
 (blue / yellow / blue) via !important rules at .lh-uni-card:nth-child()
 specificity, so this needs one more class to win. Plain paper, so the
 monogram or logo is the only thing that differs between cards. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-card:nth-child(n) .lh-uni-card-top{background:#F4F2ED !important;background-image:none !important;border-bottom:1px solid #EDEAE3}
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-cta{color:#0B5FA5 !important}
 .lh-wrap .sie-dest-hub__name{color:#12233D}
 /* Europe silhouette on the navy side. Present, never loud: a lighter blue
 at 15% so the copy on top keeps full contrast. The right edge fades out
 because the map is cut through Russia there, and a hard vertical cut
 would read as a mistake. The stroke in the fill colour closes the
 hairline seams between neighbouring countries; opacity sits on the <svg> itself so overlapping strokes cannot add up into darker lines. */
 .lh-hero-navy{overflow:hidden}
 .lh-hero-map{position:absolute;top:6%;bottom:6%;left:6%;width:92%;height:88%;opacity:.15;pointer-events:none;-webkit-mask-image:linear-gradient(to right,#000 78%,transparent 100%);mask-image:linear-gradient(to right,#000 78%,transparent 100%)}

 DESTINATIONS PANEL  — overlay + grid
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
 /* Outer layer: covers full viewport */
 .sie-dest-panel {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 2147483000;
 display: flex;
 align-items: stretch;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .25s ease, visibility .25s;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open {
 opacity: 1;
 visibility: visible;
 pointer-events: auto;
 }
 /* Backdrop */
 .sie-dest-panel__backdrop {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 background: rgba(11, 55, 112, .52);
 backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 cursor: pointer;
 }
 /* Sheet — right-panel on desktop */
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1;
 width: min(800px, 100%);
 height: 100%;
 background: #fff;
 overflow-y: auto;
 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;
 transition: transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1);
 box-shadow: -20px 0 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);
 opacity: 1;
 }
 /* Mobile: bottom-sheet */
 @media (max-width: 767px) {
 .sie-dest-panel {
 align-items: flex-end;
 justify-content: stretch;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 width: 100%;
 height: 92vh;
 border-top-left-radius: 22px;
 border-top-right-radius: 22px;
 padding: 20px 16px 40px;
 transform: translateY(28px);
 box-shadow: 0 -16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateY(0);
 }
 }
 /* ── Header ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__header {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #1e66f5;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__title {
 font-size: 1.5rem;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #0b3770;
 margin: 0;
 line-height: 1.2;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close {
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #0b3770;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 6px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 line-height: 1;
 opacity: .75;
 transition: opacity .15s, background .15s;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close:hover {
 opacity: 1;
 background: #f0f4ff;
 }
 /* Subheading */
 .sie-dest-panel__sub {
 color: #466087;
 font-size: .94rem;
 margin: 0 0 20px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 /* ── Country grid ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 display: grid;
 grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
 gap: 14px;
 /* allow this to grow and scroll */
 flex: 1;
 align-content: start;
 }
 @media (max-width: 620px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
 gap: 10px;
 }
 }
 @media (min-width: 621px) and (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
 }
 }
 /* ── Country card ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__card {
 position: relative;
 display: block;
 aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
 border-radius: 12px;
 overflow: hidden;
 text-decoration: none;
 background: #1d3557;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card--no-img .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1d3557 0%, #1e66f5 100%);
 }
 /* Hero image layer — scales on hover */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 transition: transform .4s ease;
 will-change: transform;
 }
 /* <img> fills the card exactly like background-size:cover did.
 loading="lazy" means the browser only fetches each image when the
 panel opens and the card enters the viewport — saving ~30 MB of
 upfront image requests on every page that includes this panel. */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-img {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center;
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 transform: scale(1.07);
 }
 /* Gradient overlay + text */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-body {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 padding: 10px 12px 10px;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .72) 0%,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .30) 55%,
 transparent 100%
 );
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-name {

 font-weight: 700;
 font-size: .92rem;
 line-height: 1.2;

 .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {

 margin-top: 2px;
 transition: color .2s ease, transform .2s ease;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 color: rgba(255,255,255,.9);
 transform: translateX(4px);
 }

 body.sie-dest-panel-open {

 top: 8px;
 right: 8px;
 z-index: 10;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);

 border-radius: 20px;
 padding: 4px 8px 4px 7px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 cursor: pointer;
 font-size: 13px;
 color: #94a3b8;
 box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.22);
 backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(6px);

 justify-content: center;

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

Overview

PR kann heute mehr, als nur Sichtbarkeit verwalten.

Bei getpress bauen wir an einer Marke, die zeigt, wie moderne Kommunikation für Europas ambitionierteste Unternehmen aussehen kann: strategisch, messbar, relevant und mit einem klaren Gefühl für Qualität.
Dafür suchen wir eine Person, die unsere externe Kommunikation ownt und vor allem sichtbar macht. Jemanden, der*die starke Themen erkennt, gute Formate daraus entwickelt und sie auch selbst umsetzt – von LinkedIn und Website über Podcast, Blog und Whitepaper bis zu Speaker- und Event-Content.

Deine Rolle

Du arbeitest an der Schnittstelle von Brand, Content, Thought Leadership und externer Kommunikation. Dabei bist du strategisch genug, um Themen, Kanäle und Formate kritisch zu hinterfragen und hands-on genug, um auch selbst zu schreiben, zu produzieren, zu redigieren und Dinge live zu bringen.

  • Du planst, steuerst und produzierst unseren Content für alle relevanten Kanäle und Formate – darunter LinkedIn, Website, Blog, Podcast, Whitepaper sowie Speaker-Auftritte und Events.
  • Du schreibst, redigierst und schärfst Inhalte selbst – von LinkedIn-Posts und Website-Texten über Case Studies und Blogartikel bis zu Podcast-Beschreibungen, Speaker-Profilen und Präsentationsinhalten.
  • Du denkst Visuals, Präsentationen, Social Assets und einfache Foto-/Video-Formate mit und kannst kleinere Content-Produktionen selbst umsetzen oder sauber briefen.
  • Du sparrst mit unseren Corporate Creator*innen und dem C-Level zu Personal Brands, Thought Leadership, Themen, Tonalität und Formatideen.
  • Du betreust unseren Podcast redaktionell von Gäste-Recherche und Briefings bis zur Veröffentlichung und begleitenden Kommunikation.
  • Du sorgst dafür, dass getpress über alle Touchpoints hinweg konsistent, hochwertig und markant auftritt, in Sprache, Look, Dramaturgie und Qualität.
  • Du beobachtest, wie unsere Inhalte performen, leitest daraus Learnings ab und bringst eigene Ideen ein, wie wir Formate, Kanäle und Botschaften weiterentwickeln.
  • Du repräsentierst getpress auch nach außen – auf Events, in Netzwerken und an den Stellen, an denen Marke durch echten Kontakt entsteht.

Wer du bist

Du hast mehrere Jahre Erfahrung in Kommunikation, Brand, Content oder PR, idealerweise im B2B-Umfeld und in einer Agentur oder einem dienstleistungsnahen Kontext.

Außerdem macht dich folgendes aus:

  • Ein feines Gespür für Sprache, Tonalität und Qualität. Du erkennst schnell, wann ein Text, Auftritt oder Format wirklich sitzt.
  • Du denkst strategisch mit, verlierst dich aber nicht in Konzepten. Dein Ziel ist Sichtbarkeit schaffen.
  • Du hast LinkedIn, Organic Social und Personal Branding vollständig durchdrungen und weißt, wie man echte Markenwirkung erzeugt.
  • Du kannst Themen priorisieren, Kommunikationsmaßnahmen einschätzen und Redaktionspläne eigenständig strukturieren.
  • Ein gutes Auge für Design, Ästhetik und Brand Consistency, auch bei Slides, Social Assets, Website-Elementen und Event-Content.
  • Du arbeitest sicher mit Tools wie Canva und hast keine Berührungsängste mit Adobe Creative Cloud, Adobe Lightroom oder einfachen Editing-Workflows.
  • Du bringst Foto- und Video-Basics mit oder hast Lust, dich in einfache Inhouse-Content-Produktion einzuarbeiten.
  • Du arbeitest souverän mit KI-Tools und nutzt sie für bessere Recherche, Briefings, Struktur, Workflows, Varianten und Qualität, nicht als Abkürzung für generischen Content.
  • Du hast eine eigene Meinung, gibst klares Feedback und bringst dich im Sparring mit Team und C-Level aktiv ein, statt Aufträge nur abzuarbeiten.

Was dich erwartet

  • Volle Ownership: Du bist bei uns die einzige Person in dieser Rolle und gestaltest Brand und Content ohne Doppelstrukturen, mit direktem Draht zum C-Level.
  • Eine Rolle, in der du strategisch gestaltest und selbst umsetzt, und direkt siehst, welche Wirkung deine Arbeit hat.
  • Ein Umfeld, in dem Kommunikation als echter Faktor für Sichtbarkeit, Vertrauen und Relevanz gesehen wird.
  • Die Möglichkeit, neue Tools, Formate und Arbeitsweisen auszuprobieren – besonders an der Schnittstelle von Brand, Content und AI.
  • Ein Team, das ambitioniert, warm und beweglich ist und richtig Bock hat, Dinge voranzubringen.
  • Du wirst regelmäßig vor Ort in Berlin gebraucht – für Abstimmungen, Content-Produktion, Events und die enge Zusammenarbeit mit zentralen Stakeholdern. Gleichzeitig kannst du auch remote arbeiten. Wir setzen auf flexible Arbeitsmodelle mit viel Eigenverantwortung, klarer Kommunikation und Vertrauen.
  • Gehalt: 60.000–70.000 € brutto jährlich

Wie gehts weiter?

Wenn sich das nach deinem nächsten Schritt anfühlt, dann schick uns deinen Lebenslauf oder LinkedIn-Profil, relevante Arbeitsproben oder ein Portfolio.

Uns interessiert nicht nur, was du gemacht hast. Sondern vor allem auch, wie du denkst, wie du Qualität einschätzt und welches Gefühl du für starke Kommunikation mitbringst.

Hey, wir sind Junto! 😊

Wir machen Leadership Development für das KI-Zeitalter: Wir befähigen Führungskräfte, KI in ihren Teams wirksam einzusetzen, und begleiten Unternehmen wie AOK PLUS, Henkel, Ottobock und diva-e mit blended Lernreisen. Für den nächsten Wachstumsschritt suchen wir dich als Senior Consultant AI Enablement: die Person, die KI-Expertise und Beratungsdenke in unsere Programme bringt.

Aufgaben

Deine Verantwortung

  • Du konzipierst maßgeschneiderte KI-Befähigungsprogramme für Führungskräfte unserer Kund:innen vom Vorstand bis zur Teamleitung, gemeinsam mit unserem Head of Leadership Development

  • Du arbeitest mit unserem Gründer und Geschäftsführer am Business Development und an Pitches für potenzielle Neukunden

  • Du setzt eigene, kleine Use Cases für unsere interne KI-Transformation um und testest dabei fortlaufend neue KI-Tools und Anwendungsmöglichkeiten

Deine Aufgaben

  • Discovery: Du analysierst Bedarfe und KI-Reifegrad der Zielgruppe (Interviews, Surveys, Use-Case-Workshops)

  • Design: Du entwickelst Inhalte, Übungen, Demos und Arbeitsmaterialien, z. B. Präsentationen mit Speaker Notes, Prompt-Bibliotheken, Hands-on-Labs

  • Delivery: Du moderierst Sessions und Workshops selbst (online und vor Ort) und/oder begleitest unsere Executive Trainer:innen

  • Use Cases und Prozesse: Du identifizierst mit Fachbereichen konkrete KI-Use-Cases, priorisierst sie und übersetzt sie in Prozesse

  • Iteration: Du wertest Feedback und Daten aus und entwickelst unsere Programme weiter

Deine Schnittstellen

  • Intern: Du arbeitest direkt mit Marius (Gründer und Geschäftsführer) und Andreas (Head of Leadership Development) sowie unserem Learning-Design-Team zusammen

  • Extern: Du führst Kundenbeziehungen von der Personalvorständin bis zum L&D-Experten und arbeitest mit Top-Coaches aus unserem Netzwerk (z. B. CMO bei T-Systems, Head of AI bei Mercedes)

Qualifikation

Erfahrung

  • Du bringst 3 bis 7 Jahre Berufserfahrung mit, idealerweise aus der Unternehmensberatung oder aus Transformations- und Change-Projekten

  • KI-Erfahrung: Du hast selbst schon kleinere Automatisierungen oder Agenten eingesetzt und in KI-Transformations- oder Enablement-Projekten mitgewirkt

  • Erfahrung in Learning Design oder Leadership Development ist ein Plus, aber kein Muss: Das didaktische Know-how bringen wir mit

Eigene KI-Kompetenz

  • Du nutzt KI täglich und deine Begeisterung für die Potenziale ist ansteckend

  • Du hast bereits praktische Erfahrung mit fortgeschrittenen KI-Tools gesammelt, z. B. Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Copilot Studio oder Agenten in Microsoft Foundry

  • Du erklärst Konzepte wie Agenten, Automatisierung oder KI-Governance so, dass auch nicht-technische Führungskräfte sie verstehen und für sich nutzen können

  • Wenn du etwas noch nicht weißt, weißt du, wie du es dir mit KI beibringen kannst

Mindset und Arbeitsweise

  • Human-first: Du kombinierst deine Begeisterung für KI-Technologie mit Verständnis für menschenzentrierten Change und einer klaren Business-Denke (Workflows, Use Cases)

  • Präsentationsstark: Du stehst gern vor Gruppen, von der Teamleitung bis zum Top-Management

  • Neugier: Du bleibst bei KI-Entwicklungen dran und teilst dein Wissen gern

  • Sehr gutes Deutsch und Englisch in Wort und Schrift

Benefits

  • Urban Sports Club und Co. gibt's natürlich auch ;-)

So sieht der weitere Prozess aus

  2. Fachliches Gespräch mit Marius (ca. 45 Min.)

  4. Vertragsangebot 🚀

Vollzeit · Festanstellung · Hauptverwaltung Düsseldorf · Direkt an die Geschäftsführung angebunden · Start kurzfristig, spätestens zum 01.01.2027

„Jeden Tag einen Menschen in eine sinnstiftende Tätigkeit bringen.“

Stell dir vor

Montagmorgen. Eine Standortleitung braucht bis Mitte des Monats eine neue Dozentin, also geht die Anzeige heute noch raus. Daneben wartet ein Arbeitsvertrag auf die Unterschrift, zwei Krankmeldungen müssen ins System, die Lohndaten gehen diese Woche an die Steuerberatung, und ein Kollege braucht bis morgen eine Bescheinigung. Du sortierst, legst los – und am Abend ist alles erledigt und sauber in Personio dokumentiert.

Das ist kein Werbetext. Das ist der Job. Wir suchen jemanden, der Personalarbeit nicht delegiert, sondern macht: von der Stellenanzeige bis zum Zeugnis, selbstständig und mit Tempo.

Wer wir sind

Die EuBiA (Europäische Bildungsakademie) ist als operative Tochtergesellschaft der IWQ Holding ein Bildungsträger mit Standorten in NRW, Schleswig-Holstein, Hamburg und Berlin sowie in Marokko. Wir konzipieren und realisieren geförderte Bildungsmaßnahmen, Coachings, Sprachkurse und Weiterbildungen – für Privat- wie Firmenkunden, national und international.

Was uns ausmacht: Herzlichkeit, Kompetenz und Engagement. Bei uns arbeiten Kolleginnen und Kollegen unterschiedlichster Herkunft zusammen, wir beraten und unterrichten in mehreren Sprachen. Diversity ist für uns kein Schlagwort, sondern gelebter Alltag.

Worum es geht

Wir wachsen – mit mehreren Gesellschaften, mehreren Standorten und einem Team, das größer wird. Dafür brauchen wir kurzfristig eine Person, die unsere Personalarbeit operativ in die Hand nimmt: das gesamte Handwerkszeug der Personalsachbearbeitung, schnelles Recruiting und eine Personalabteilung, die vollständig über Personio läuft.

Du arbeitest sehr eigenständig, verantwortest die operative Personalarbeit ab Januar in eigener Hand und hast den direkten Draht zur Geschäftsführung. Wenn du gern selbst anpackst, statt Zuständigkeiten zu verteilen, bist du hier richtig.

Was du bewegst

  • Personalabteilung über Personio führen – Du führst unsere Personalarbeit in Personio: Stammdaten, digitale Personalakte, Abwesenheiten, Dokumente, Workflows und Auswertungen. Was noch nicht sauber läuft, richtest du ein.
  • Personalsachbearbeitung von A bis Z – Arbeitsverträge, Vertragsänderungen, Bescheinigungen, Zeugnisse und Schreiben erstellst du selbst. Du pflegst die Personalakten und behältst Fristen wie Probezeiten und Befristungen im Blick.
  • Kurzfristig einstellen – Du schreibst Stellen aus, sichtest Bewerbungen, führst Erstgespräche, stimmst Termine ab und bringst Einstellungen bis zur Vertragsunterschrift – auch wenn es schnell gehen muss.
  • On- und Offboarding – Du begleitest Eintritte und Austritte vollständig: Unterlagen, Unterweisungen, Zugänge, Übergaben.
  • Vorbereitende Lohnabrechnung – Du bereitest die monatlichen Lohndaten vor, klärst Rückfragen und hältst den Kontakt zur Steuerberatung.
  • Ansprechperson im Alltag – Du bist erste Adresse für Mitarbeitende und Führungskräfte bei allen Personalfragen und bereitest arbeitsrechtliche Vorgänge wie Abmahnungen oder Kündigungen sauber vor.
  • Mitdenken und anpacken – Du kümmerst dich um das, was anfällt – auch wenn es nicht in der Stellenbeschreibung steht.

Was du mitbringst

  • Qualifikation – Abgeschlossene kaufmännische Ausbildung mit Weiterbildung zur Personalkauffrau bzw. zum Personalkaufmann, ein Studium mit Schwerpunkt Personal oder eine vergleichbare Qualifikation mit entsprechender Praxis.
  • Erfahrung – Mehrjährige Praxis in der operativen Personalarbeit. Du beherrschst das gesamte Handwerkszeug der Personalsachbearbeitung und hast es selbst gemacht, nicht nur begleitet.
  • Personio – Du arbeitest sicher mit Personio und hast das System idealerweise selbst eingerichtet oder administriert.
  • Arbeitsrecht – Solide Grundkenntnisse im Arbeitsrecht für das Tagesgeschäft – und das Gespür dafür, wann du dir Rat holst.
  • Hands-on-Mentalität – Du packst an, kümmerst dich und arbeitest gern selbstständig. Du priorisierst sicher, wenn vieles gleichzeitig kommt.
  • Verfügbarkeit – Du kannst kurzfristig einsteigen, bestenfalls zum 01.01.2027 oder früher.
  • Persönlichkeit – Verbindlichkeit, strukturierter Arbeitsstil, klare Kommunikation in Wort und Schrift und absolute Diskretion.
  • Von Vorteil – Erfahrung bei einem Bildungsträger oder im SGB-II/III-Umfeld ist ein Plus, aber keine Voraussetzung.

Was du bei uns findest

SumUp is preparing to build a CRR (Capital Requirements Regulation) licensed bank in Germany—an important next chapter in our journey to help small businesses thrive. As Managing Director, Front Office, you'll be part of the team that shapes how this bank serves customers: the proposition we bring to market, the products we build, and the standards by which we grow.

This is a rare opportunity to take an executive management role in a new, digitally native bank. You'll combine commercial leadership with direct accountability for customer-facing governance, and represent the market perspective in dialogue with supervisors. We're looking for a leader who sees customer trust and sustainable growth as inseparable—and who can build with the pace of a technology company and the discipline of a bank.

What you'll do

  • Together with the other members of the executive management team contribute to the strategic and corporate development of the bank.
  • Lead the market facing part for the German banking licence application. Represent the bank in supervisory dialogue on commercial strategy, products, distribution and customer treatment, including with BaFin, Deutsche Bundesbank and the European Central Bank where relevant.
  • Support building  the go to market operating model and ensure it is integrated into the bank's governance, risk and control framework. Work closely with the Managing Director, Back Office (Geschäftsleiter Marktfolge) to ensure product, conduct and outsourcing risks are understood and managed.
  • Partner with the wider SumUp and bank leadership teams—including Finance, Global Banking, Product and Engineering—to turn the strategy into a viable, well-governed business.
  • Coach the next generation of SumUp leaders on their path to a §25c Abs 1 KWG qualification.

You'll be great for this role if…

  • You bring 15 - 20+ years of senior leadership experience in credit institutions, including the qualification according to §25c Abs. 1 KWG.
  • You have led commercial, product or customer activity in a regulated bank and can show how you balanced business performance with customer outcomes, conduct requirements and effective controls.

About Wolt

At Wolt, we create technology that brings joy, simplicity and earnings to the neighborhoods of the world. In 2014 we started with delivery of restaurant food. Now we're building the delivery of (almost) everything and you'll find us in over 500 cities in 30 countries around the world. In 2022 we joined forces with DoorDash and together we keep on dreaming big and expanding across the globe.

Working at Wolt isn't always easy, but it's definitely exciting. Here you'll learn more, build more, and ship more than in most other companies. You'll be challenged a lot, but also have a lot of fun on the way. So, if you're a self-starter with drive and entrepreneurial spirit, this could be the ride of your life.

What you'll be doing

As part of Wolt's Platform department (Core Group), you'll help improve and automate operations for our storage access platform - our real time database abstraction layer solution designed with scale and resiliency in mind . The product you will build enforces best practices by design, abstracts database infrastructure, and supports Multi-Region architecture through data sharding and replication. You join a team of highly skilled engineers in designing, building and optimizing this platform and ensuring smooth developer onboarding, constant improvement and optimization. 

As an engineer on the Storage access platform team, you'll work on platform features such as UI for developer teams, storage abstraction layer, database automation, client SDK and proxy, Change Data Capture pipelines, caching and ephemeral storage, Hot & Cold storage management and more.

Our humble expectations

You'll be a great fit for this role if you have the following skills and experience:

  • A strong developer-to-developer mindset, with a genuine enjoyment of building for internal customers and treating other engineers as your primary users.
  • Adaptability and strong motivation for working with distributed systems.
  • A data-driven approach to decision-making and a collaborative mindset, with the ability to navigate disagreements constructively and deliver consistently.
  • Autonomy in dynamic, fast-paced environments with frequent change.
  • A product- and platform-oriented approach to engineering challenges.
  • Excellent communication skills, with the ability to engage effectively with stakeholders and cross-functional teams.
  • A collaborative spirit and experience contributing to diverse and inclusive work environments.

Technical proficiencies:

  • Expertise in NoSQL databases, particularly Cassandra or DynamoDB.
  • Experience with large-scale distributed systems, emphasizing both velocity and scalability.
  • Familiarity with SRE principles; however, a background in Backend Development is essential.
  • Practical knowledge of Kubernetes, including EKS, as an end user.

You don't need to tick every box, but if you see yourself in many of these points, we'd love to hear from you!


What we offer

At Wolt, we're committed to building an environment where engineers can make an impact while enjoying meaningful challenges. As a member of the the team you'll enjoy:

  • Working on solutions that support millions of users
  • Solving complex problems in performance, reliability and automation
  • A collaborative and inclusive culture that supports your professional and personal well-being

We also offer flexible work arrangements, competitive compensation, and ongoing learning opportunities to help you thrive.

 

Our Commitment to Diversity and Inclusion

We're committed to growing and empowering a more inclusive community within our company, industry, and cities. Few people get to build a bank from scratch. Even fewer get to build one at a moment when banking itself is being reinvented.


The Dollar is the best product in the history of the world - there is infinite global demand. But international fintechs and banks are left with two unsatisfying options to choose from: Either build on legacy correspondent banks that are slow and unreliable, or interface with middleware providers that neither move nor hold the dollars directly, but instead rely on underlying legacy banks themselves. At Augustus, we collapse the stack by combining two things: A real, national bank charter (in organization), and Marble, our proprietary core banking system, built around intelligence, made of code.


We are a group of ex-founders, founding employees of unicorns, and people who dropped out of university because they believe this is an industry and career defining opportunity. We are backed with more than $200M from Peter Thiel's Valar Ventures, Tiger Global, Hummingbird, QED, Creandum, and the founders of Nubank, Ramp, Deel, Circle, Fluidstack, Fuse, and Etched.


We are regulated in Europe and live with Euro and Stablecoin clearing today. Now, we are building the US team from the ground up, while continuing to grow rapidly in Europe.

The Role

You generate pipeline for our account executives (AEs) in the markets where dollar access is hardest. Most of it happens in person, at conferences and the events around them. In between, you find the next targets and make sure every lead lands with the right AE.

You also own the numbers behind the top of the funnel and use them to recommend where the team spends its time next, including which new markets are worth testing. You'll help shape how we run Growth, with real autonomy and a scope that grows with what you show.

Your First Six Months

  • Months 1-2: Learn the product, our ICP and how we sell to banks and fintechs. Shadow our sales conversations, and get to know our stack, our playbooks and the way we operate. Go to your first conference with the team: help with pre-booking, work the floor alongside our Sales and Growth teams, and book your first meetings. By the end of month two, you can pitch Augustus on your own.

  • Months 3-4: Execution is yours. Own a conference end to end, from the target list to the follow-up: book the meetings, route each one to the right AE and make sure it happens. Take meetings on your own and work closely with Sales and Marketing.

  • Months 5-6: Own the pipeline for a set of markets and run your first event. You've turned what you've learned into data: which conferences, intros and markets bring deals that close, and which don't. You sync with the rest of GTM to bring in what they see and use it to shape our market strategy: where we go next, how we go in, who we target first and what we lead with.

Who Will Thrive At Augustus

We believe that throwing smart people with high agency at big problems produces the best outcomes. We’re building a modern correspondent bank, and we win by having a better team. The people who succeed here share the following traits:

  • American Dream: You’d rather shoot for gold than settle for mediocrity. You pick the harder goal and stay optimistic when the odds are against you. If it feels easy, we aimed too low.

  • Live Player: You don’t need permission. You rebuild what’s broken without being asked, challenge how things are done, and move before the perfect moment.

  • Ever to Excel: You can’t accept good enough and you take your work personally. When it matters, you do what it takes and keep raising the bar for yourself and your team.

  • Genuine: You play for the company, not your title or turf. Low ego, low drama, no politics. You say it straight, also upwards and always assume good intent.

This role is for you if:

  • You're outgoing and at your best in front of people. You can start a conversation with a stranger at a booth and hold it with a bank's CFO.

  • You do what needs to be done, even when it's not glamorous: building a prospecting list, chasing a follow-up, carrying boxes to the booth.

  • You think clearly and work from data. You take an unstructured dataset and come back with answers and insights.

  • You're diligent and organised. Nothing falls through the cracks.

  • You use AI to move fast, but don't trust the output blindly. You check results, question the systems and don't ship anything you wouldn't put your name on.

  • You're curious: when something takes too long, you find a faster way to do it.

  • After every conference, you know what you'd do differently next time, and you do it.

This is not for you if:

  • You'd rather work behind a screen than in front of people. Most of our pipeline starts with a conversation in person.

  • You want a well-defined scope and clear processes. Ours change as we grow, and you'll help build many of them.

  • You want a predictable week. Plans change, the bar is high and the hours are long.

  • You expect your degree to count for more than your results.

Hard Requirements

  • You are currently pursuing or have obtained, in the last two years, a Bachelor's or Master's degree from a stellar institution.

  • You have 1-2 previous internships or roles in high-growth startups, venture capital, private equity, consulting or investment banking, and/or you have demonstrated initiative through side projects, student organizations or entrepreneurial experiences.

  • Fluent English. Spanish is a strong plus.

  • You can travel regularly, often at short notice.

  • Based in Berlin or willing to relocate.

Pay transparency

Compensation packages at Augustus include base salary, equity, and benefits. New hire offers are made based on a candidate's experience, expertise and geographic location. The annual base salary range for this role is €60,000-€80,000 + equity and benefits.

What We Offer

  • Career Growth: You will be given more responsibility and pushed to grow faster than ever before.

  • Network: Your peers are brilliant, highly motivated people. These people will be foundational in your future opportunities.

  • Real Participation: Employees are shareholders. You will think and act like an owner.

  • Perks & Benefits: Relocation support, visa support, the latest Apple gear (MacBook + AirPods), lunch benefit, gym benefit, a beautiful office in the heart of the city, 4x on-/offsites per year, and an annual development budget.
